title: DHS starts deportation flights after end to remaining protections for TPS holders - The Hill
description:
Beyond Haiti and Syria, TPS holders from Venezuela, Nicaragua, Honduras, Afghanistan, Cameroon, Nepal, South Sudan, Burma, Ethiopia, Yemen and Somalia can now be deported.
Many TPS holders are now being pressured to return to countries where the State Department has actively highlighted the dangers on the ground.
Also frightening for TPS holders is they have little control over where they may be deported.
While some might be returned to their home countries, TPS holders could be sent to a third country if their home nation doesn’t accept flights.
Thursday night’s deportation flight, while not the first to Haiti, represents the beginning of an expected uptick in such removals, particularly for TPS holders.
text:
Lower court judges have now fully lifted certain limitations on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in the wake of a Supreme Court decision that cleared the end of temporary protected status (TPS), removing any final roadblock to deportations.

A federal judge earlier this week lifted the final stay that barred immigration officials from carrying out deportations to Ethiopia. That was the last of various court cases by TPS recipients challenging the termination of their protections.

Immigration officials are now free to deport nationals from 13 countries that prior administrations determined were not sufficiently stable because of natural disaster or civil unrest to safely return migrants.

The additional four countries that still retain their TPS designation are set to expire shortly, meaning more than 1.3 million protectees either have or are likely to soon lose their legal status.

“Effectively, this signals the end of the program,” Nayna Gupta, policy director at the American Immigration Council, told The Hill.

“This an unprecedented delegalization campaign. It’s the largest effort to strip people of lawful status in U.S. history.”

The Supreme Court in its June ruling didn’t end the TPS program but determined the courts did not have the power to review the administration’s decision to end protections for citizens of Haiti and Syria — two countries marred by violence.

While that left very narrow grounds to continue litigation, the ruling has real-life impact now.

Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, a nonprofit advocacy group that also provides legal services to TPS holders, shared the story of one Haitian woman who fled to the U.S. at age 19.

“For the first time when she got to the United States, she woke up and was not worried about being kidnapped by armed groups in Haiti. For the first time, she wasn’t worried about seeing a dead body on the street of where she lived. For the first time, she went to bed not hearing gunshots,” Jozef said.

“After the termination of TPS, when she saw an ICE car for the first time she felt so unsafe again, fearful that she would be taken by ICE, so the same fear that she had about being kidnapped by armed groups in Haiti came back in the form of being kidnapped by ICE,” she said, using an abbreviation for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Beyond Haiti and Syria, TPS holders from Venezuela, Nicaragua, Honduras, Afghanistan, Cameroon, Nepal, South Sudan, Burma, Ethiopia, Yemen and Somalia can now be deported.

Lower courts had blocked DHS from carrying out deportations, but those rulings had to be reexamined in the wake of the high court’s ruling, even though many judges had initially sided with TPS holders in temporarily blocking deportations.

James Percival, the top attorney at DHS, celebrated when the final stay was lifted by a lower court judge based in Massachusetts.

“Judge Brian Murphy just lifted the stay of Ethiopia TPS termination. All TPS terminations are in effect!” he wrote Tuesday on the social platform X, sharing a graphic modeled after one used by Facebook that allows users to mark themselves as safe after an event, with the attorney writing he was now safe “from TPS judges today.”

Haitians are among the largest groups of TPS holders, with nearly 350,000 protected under the status prior to the Supreme Court ruling.

Many are now contemplating what to do next as their once-legal status evaporates.

“It’s been an incredibly difficult, painful time,” said Jozef, who added that it comes after “a difficult day, week, month, and year.”

On Thursday night, the Trump administration conducted its first deportation flight to Haiti since the end of TPS, a plane Jozef said carried roughly 170 people, including one of her clients.

Many TPS holders are now being pressured to return to countries where the State Department has actively highlighted the dangers on the ground.

That’s particularly true for Haiti and Syria.

The Caribbean nation has been dominated by gang violence in the wake of an assassination of their prime minister in 2021 that has left the country with a transitional government.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.) visited Haiti earlier this summer as part of a congressional delegation, describing the country as having areas “like Afghanistan” — where he was deployed while in the military — and adding “it is probably the poorest place I’ve ever been through in my life.”

In Syria, warring factions are still feuding across the country after ousting leader Bashar Assad, who deployed chemical weapons against his own people.

The State Department has rated each a “Level 4 Do Not Travel” country.

The Haiti deportation flight carried out Thursday night landed in the northern coastal city of Cap-Haitien, as the U.S. bars commercial flights into Port-au-Prince — where gang members who largely control the capital city routinely fire at landing planes.

Jozef noted a high-ranking military leader, charged with protecting the public, was ironically kidnapped earlier this summer by gangs.

“If the department that is in charge of protecting the people, they themselves have been kidnapped, how will they be able to protect people being deported to Haiti right now?” she asked.

“Even the Department of Defense is unable to defend themselves against the armed groups in Haiti right now.”

Many judges made it clear the Supreme Court had tied their hands after they issued rulings backing TPS holders on a number of grounds, including that the Trump administration had acted with racial animus in terminating the protections.

Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs wrote an emotional order last week lifting her earlier block on deporting citizens of Somalia.

“Plaintiffs have made a convincing showing that they will suffer irreparable harm if the injunction is withheld … and the balance of hardships and the public interest also favor Plaintiffs, given that the government has made no showing that maintaining TPS status for the duration of this litigation would impose an undue burden,” she wrote.

Also frightening for TPS holders is they have little control over where they may be deported. While some might be returned to their home countries, TPS holders could be sent to a third country if their home nation doesn’t accept flights. Eswatini and Liberia are among those that have agreed to accept deportees.

Jozef noted that many times, those sent to third countries are often placed in “confinement” in a prisonlike setting.

“The deportations are costing U.S. taxpayers money — it is not free,” she said, noting that the U.S. has agreed to pay other countries millions to accept deportees.

And though not a TPS holder, one deportee sent to Haiti was from the Dominican Republic, according to The Associated Press.

Thursday night’s deportation flight, while not the first to Haiti, represents the beginning of an expected uptick in such removals, particularly for TPS holders.

Gupta noted that plan is not without challenges in countries like Haiti, “where conditions are so horrific on the ground that it’s difficult for airplanes to land in the country,” meaning the Trump administration “is likely facing greater logistical barriers on that front.”

Jozef noted that many TPS holders, particularly from countries that have been more recently designated, have few options for attaining some other form of legal status. Many do not have U.S. citizen children who have reached age 21, where they would be able to sponsor them to adjust their status.

“There are a lot of people who have applied for asylum. Unfortunately, 90 percent of those cases have been denied,” she said.

Gupta and other immigration advocates have for years advocated for TPS holders to be able to obtain a permanent path to citizenship, but like many immigration efforts in Congress, those pushes have stalled.

“While it is absolutely shocking because it violates American norms,” she said of the TPS deportations, “it’s unsurprising in that we knew this was always a risk, and that these were folks who are always vulnerable, given their liminal status, which inherently means not having a permanent place here in the United States.”

title: Washtenaw County may continue 'sanctuary policies,' federal judge rules - The Detroit News
description:
The ruling, issued Friday by Judge F. Kay Behm of U.S. District Court in Flint, allows Washtenaw County to continue its so-called sanctuary policies, including banning federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from county property.
The county board of commissioners' policy barring federal immigration officers from county property without a judicial warrant or court order.
In the suit against Washtenaw County, filed in April, the White House argued that federal law preempts state or local restrictions on cooperation with immigration enforcement.
It alleged that county policies conflict with federal immigration law and are therefore invalid, and also that those policies improperly interfere with or discriminate against the federal government in violation of the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause.
Cases in Illinois, California, New York, Colorado and Minnesota have been dismissed, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, which compiles all Trump immigration policy.
text:
A federal judge has handed a Michigan county a key win against President Donald Trump, ruling that the federal government cannot force it to participate in immigration enforcement activities.

The ruling, issued Friday by Judge F. Kay Behm of U.S. District Court in Flint, allows Washtenaw County to continue its so-called sanctuary policies, including banning federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from county property.

"This is one of a series of lawsuits in which the President of the United States has sought to compel states and localities to do the work and bear the cost of enforcing his preferred immigration agenda ..." Behm wrote in her 86-page ruling. "... But neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will."

The United States’ Complaint fails to allege that Washtenaw County has done anything more than exercise its constitutional authority under the Tenth Amendment, Behm, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote.

Trump has made immigration enforcement a cornerstone of his second term, vowing to target and deport violent criminals.

Washtenaw County Sheriff Alyshia Dyer said in a statement on Friday that as sheriff, her role is to protect the people of the community, not to advance Trump’s political agenda.

"Our community stands in solidarity with immigrants and supports the civil and constitutional rights of all people regardless of immigration status," Dyer said in a statement. "The current climate demands bold, courageous leadership to defend our constitutional freedoms. I will not be intimidated by Donald Trump and my office will continue to prioritize providing just, compassionate public safety for our local community as local public servants.”

The lawsuit centered around several Washtenaw County policies deemed by the Trump's administration as "sanctuary policies":

The prosecutor's policy of considering consequences related to suspects' immigration status when making decisions involving charges or pleas.

The sheriff's policy of not asking individuals about their immigration status in the course of their duties, or detaining individuals solely due to ICE-issued detainers or warrants not ordered by a judge.

The county board of commissioners' policy barring federal immigration officers from county property without a judicial warrant or court order.

The Trump administration asserted that Washtenaw County's policies "aim to obstruct federal law enforcement and celebrate thwarting the constitutional obligation of the President of the United States to take care that federal immigration law be faithfully executed."

In the suit against Washtenaw County, filed in April, the White House argued that federal law preempts state or local restrictions on cooperation with immigration enforcement. By "shielding criminal offenders from apprehension," the county officials "jeopardize the public safety of all Americans," the federal government said in its complaint.

However, Behm wrote that the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) "contemplates the possibility of state and local cooperation with federal immigration officials, but it generally does not require cooperation with any particular federal request."

The U.S. Department of Justice didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The federal government had also argued the Washtenaw County's Sheriff's Office's stated policy of not using its “resources to enforce federal immigration law or assist in immigration related matters" amounted to discrimination.

Behm, however, concluded that by not identifying another entity that the county treated more favorably, the White House failed to prove discrimination.

The lawsuit was filed against Dyer, County Prosecutor Eli Savit and the board of commissioners. It alleged that county policies conflict with federal immigration law and are therefore invalid, and also that those policies improperly interfere with or discriminate against the federal government in violation of the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause.

Behm dismissed the full case.

Soon after beginning his second term, Trump signed an executive order taking aim at what he called "sanctuary jurisdictions," threatening to pull federal funding from those areas that interfere with federal enforcement operations and ordering the attorney general and secretary of Homeland Security to take legal action against them.

The White House has filed at least 14 lawsuits similar to the Washtenaw litigation against states and municipalities across the country. Cases in Illinois, California, New York, Colorado and Minnesota have been dismissed, according to the Immigration Policy Tracking Project, which compiles all Trump immigration policy.

In some cases, the Trump administration has appealed. Other cases remain pending.

text:
The US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction Tuesday barring the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from conducting immigration enforcement actions at or near Quaker, Sikh and Baptist houses of worship that sued the Trump administration over the policy permitting them.

The Fourth Circuit’s opinion recounts sworn declarations describing how congregations have changed how they worship since DHS lifted the enforcement limits. Roni Kingsley, clerk of the Richmond Friends Meeting, one of six Quaker organizations that sued, said in a declaration that a member “expressed concern that he could be mistaken for being undocumented and feared the idea of enforcement actions in or around the meeting.” At Oakland Baptist Church, affiliated with the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship (CBF), Rev. Dr. Jeff Hayes said immigrant congregants “are now afraid to come to our sacred space…since DHS’s policy means they might be targeted.” Another CBF congregation reported a 66 percent drop in attendance at its English-as-a-second-language classes.

In Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of the Religious Society of Friends v. US Department of Homeland Security, No. 25-1512, a unanimous three-judge panel held that the documented attendance declines were a “predictable effect” of the 2025 policy sufficient to establish standing, and that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the policy violates the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). Senior Judge Barbara Milano Keenan wrote the opinion, joined in full by Judges Pamela Harris and G. Steven Agee, who also concurred separately. The panel found DHS waived any compelling-interest defense by failing to raise it or present evidence below.

DHS rescinded a 2021 policy limiting enforcement near “protected areas,” including churches, schools, and hospitals, in a January 20, 2025 memo signed by then-Acting Secretary Benjamin Huffman, President Trump’s first day back in office. The memo dispensed with “bright line rules” on enforcement locations, instructing agents to rely on their own discretion instead.

Six Quaker organizations, Sikh Temple Sacramento, and CBF sued DHS in the US District Court for the District of Maryland. Judge Theodore Chuang granted a preliminary injunction in February 2025 covering the plaintiffs’ congregations but declined to extend it nationwide. Judge Agee’s concurrence stressed the injunction’s narrow scope, noting DHS may still make arrests at the plaintiffs’ properties with a warrant, in hot pursuit, or during genuine emergencies.

The plaintiffs said in a joint statement that the ruling “reaffirms a fundamental promise of religious liberty” and that they would keep litigating “to ensure that religious freedom remains meaningful for every congregation.” DHS’s original statement announcing the policy said “criminals will no longer be able to hide in America’s schools and churches to avoid arrest” and that the administration trusted agents “to use common sense,” language a DHS spokesperson repeated to Government Executive when asked about Tuesday’s ruling.

A federal judge on Friday dismissed a lawsuit the Trump administration filed against Washtenaw County over its immigration enforcement policies, ruling that the county’s sheriff, prosecutor and Board of Commissioners had not violated federal law.

text:
A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump administration that accused Washtenaw County officials of obstructing federal immigration enforcement operations.

The lawsuit filed on April 9 against Washtenaw County Sheriff Alyshia M. Dyer, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, and the Washtenaw County Board of Commissioners challenged a resolution that restricted federal agents from entering county-owned buildings. Federal officials sought to have the resolution declared invalid.

However, Judge F. Kay Behm wrote on Friday that federal officials failed "to allege that Washtenaw County has done anything more than exercise its constitutional authority under the Tenth Amendment."

"The Constitution imparts much authority on the federal government. But neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will ... nothing in the text of the INA (Immigration and Nationality Act) requires the result the government seeks, and the government cannot otherwise compel localities to enforce the President's priorities in the manner it wishes," Behm wrote.

CBS News Detroit reached out to the Justice Department on Friday night and is awaiting a response.

Behm's decision came more than two months after county officials filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit in June.

At the time the lawsuit was filed, federal officials claimed the county had "taken steps to shield illegal aliens from the reach of federal enforcement" by prohibiting county employees from sharing immigration information with federal immigration authorities, along with barring federal immigration law enforcement from Washtenaw County properties.

Dyer issued the following statement on Friday:

"As Sheriff, my role is to protect the people of our community, not to advance Trump's political agenda. Our community stands in solidarity with immigrants and supports the civil and constitutional rights of all people regardless of immigration status. The current climate demands bold, courageous leadership to defend our constitutional freedoms. I will not be intimidated by Donald Trump and my office will continue to prioritize providing just, compassionate public safety for our local community as local public servants."

The bill honors Dalilah Coleman, a first-grader who was critically injured when an illegal immigrant driving a big rig caused a multi-car pileup on an Indiana highway. Partap Singh, an Indian national licensed in California, was driving the truck. Coleman suffered catastrophic injuries, spent months in the hospital and had a craniectomy.

Immigration attorneys argued Banks’ bill would make the U.S. "far less attractive as a study destination" and encourage foreign talent to look to Canada instead.

"Many employers would be unable or unwilling to meet this threshold, effectively limiting H-1B hiring to top tech companies or highly specialized roles," Texas firm Reddy Neumann & Brown said on its website.

AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN

text:
TRENTON, N.J. — New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport is co-leading a multistate lawsuit challenging immigration-enforcement conditions imposed by the Trump administration on federal grants used to support law enforcement and public safety programs.

Davenport joined a coalition of 22 attorneys general and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in filing an updated and amended lawsuit challenging conditions the U.S. Department of Justice has placed on congressionally authorized grants.

“This is an outrageous maneuver that uses our dedicated law enforcement personnel as pawns in a political game,” said Attorney General Davenport. “This administration is holding up funding that helps pay for protective equipment for law enforcement, fight drug trafficking, enforce Megan’s Law, and find violent criminals. We will not let this administration attach illegal conditions to essential federal funding – funding that New Jerseyans send to Washington, D.C., through our tax dollars.”

According to the New Jersey Attorney General’s Office, the Trump administration last year declared that states would be unable to access Victims of Crime Act funds unless they agreed to immigration-related conditions. A multistate coalition successfully challenged those conditions, resulting in their removal from more than $1.3 billion in VOCA funding.

The Attorney General’s Office said the U.S. Department of Justice this year applied similar conditions to new grants, including funding for law enforcement and juvenile justice programs.

Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant Program, commonly known as Byrne JAG. The program provides federal criminal justice funding to state and local governments.

New Jersey law enforcement agencies received more than $21 million in Byrne JAG funding through the state from fiscal years 2019 through 2024, according to the Attorney General’s Office. The challenged conditions also affect funding for crisis intervention and youth justice programs.

The coalition argues that civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and that the administration’s attempt to condition the grants on state participation in immigration enforcement violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

The attorneys general are asking the court to declare the conditions unlawful and permanently block their implementation or enforcement.

In addition to Davenport, the lawsuit is being co-led by attorneys general from California, Delaware, Illinois and Rhode Island.

Attorneys general from Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia have also joined the lawsuit, along with Pennsylvania.

title: As Denaturalization Lawsuits Surge, Their Basis Lacks Transparency
description:
This brought the total during the first seven months of 2026 to at least 105 denaturalization suits filed this year.
Seven of these states had not seen any denaturalization suits filed previously in records stretching back to 2008.
California, which had seen numerous denaturalization suits in the past, saw only two (2) new suits filed in July; and both New York and Illinois had none.
Across this entire period, California was second with a total of 26 denaturalization suits filed and Texas was third with 16 denaturalization suits filed.
Civil Denaturalization Complaints Filed by Calendar Year in Federal District Courts Seeking to Revoke the U.S.
text:
Published Aug 21, 2026

Denaturalization remains an ongoing Department of Justice (DoJ) civil enforcement priority. In July 2026 at least 50 denaturalization complaints were filed in that single month, an all-time high. This brought the total during the first seven months of 2026 to at least 105 denaturalization suits filed this year. Yet despite this surge in denaturalization suits, the government has released very little information about the underlying basis for these suits and current rules prevent public access to almost all of these court filings.

Suits were filed in 23 states during the month of July 2026 alone. Seven of these states had not seen any denaturalization suits filed previously in records stretching back to 2008. The largest number of denaturalization suits identified in July were filed in Florida (9), Texas (7), and Maryland (6). California, which had seen numerous denaturalization suits in the past, saw only two (2) new suits filed in July; and both New York and Illinois had none. Figure 1 displays the states and federal judicial districts which have had denaturalization suits in July.

Thirty-six (36) states plus the District of Columbia saw federal actions in their communities to strip naturalized citizens of their citizenship over this entire period. The largest number of suits have been filed in Florida where a total of 49 have been filed since 2008. Across this entire period, California was second with a total of 26 denaturalization suits filed and Texas was third with 16 denaturalization suits filed. See Table 1 for a state-by-state breakdown for the entire period. Figure 2 shows the dramatic growth in denaturalization filings this year.

Figure 1. Civil Denaturalization Lawsuits Filed in July 2026 by State in Federal District Courts Seeking to Revoke the U.S. Citizenship of Individuals

Figure 2. Civil Denaturalization Complaints Filed by Calendar Year in Federal District Courts Seeking to Revoke the U.S. Citizenship of Individuals, January 2008 to July 31, 2026

True Number of Suits Lacks Transparency

The true number of denaturalization suits may be higher since there is no reliable way to identify every court action. While claiming that it is filing a record number of denaturalization suits, the DoJ is highly selective about which suits it publicizes and which ones it fails to make public. For example, the DoJ issued press releases on July 20, 2026, and August 3, 2026, purporting to describe each denaturalization suit it recently filed. However, for all of July, these press releases listed just 29 denaturalization suits when it appears at least 50 were actually filed for that month. Clearly, the DoJ cannot be relied upon to publish a comprehensive list.

While federal courts are usually assumed to make court records readily accessible to ensure citizens and the press can monitor the integrity of the federal judicial system, the U.S. courts in fact severely restrict public access to court actions seeking to strip individuals of their citizenship. Unlike most court records which are available online, denaturalization complaints setting forth the government’s allegations fall under special provisions that block public access allegedly to protect personal privacy.

Assuring public access to the denaturalization complaints is clearly vital. A court filed complaint is largely the sole means of systematically monitoring these actions. It is clearly preposterous to block public access to this information on privacy grounds while at the same time the DoJ is publicizing the names and alleged violations of these same individuals in its press releases. Without access to the complaint, the public has little means to check that a press release fairly and fully describes the rationale for the government’s action.

Further, without access to the complaints, it is difficult even to identify denaturalization suits when they are filed. While the federal courts online system called PACER tags each civil filing by a “nature of suit” code, these are not always reliably assigned and there is no nature of suit code that specifically identifies denaturalization suits.

The methodology TRAC used to compile its list of denaturalization cases filed since 2008 is described in Appendix A in its June 17, 2026, report. Through these painstaking efforts reviewing federal court dockets, TRAC identified 21 additional denaturalization cases filed during July 2026 beyond the 29 listed in the DoJ’s press releases. See Appendix.

However, there is no assurance that this is the complete set of denaturalization cases. Indeed, at least one of the cases identified in DoJ’s latest press release could not be located through a PACER search as of the date of this report. Further, when the person’s identity is not released, the available court docket information is limited and therefore may be insufficient to pinpoint a denaturalization filing.

Denaturalization Grounds Lack Transparency

Because of these access barriers, only two of the 50 complaints filed in July were available through a search of court records. As a result, the public is largely left in the dark on the grounds the government used and the reasons why it chose these individuals to pursue denaturalization.

DoJ’s press releases for denaturalization complaints filed during July 2026 cited alleged convictions for significant unlawful acts prior to naturalizing and/or falsely representing their identity to obtain naturalization in the first instance. Most denaturalization complaints featured in these press releases, however, were premised on unlawful conduct versus false identity.

Unlike the earlier denaturalization cases shared in TRAC’s initial report, sexual abuse of a minor or similar conduct was the largest single underlying basis for denaturalization complaints filed in July 2026. Given that the DoJ was highly selective in which lawsuits were publicized, it is impossible to say whether sexual abuse cases were cited because it chose to feature lawsuits based on these grounds or this was generally true for denaturalization lawsuits that the administration filed during July 2026.

Extraordinary Efforts Required to Obtain Denaturalization Complaints Directly from Courts Yielding Divergent Responses

After publishing its first report on denaturalization suits, TRAC launched a project to obtain copies of unavailable denaturalization complaints directly from the federal judicial district where they were filed. A series of letters listing the cases in which complaints were sought were written and emailed to the court clerk in each of 37 separate federal judicial districts. The courts’ responses to TRAC’s requests, including the process required, varied widely from one court to the next.

In total, these letters sought copies of 142 denaturalization complaints. These covered all complaints which TRAC had been unable to obtain covering the period January 2008 through June 14, 2026, discussed in TRAC’s June 17, 2026, report. This effort is still ongoing as some courts have not yet provided copies of the complaint or advised that they wouldn’t be able to send them.

For forty (40) of the requested complaints, the court responded that they could not furnish us copies. The reasons given were as follows:

For nineteen out of these forty, TRAC was advised that someone would have to travel to the court and obtain copies by using public terminals at the courthouse.

For an additional four of these requested denaturalization complaints, TRAC was advised that these could only be viewed on public terminals at the courthouse, but that copies were not permitted, just viewing.

For nine further complaints, the court advised that copies could only be obtained either by a motion to the court or from the parties themselves.

For the remaining eight of these requested denaturalization complaints, TRAC was advised that the complaints were unavailable altogether.

As of the date of this report, TRAC successfully obtained forty-three (44) of the requested denaturalization complaints without traveling to the courthouse. It is disappointing that just 44 out of the 142 complaints sought, just 31% have been provided.

As of the date of this report, a total of $1,496.00 was paid for copies of these 44 complaints, or an average of $34 per case. Most charged a copying fee of $0.50 per page and the payment had to be received by the court before copies were released. Only six charged the standard PACER rate of $0.10 per page. One court did offer a free courtesy copy, however, future requests for docket sheets, transcripts, or other documents require prepayment of copy expense at $0.50 per page. None of the other courts offered to waive or cap the fee even though PACER has provisions for doing this for electronic access. For those denaturalization complaints that were often very lengthy, fees were as high as $719.00 from one court for copies of multiple complaints. This can be a considerable financial cost barrier limiting public access to these records. Apart from copying fees, occasionally other charges were imposed. These included electronic retrieval charges, additional search fees, and certified copy fees from a several of the courts.

Considerable delays were inevitably involved before complaints were received. Only five courts allowed electronic payment, so checks had to be physically sent and received by the court before complaints were provided. And only five courts were willing to provide digital copies, the rest only made paper copies. Often considerable back and forth communications has had to be exchanged with the court clerk.

This cost assessment omits both the administrative overhead of managing court communications and the technical infrastructure required to sustain this project. Other administrative expenditures include PACER fees, postage, certified check processing fees, office supplies, and staff time.

Considerable time and effort required to communicate with each court. The process of identifying which complaints were within the jurisdiction of each district and then preparing letters to each of these courts was a significant administrative undertaking that would have otherwise been unnecessary in the absence of current public records access policies.

Conclusion

In July 2026 the increase in denaturalization complaints filed continued unabated and reached what appears to be an all-time high. At the same time, the government provided even less transparency as to the underlying bases for these suits. The establishment of denaturalization as a civil enforcement priority now includes robust administrative processes and infrastructure to support an expansive system for civil denaturalization proceedings for which the government provides little publicly accessible information. This lack of transparency should concern all citizens.

Continued empirical monitoring of this administration’s efforts to strip individuals of their citizenship will be increasingly important.

Appendix: Methodology Using Court Docket Information and Nature of Suit Codes

Federal civil lawsuits are organized in PACER according to nature of suit codes. Nature of suit codes are assigned based on the checkbox the person filing the complaint marks on the civil cover sheet. For this updated report, these three nature of suit codes were again used:

462: Naturalization Application

465: Other Immigration Action

890: Other Statutory Actions

TRAC examined every case listed under each of these three codes and reviewed the PACER Docket Report screen to determine whether the case was a civil denaturalization proceeding. This over-inclusive review required manual querying and reviewing large numbers of individual federal civil lawsuits in PACER.

In most instances, the Docket Report screen in PACER includes the statutory provision and subsection for the cause of action. For example, for many of the cases reviewed, a reference to “1451(a)” is presented on the Docket Report screen cause of action field. In other instances, however, no statutory reference is provided.

In instances where no statutory reference is provided as the cause of action, many of the cases include language that appears to reference the relevant statutory section. For example, if the language in the cause of action field in the Docket Report screen references “revocation of citizenship,” this is likely a reference to 8 U.S.C. § 1451(a) since that provision contains the word “revocation” in the statutory text. In still other instances where no statutory reference for the cause of action is provided, there is language such as “Motion to Correct Order & Judg. of Naturalization.” This is presumably a reference to 8 U.S.C. § 1451(h) since the word “correct” appears in the statutory text of that subsection.

For the period January 1, 2008 to July 31, 2026, the denaturalization complaint case list now includes a total of 229 identified civil denaturalization cases. Of these 229 cases, 137 or 59.83% of the cases were filed under a cause of action of 8 U.S.C. § 1451(a) and 56 or 24.45% were filed under a cause of action of 8 U.S.C. § 1451(j). These two causes of action together account for 193 or 84.28% of the 229 denaturalization cases reviewed.

For July alone, approximately 19 of the 49 denaturalization cases were filed under 8 U.S.C. § 1451(a) and 9 were filed under 8 U.S.C. § 1451(j). Together, these two causes of action account for 28, or 57.14% of the denaturalization cases reviewed. Notably, this is a much lower percentage than it was for the entire period from 2008 through July.

Over eight out of ten (85.59%) of the 229 denaturalization complaints filed between 2008 and July 31, 2026 reviewed for this updated report were filed under a nature of suit code 465. For those filed during July 2026, all but two were filed under this nature of suit.

Between 2008 and July 31, 2026, 7.86% were categorized under the miscellaneous code 890, while 5.68% were assigned nature of suit code 462. Two suits, or 0.87% of the denaturalization complaints were filed under code 460. Two suits were filed under one of the above nature of suit codes, but were subsequently determined not to be denaturalization complaints upon further review of information contained in the Docket Report screen of PACER.

text:
Last year, Cuban immigrant Yasmany Moreno de Armas was working and living in Florida. He's now in the Central African Republic, after the Trump administration sent him and dozens of deportees to the deeply impoverished and conflict-ridden nation.

The 31-year-old said he only learned the U.S. government was deporting him to Africa after he arrived there in late July, alongside detainees from countries across the globe, including Ecuador, Honduras, Serbia, Russia and Vietnam.

"We cannot leave, we don't have documents and we're suffering and missing our families, in a continent we don't know," Moreno de Armas told CBS News in Spanish over a video call from inside a building in Bangui, the country's capital, where the deportees have been living.

Asked if he had ever heard of the Central African Republic prior to his deportation, he said "never."

The Central African Republic is one of the poorest countries in the world. Armed conflict, political instability and Russian mercenaries have also made it one of the most dangerous. The State Department warns Americans through a Level 4 travel advisory not to visit the country, citing the widespread insecurity there.

The landlocked nation is one of more than 30 countries the U.S. government has convinced to accept third-country deportees arrested as part of President Trump's large-scale crackdown on illegal immigration. The list includes a growing number of African countries, many of which are plagued by armed conflict, repressive governments and human rights abuses.

Eritrea native Zena Gebrgzabher, 39, is also stranded in the Central African Republic after being ejected from the U.S.

"I miss my family," Gebrgzabher told CBS News over a video call.

"My son. He asked like every day to my wife, '(where) is my daddy?'" he added.

Gebrgzabher's wife and their 5-year-old son, both of whom are American citizens, live in Maryland, where he said he worked as a truck driver. Like Moreno de Armas, Gebrgzabher said he was not given any notice of his deportation to the Central African Republic or allowed to challenge it.

Yrgalem Gehrehiwet called her husband's deportation unfair and inhumane. She said their son, Nathan, has been particularly affected by his father's absence, though she has refrained from telling him about Gebrgzabher's predicament.

"More than us because he loves his dad," she told CBS News.

CBS News could not find any criminal record for Moreno de Armas or Gebrgzabher, beyond traffic and immigration violations, like entering the U.S. illegally. But both men's cases do match the description of many of those targeted by the Trump administration for deportation to far-flung "third countries."

For the most part, the Trump administration has sought to use third-country deportation agreements to deport immigrants whose home countries, like Cuba, reject or limit U.S. deportations or who have won legal protections in U.S. immigration courts that shield them from being returned to their homelands due to concerns about their safety.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to questions about the men sent to the Central African Republic and the nature of its agreement with that country, including what it is getting for accepting deportees from the U.S.

Moreno de Armas said he could be in danger in Cuba, since he was once imprisoned there after his first attempt to flee the communist-ruled island. Cuban government documents show he was imprisoned for "illegal exit from the national territory." His second attempt proved successful.

U.S. government documents show he arrived in Florida by boat in September 2016 and was allowed into the U.S. under the "parole" legal authority that Cuban arrivals benefited from under the now-defunct "Wet Foot, Dry Foot" policy. He applied for a green card under the Cold War-era Cuban Adjustment Act, but was denied on the grounds that he filed the application after his parole expired.

Lacking legal status, Moreno de Armas was arrested by immigration officials in May 2025 and spent roughly a year in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody before his deportation to Africa this summer.

Gebrgzabher won his legal case in immigration court in 2017, when an immigration judge found him eligible for protection under the Convention Against Torture and barred his deportation to Eritrea.

Court documents show Gebrgzabher did not get asylum, a more permanent legal status, because he served as a checkpoint guard in the Eritrean military. Even though judges noted he was forcibly conscripted as an 18-year-old, they found him to be ineligible for asylum because of a rule that disqualifies those who may have assisted in the persecution of others. While he said he did not harm or arrest anyone passing through the checkpoint, the judges said he impeded the escape of political prisoners.

The documents indicate Gebrgzabher was imprisoned by the Eritrean military after overstaying his leave, and subsequently fled the country. He then traveled to the U.S.-Mexico border, where he requested asylum at a port of entry.

After being granted protection under the Convention Against Torture, Gebrgzabher said he started a family and checked in with ICE regularly, without incident, until he was arrested during an appointment last year. While his protection barred his deportation to Eritrea, it did not legally prevent officials from sending him to a third country like the Central African Republic.

Both men CBS News spoke to described being effectively stateless, stuck in a foreign nation where they don't speak the language and lack any ties or relatives.

"If you're going to be deported, it should be to your home country, not to another country where you don't know the culture," Moreno de Armas said.

text:
A United States judge has struck down a policy introduced by the administration of President Donald Trump suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.

Judge Jeannette Vargas of Manhattan said in her ruling on Friday in the Southern District of New York that the policy was “patently unlawful” and conflicted with federal immigration law, which explicitly stripped the secretary of state of authority over consular officers’ adjudication of immigrant visas.

Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3Why are some African countries banning US citizens from entry?

list 3 of 3Why are some African-Americans moving to Africa?

end of list

“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.

Vargas, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together, along with applicants for immigrant visas and US citizens sponsoring family members from the designated countries.

The suspension, which took effect in January of this year, affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh; and many nations in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean.

The Department of State said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”.

President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown during his presidency that he argues is aimed at improving domestic security. According to the Center for Constitutional Rights, the freeze was one of several restrictions the administration has imposed in rapid succession, following a broader travel ban covering 39 countries that took effect January 1, and a pause on diversity visa issuance in late December.

Rights groups have suggested that the crackdown violates free speech and due process rights, particularly for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The State Department has not yet commented on the ruling.

text:
New York — In a major victory for families, fairness, and the rule of law, a federal court in New York struck down the Trump administration’s blanket, nationality-based “public charge” ban on immigrant visa processing for people from 75 countries. The court held that the ban exceeds the Secretary of State’s statutory and regulatory authority and violates Section 1152(a)(1)(A) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965’s prohibition on nationality-based discrimination in issuing a visa. In its decision, the court also vacated and set aside any visa denial based solely on the ban and ordered the State Department to restore lawful, case-by-case evaluation of visa applications.

“We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together,” said Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC). “The suspension of lawful visa processing across 75 countries separated spouses, parents, and children who were simply following the legal immigration process. Catholic social teaching calls us to uphold the dignity of every person and recognize the family as the foundation of society. Today’s decision affirms both those values and the rule of law, allowing families to once again move forward toward reunification.”

“This decision is a tremendous victory for the rule of law,” said Diana Konate, Deputy Executive Director for Policy and Advocacy at African Communities Together, an associational plaintiff in the case. “This unlawful and racist ban caused immeasurable harm, cruelly keeping families and loved ones apart. Today, we are elated to tell our community members: this ban is no more.”

“Today’s decision is a significant victory for the hundreds of thousands of families across the country and the world whose lives were thrown into chaos by this administration’s unlawful and discriminatory visa ban,” said Joanna Cuevas Ingram, Senior Staff Attorney at the National Immigration Law Center. “The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination. We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.”

“This is a victory for justice and fairness,” said Susan Welber, Supervising Attorney with the Civil Practice at The Legal Aid Society. “The Administration cannot weaponize the public charge ground of inadmissibility to keep families apart. We call on the State Department to immediately resume consular processing for our individual plaintiffs and all others impacted by this blatant lawlessness.”

“Today’s ruling is a critical rebuke of an unlawful and discriminatory policy that inflicted enormous harm on families and communities across the country,” said Skye Perryman, President and CEO of Democracy Forward. “The Trump-Vance administration cannot weaponize immigration law to blacklist entire countries, separate families, and deny people rights guaranteed by the Constitution without being held accountable. We are honored to represent our clients and grateful that the court took action to protect their rights.”

“Today’s ruling is a significant victory for the families and communities harmed by this policy. After months of separation and uncertainty, our clients can finally move forward, free to pursue the legal immigration pathways this administration unlawfully tried to block,” said Sarah Wilson, Partner & Federal Immigration Litigation Practice Leader at Colombo & Hurd.

“This ruling is a resounding rebuke of a discriminatory policy that tore families apart and treated entire nationalities as unworthy of due process,” said Antionette Dozier, Senior Attorney for Western Center on Law & Poverty. “Congress set out clear, individualized criteria for immigrant visa eligibility—not a blanket ban that drew, in the words of District Judge Hon. Jeannette A. Vargas, ‘pernicious distinctions based upon nationality’. For 75 countries’ worth of families, this decision means a return to fair, case-by-case review, and a chance to be reunited with their loved ones. No administration gets to override the law because it deems an applicant’s nationality unacceptable.”

“This latest attempt by the Trump administration to enforce its white nationalist worldview through U.S. immigration policy is, like the others, equal parts retrograde and unlawful,” said Baher Azmy, Legal Director of The Center for Constitutional Rights. “We are proud to stand by communities that will not stop fighting against the administration’s attempts to project its racist insecurities to tear apart families.”

The National Immigration Law Center, Democracy Forward, The Legal Aid Society, the Western Center on Law & Poverty, the Center for Constitutional Rights, and Colombo & Hurd brought the lawsuit on behalf of Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC); African Communities Together; and individuals whose lives were upended by the ban. The case was filed on February 2 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, and the legal team at Democracy Forward includes Elena Goldstein, Erez Reuveni, and Catherine Carroll.

The lawsuit argued that the U.S. Department of State imposed an unlawful, discriminatory nationality-based barrier to legal immigration that strips families and working people of the process guaranteed by law. The Trump administration baselessly cited “public charge” risk as its stated justification for the ban, after relentlessly and cruelly smearing immigrant communities, particularly communities of color.

The defendants in the lawsuit are U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. Department of State.

text:
United States

N.C.

Letter

An Open Letter

To: Sen. Budd, Sen. Tillis, Rep. Harris

From: A verified voter in Waxhaw , NC

August 22

As your constituent, I urge you to support a comprehensive congressional investigation into the relationship between the Trump administration, the GEO Group, and federal immigration detention contracts. Recent campaign finance disclosures show that GEO Reentry Services, a GEO Group subsidiary, donated $1 million to MAGA Inc. on July 16, three days after GEO announced an $85 million per year, five year contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to operate a 1,188 bed detention center in Hudson, Colorado. GEO donated another $413,000 on July 31, two days after announcing a second five year ICE contract worth $80 million annually to operate a 1,320 bed facility in Winton, North Carolina. There is no publicly established evidence that these donations directly caused the contracts. However, their timing and scale create a serious appearance of potential pay to play influence. Together, the contracts could provide GEO with $165 million annually, or approximately $825 million over five years. GEO Reentry Services has donated more than $4.4 million to MAGA Inc. since the beginning of last year. The need for scrutiny is reinforced by GEO’s reliance on ICE contracts and its sharp increase in profits during the administration’s mass deportation campaign. GEO reported $254.3 million in net income last year, compared with $31.9 million during the final year of the Biden administration. The North Carolina facility, which GEO owns, had been closed since 2021 after the federal government moved away from for profit prison contracts. Congress should investigate the procurement process, including contract evaluations, approvals, communications, and contacts among ICE, the Department of Homeland Security, GEO, MAGA Inc., and administration officials. It should also examine whether the appointment of former GEO official David Venturella as acting head of ICE created a conflict of interest or required recusal. Please request inspector general investigations into procurement integrity, ethics compliance, contractor access, and conditions at GEO operated facilities. Congress should require greater transparency regarding detention costs, inspections, incidents, ownership, and performance. Future contracts should be suspended or terminated when operators fail to meet health, safety, and humane treatment standards. Political donations should never create the appearance that public contracts are awarded in exchange for financial support. Please act promptly to protect taxpayers, detainees, and the integrity of federal contracting.

text:
Yulia Gómez held her infant son during a doctor’s appointment in Alabama as part of his care for health complications he’s faced since birth. Until a month ago, her husband Olinder Calderon was by her side to translate and help her understand their child’s care.

But on this day, Gómez was by herself because Calderon is hundreds of miles away in a Mississippi immigration detention center facing deportation to Guatemala, a country he left nearly 20 years ago.

Calderon plans to ask a judge to cancel removal proceedings against him because of his son and how much of a role he plays in the infant’s medical care. If deported, his wife said she would have to stay so that their American-born son can continue to receive specialized medical care.

“(It) would completely change our lives,” Gómez said in Spanish in a phone interview from the doctor’s office. “I’d have to start our whole life over, and I think we’d even end up separating because you can’t put love above our baby’s well-being and health.”

The 27-year-old has been especially worried because Calderon was the family’s main source of income and transportation to the baby’s appointments, some hours away.

Since he’s been away, Gómez said she has used their small savings to continue their son’s medical care. She is looking for support from organizations and searching for a pro bono immigration attorney because money is limited.

Calderon’s immigration case took a step forward Wednesday with a virtual preliminary hearing with Immigration Judge Larry Downend from the LaSalle Immigration Court in Jena, Louisiana.

That morning, Gómez logged on through a link provided by the federal government to watch the hearing, but she spent hours in a virtual waiting room unable to see anything before she was kicked off.

Later that day, she talked with her husband who told her the hearing was brief. Downend, who was appointed to the court in June, asked if Calderon had an attorney and if he needed more time to get one, Gómez said. The judge also asked about the possibility of voluntary self-deportation, but she said Calderon does not plan to do that because of their son.

His next hearing date is set for Sept. 1. At that hearing or a future one on his case’s merits, Calderon will have the chance to argue why he should stay in the country.

As Calderon’s case makes its way through immigration court, Gómez said she has been in contact with the office of Alabama U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, who has offered help to look into Calderon’s case, including reaching out to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

A spokesperson for Rogers, a Republican who chairs the House Armed Services Committee, was not immediately available for comment Friday.

Calderon, 37, came to the U.S. through a work visa and he stayed after it expired. He has worked as a painter and joined a Latino Christian church, where he became a member of the worship team, played bass guitar and sang in the church band. A friend introduced him to Gómez, and the couple married three years ago. Their son Oliver David was born in Georgia, near the Alabama border, in November.

Gómez said she doesn’t have a driver’s license and can’t leave her son with others because of his special care needs. She stopped working during her high-risk pregnancy.

Oliver developed bacterial meningitis after he was born, and the infection resulted in problems with his swallowing and coordination with his breathing. Gómez said eating poses a choking risk for him. The infant receives therapy at a Birmingham, Alabama, hospital and has appointments at a children’s clinic in Auburn, Alabama.

Because Gómez and Calderon don’t have family in the U.S., people from church and the community have stepped in to help her get to doctor’s appointments and buy milk and supplies for Oliver.

In a letter shared with Mississippi Today, Oliver’s pediatrician wrote that Calderon’s absence would have a physical, mental and emotional impact on the infant. The first week Calderon was gone, Gómez said their son had trouble sleeping because the baby was used to sleeping with his father.

On July 19, Calderon was driving home from church when a police officer in Jackson’s Gap, Alabama, pulled him over. The officer found Calderon had a suspended license due to an outstanding ticket from another state, Gómez said. Then the officer asked Calderson if he was a citizen. He told the truth: No, I don’t have papers.

Police put cuffs on his hands and legs and put him into the back of a cruiser, which Gómez said she saw through a video call from friends who met Calderon at the scene.

“What impacted me the most was seeing my husband … accused like a person who committed a crime,” she said, adding that he does not have a criminal record.

Coordination between local and state law enforcement and ICE is possible especially through the 287(g) program. Participation has exploded during the Trump administration. Jackon’s Gap’s agreement with ICE gives the force some authority to enforce federal immigration laws during routine policing, according to ICE records.

Similar 287(g)agreements have also been signed in Mississippi, and more departments and state agencies are expected to ink them because a new state law requires all counties with a jail to have one. As of August, 25 of the state’s 82 counties have signed them, as well over 20 police departments, five state agencies and a county constable’s office.

The Trump immigration crackdown has led to increased immigration arrests and restricted eligibility for bond hearings. At one point, anyone who entered the country illegally at any point in time could not receive bond to leave detention and await court proceedings from home, leading to indefinite detention. In July, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that those arrested are entitled to a bond hearing within 90 days of detention.

Calderon had a bond hearing and provided written support from his church. The pastors highlighted his service and devotion to the church, his family and the community.

If released on bond, they said the church would continue to support Calderon and his family. The pastors said he earned their trust over the years and they are confident he would attend future immigration hearings, according to the letter shared with Mississippi Today.

Downend denied the request July 30, saying Calderon failed to meet the burden to show he wasn’t a flight risk, according to documents reviewed by Mississippi Today.

Calderon was moved from one immigration center to another, and Gómez was not able to talk to him. She said she tracked his movement through an app until he ended up in the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi.

She talks to him daily, and through a tablet. Calderon can have video calls where he can see their son.

Since coming to the Natchez facility, Calderon has had a fever and sore throat, making it difficult for him to speak, Gómez said. She worries he has been receiving inadequate medical attention because he has asked a nurse to treat him, but Calderon said he hasn’t received treatment. Others at the immigration detention center are sick, too, he told her.

“What I want people to take from this story is that Olinder, my husband, is not a criminal. He’s a father, a hard worker, a man who for years has served the church and been part of the community. His criminal record is clean,” Gómez said.

“I want people to understand that behind an immigration detention there are human beings — families.”

Claudia Amendoeira and Sarah Whites-Koditschek contributed reporting
