title: In LA immigration courts, Indigenous migrants face deportation because they don't have interpreters
description:
In federal immigration courts across Los Angeles, Indigenous migrants who speak Mixtec, K’iche’ or many of the dozens of Indigenous languages spoken in LA County don’t receive translation services they need and are legally entitled to, advocates tell LA Public Press.
Across the 72 U.S. immigration courts, non-citizens in court proceedings are guaranteed due process under the Constitution.
López Resendiz told LA Public Press the immigration court system operates under a harmful assumption that all Latin American immigrants speak Spanish.
Hundreds of Indigenous languages are spoken across the Americas, including 364 in Mexico alone.
Concerns about language access for Indigenous migrants emerge as immigration courts struggle to clear a 3.2 million case backlog.
text:
In federal immigration courts across Los Angeles, Indigenous migrants who speak Mixtec, K’iche’ or many of the dozens of Indigenous languages spoken in LA County don’t receive translation services they need and are legally entitled to, advocates tell LA Public Press.

Attorneys and organizers said by not providing translation services, the federal government is unfairly punishing people who might not understand their immigration hearings.

Across the 72 U.S. immigration courts, non-citizens in court proceedings are guaranteed due process under the Constitution. That means immigrants have the right to defend themselves in court proceedings by requesting government-provided interpretation in their preferred language.

With nearly 26 million people living in the U.S. with limited English proficiency, according to a 2025 federal report, timely access to interpreters can determine whether some remains in ICE custody indefinitely or accepts a deportation order without understanding its legal consequences.

Indigenous migrants from Mexico and Central America aren’t receiving interpretation of court hearings in their preferred languages, according to Luis López Resendiz, director of operations for the Indigenous-led, LA-based organization Comunidades Indígenas en Liderazgo, or CIELO.

López Resendiz told LA Public Press the immigration court system operates under a harmful assumption that all Latin American immigrants speak Spanish.

“A lot of these immigrants are Indigenous, and language rights are not being respected in any setting,” López Resendiz said. “This administration does not prioritize [Indigenous] languages, so it’s hard for us to see who is being detained and who is requesting an interpreter. People are falling through the cracks.”

CIELO has observed cases of Indigenous migrants who were deported without being provided an interpreter, according to López Resendiz.

“[T]hey perhaps didn’t know why they were being deported or being detained,” López Resendiz said.

Inadequate immigration court interpretation can lead to wrongful deportation

LA County is home to a vibrant tapestry of Indigenous communities from across Latin America who live and work in places like the “Oaxacan Corridor” in the Pico-Union neighborhood or “Little Guatemala” in Westlake.

Indigenous people have been swept up in ICE operations in LA. At a June 6, 2025 ICE raid at a clothing supply warehouse, 14 Zapotec workers were detained.

A 2024 report by CIELO found that LA County is home to at least 24 distinct Indigenous migrant communities from Mexico and Central American countries, including Zapotec, K’iche’, Chinanteco, Mixteco, and Mixe people. Hundreds of Indigenous languages are spoken across the Americas, including 364 in Mexico alone.

But the diversity of Latin American languages hasn’t been reflected in the interpretation services provided in immigration hearings, placing Indigenous language speakers at a significant disadvantage, according to the American Immigration Council.

Although CIELO is contracted to provide interpretation in courts, and has a team of 250 interpreters to do so for more than 60 Latin American Indigenous languages, López Resendiz said courts still fall short of ensuring immigrants’ due process rights are enforced.

“We’re careful in training our interpreters to make sure they follow all ethics and codes in order to provide a quality service,” López Resendiz said. “A lot of these courts fail at providing an interpreter because they all consider, and some courts classify Indigenous languages as rare languages that are hard to get an interpreter for.”

In response to questions about ICE’s protocol for translating immigration proceedings, the agency said in an email to LA Public Press that when detainees are in ICE custody they aren’t required to translate court-related documents.

The agency also said it doesn’t have the authority to translate another agency’s forms or documents.

Justice Department policy states that “all documents filed with the immigration court” must be in English “or accompanied by a certified English translation.”

Federal policies, case backlogs now make it more difficult for immigrants to get interpreters

In February 2025, Sirce Elliot Owen, acting director of the Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review, rescinded a Biden-era policy requiring judges to ensure immigrants with limited English proficiency are provided with in-court interpretation in their preferred language.

The 2023 policy also recommended that immigrants receive “reasonable access to out-of-court translation services” to assist them in reading and completing court documents.

In the February 2025 memo, Owen wrote the policy had “questionable lawfulness.” Non-citizens in immigration court, he said, “may either not need language access services at all or may choose to waive them.”

Cynthia Santiago, a Zapotec Kiche immigration and deportation defense attorney, told LA Public Press that although immigrants have a right to interpretation, Indigenous migrants do often waive those rights under pressure from the court.

“Because of how intimidating [immigration court is], and with the lack of information about their rights, individuals will [proceed with] a case with very limited Spanish, and many times waive important and essential rights they have,” Santiago said.

In one case Santiago observed this summer, she said an entire hearing had been conducted before a judge asked whether an Indigenous immigrant in ICE detention had understood proceedings. When the immigrant said they didn’t, Santiago said the judge rescheduled the hearing until a proper interpreter was contracted.

“It’s rare for a judge to be able to spot those issues because they are running these processes like a mill, trying to get through as many cases as possible,” Santiago said, adding that many immigrants can still be “lost in the system for months” or be subjected to delays in their cases until a proper interpreter is found.

At Van Nuys Boulevard Immigration Court on July 28, LA Public Press observed a hearing in which several cases were rescheduled by Judge Arlene E. Dorfman after immigrants requested a Mixtec interpreter.

At the hearing, Dorfman didn’t say when the Mixtec interpreter would be available, meaning it’s unclear when those immigrants’ cases will be resolved.

The Justice Department didn’t respond to an email from LA Public Press asking what steps the federal agency is taking to ensure Indigenous people can access interpretation in their preferred language and what it’s doing to guarantee that people fully understand their immigration court hearings.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, whose prosecutors present evidence for the deportation of non-citizens, said in an email the department adheres to federal requirements for language access and that immigrants in ICE detention are made aware of their rights via the ICE detainee handbook.

ICE’s website says the handbook is translated into multiple languages including K’iche’ and Q’eqchi’, two of the 29 Mayan languages spoken by more than 6 million people in the Americas. The agency’s website also encourages people to use Google Translate, but notes that it may not be accurate or secure for confidential translations.

“Where the handbook is not available in a detainee’s language, the information (or pertinent parts) must be orally interpreted for that alien,” the DHS email said, adding that the agency encourages immigrants to self deport.

“Being in detention is a choice,” the email said, repeating the Trump Administration’s offer to pay migrants to self-deport.

DHS didn’t respond to a request to provide a name for its spokesperson.

Concerns about language access for Indigenous migrants emerge as immigration courts struggle to clear a 3.2 million case backlog. Federal officials are seeking to increase deportations ordered by immigration judges by fast-tracking cases for asylum and other claims that advocates say aren’t getting a fair argument in court.

Immigration officials have also increasingly used “mega master” hearings, which inform non-citizens of their rights and responsibilities, scheduled with little to no advance notice to immigrants. The scheduling changes have led to judges issuing deportation orders for people who don’t show for a hearing they may have had no awareness of.

Democratic lawmakers have called for an end to mega master hearings, saying they “weaponize the immigration courts to facilitate mass removals.”

Advocates said translation also needs to be vetted

Anna Solodovnikova, an interpreter for immigration cases who was previously detained at Adelanto ICE Processing Center for two years, told LA Public Press that beyond access to interpreters, there also needs to be a vetting process to ensure translations are accurate.

Solodovnikova said a fellow immigrant detained at Adelanto had issues with their asylum application because an interpreter made several mistakes during a preliminary interview.

“Ideally, the courts would provide an interpreter who is competent,” Solodovnikova said. “In those situations, a human life depends on [correct interpretation.]”

The lack of access to adequate interpretation is a problem that Court Watch LA, a nonprofit that trains volunteer court observers, noted in its report in May, finding that immigrants in immigration court often lacked interpretation or encountered dialect mismatches.

Volunteer observers said in the report that immigrants who lacked interpreters or attorneys abandoned viable claims for relief or chose deportation without understanding their legal options or the charges against them.

Bryanna Siguenza, a judicial accountability organizer with Court Watch LA told LA Public Press she observed three hearings at Santa Ana Immigration Court in February that were held in Spanish even after immigrants requested interpretation in Miskito, a Central American indigenous language.

“The judge said it would cause significant delays in their hearings, and so they decided to opt for Spanish,” Siguenza said. “You can tell that the respondents probably had very minimal understanding of what was happening in the proceedings.”

Even though immigrants in the hearings had attorneys, Siguenza said they might have felt neglected by the process.

“They’re sitting there feeling alienated because of the fact that they cannot understand what’s actually going on,” Siguenza said. “You have no idea what these people are saying about you and about your case. You might be removed to a country that is quite literally dangerous for you.”

How to support Indigenous immigrants in immigration proceedings

López Resendiz said people can demand their Congressional representatives pass legislation requiring immigration courts to have language access plans that provide Indigenous interpretation services.

“It’s important that people understand everything they’re being told, in the language that they speak,” López Resendiz said. “It’s a fundamental human right.”

Siguenza said people can support Indigenous immigrants by attending a training on how to observe immigration court proceedings, remotely or in-person, which she said is a crucial way of holding judges accountable.

“The first step is going to these courts and forcing them to acknowledge that the public is paying attention and that they cannot get away with the misconduct, degradation and incompetency,” Siguenza said.

Siguenza said people can also attend immigration court or check-ins with immigrants and their families as trained observers who can document proceedings and provide emotional support.

“Seeing your community behind you is so supportive and helps you feel less alienated during this process,” Siguenza said, adding that volunteers can also alert families and advocates if someone doesn’t get home safely from court or an ICE check-in.

Santiago said community members can direct donations and volunteer hours to organizations that are Indigenous-led and that increase the visibility of Indigenous communities throughout LA County.

Advocates for Indigenous immigrants can also work with grassroots organizations like Aetna Street Solidarity or Community Self Defense Coalition LA to ensure immigrants not only have access to interpreters but also to housing, food, and other resources after an encounter with ICE, Santiago said.

“We have to understand how pressing it is to recognize Indigenous people as human beings,” Santiago said. “We need to be making a very deliberate and conscious effort to provide materials and resources to families in LA that speak Indigenous languages.”

title: Migrants flown to Equatorial Guinea after resisting Liberia deportation under Trump deal, sources say
description:
Liberia announced on Tuesday that it had agreed to receive deportees and that the first group of 20 would arrive on Thursday.
Authorities then told them they would be flown to the U.S., but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said.
It then departed for Malabo arriving at 8:50 p.m. (1950 GMT), according to the ICE Flight Monitor.
"The Trump Administration is using these deportation agreements to shuffle people around to different countries like objects," said Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta.
Equatorial Guinea's government did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.
text:
DAKAR — Five people who the U.S. attempted to deport to Liberia this week resisted getting off the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea, another African country to which the Trump administration is removing migrants it cannot legally send home, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The incident represents an early snag in Washington's plan to send up to 1,200 so-called third-country deportees to Liberia, one of the largest such deals it has struck in Africa despite criticism from immigrants' rights advocates.

Third-country deportees have, in most cases, obtained legal protection against repatriation after U.S. immigration ​judges ruled they risked torture or other abuses in their home countries.

Liberia announced on Tuesday that it had agreed to receive deportees and that the first group of 20 would arrive on Thursday. But a Liberian official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, told Reuters on Friday that only 15 deportees disembarked.

At least five others - three Cuban men, one Brazilian man and one Cameroonian woman - refused to get off the plane in Liberia, according to three sources familiar with the incident, one of whom was a Honduran deportee on the flight.

Authorities then told them they would be flown to the U.S., but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said.

Liberia's information ministry did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

The five deportees are now being held with more than 30 other migrants who the Trump administration had previously sent to Equatorial Guinea under a deal that, like others in Africa, has been denounced by human rights groups and advocates who say many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.

The State Department on Friday said it remained "unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America's border security".

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said all the migrants "were deported to a safe third country", adding, "If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period".

40 deportees held in Equatorial Guinea, sources say

The plane carrying the deportees arrived in Monrovia at 12:45 p.m. (1245 GMT) on Thursday after taking off from Louisiana and stopping in Dakar, Senegal, according to the ICE Flight Monitor managed by Human Rights First.

It then departed for Malabo arriving at 8:50 p.m. (1950 GMT), according to the ICE Flight Monitor.

There are now 40 deportees detained at a decommissioned hotel in Malabo, according to Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian migrant who arrived there four months ago.

Conditions at the hotel are grim, characterized by "inadequate medical care", "severe psychological distress" and denial of legal assistance, according to a statement published last month by five rights groups, including Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta and EG Justice.

"The Trump Administration is using these deportation agreements to shuffle people around to different countries like objects," said Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta.

Equatorial Guinea's government did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

Additional reporting by Jessica Donati and Alphonso Toweh; Editing by Alex Richardson

text:
Why It Matters

United We Dream, a major immigrant advocacy organization, ended its lobbying relationship with Masa Group LLC after just over a month (a strikingly brief engagement for a firm) client relationship. The organization paid nothing for the services. The termination comes as the Trump administration has prioritized immigration enforcement and mass deportation policies, making legislative advocacy on behalf of immigrants increasingly difficult. The bills United We Dream targeted, the American Dream and Promise Act of 2025 (H.R. 1589) and the DREAM Act (S. 3348), have stalled without committee action in a Congress controlled by Republicans skeptical of expansive immigration protections.

By The Numbers

United We Dream engaged Masa Group LLC on June 1, 2026, and terminated the relationship on July 1, 2026, according to a termination filing signed on Wednesday, August 19, 2026. The engagement lasted just over a month. Masa Group LLC charged United We Dream $0 for lobbying services during quarter two of 2026.

Broader Context

On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Mullin v. Doe that Congress barred judicial review of most Temporary Protected Status termination decisions. The Fifth Circuit upheld a district court ruling that DACA is unlawful under the INA, and DACA renewals continue for existing holders only.

H.R. 1589, sponsored by Reps. Sylvia Garcia (D-TX) and Nydia Velazquez (D-NY), has not advanced beyond introduction and has received no committee vote. The Senate companion bill, S. 3348, similarly has not advanced beyond introduction. Historically, approximately 11 percent of bills make it past committee, and roughly 2 percent are enacted into law.

Bottom Line

Kalyani Menon, a Senior Director at Masa Group, was assigned to the United We Dream account. Menon's work on the engagement reflects a broader pattern: she also handled immigration policy matters for the Vera Institute of Justice Inc. through Masa Group in quarter one of 2026. Both clients paid nothing for her services. The rapid termination suggests that pro bono advocacy on immigration issues may be unsustainable in the current political environment.

With the Supreme Court restricting DACA and TPS protections, and Republican-controlled committees blocking bills that would expand immigration protections, immigrant advocacy organizations face a narrowing window for legislative strategy. The one-month engagement signals that even well-resourced groups like United We Dream may be shifting away from federal lobbying toward other advocacy channels.

title: Louisiana judge holds ICE official in contempt | The Lens
description:
It appears to be the first time an individual ICE official in a leadership position has been cited in contempt of court.
Without the protection of deGravelles’s court orders, Mohammed could have remained detained months or years while his immigration case proceeded.
It’s also possible that an immigration judge would ultimately rule ICE can’t deport Mohammed to any of those three countries, deGravelles pointed out.
On Wednesday, the judge ordered ICE to pay Mohammed’s attorney’s fees and $180 for the time he lost while detained.
Earlier this month, a judge in California gave contempt citations to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which has authority over ICE, while a Maryland judge held ICE in contempt.
text:
A federal judge in Baton Rouge has ordered that an ICE official overseeing offices across the East Coast be held in contempt for repeatedly violating court orders to respect due process.

It appears to be the first time an individual ICE official in a leadership position has been cited in contempt of court.

“The Court finds Respondents’ agent-then-Acting Field Office Director Vernon Liggins in contempt for violating the Court’s Orders,” reads the order that U.S. District Judge John deGravelles handed down on Wednesday, in a ruling that indicates the judicial branch is increasingly ready to sanction ICE and its employees for violating court orders.

On July 28, Liggins, on his last day as acting field officer in Baltimore, personally instructed his agents to detain Ibrahim Mohammed, an Ethiopian man living in Maryland. Liggins was being promoted to ICE’s acting deputy assistant director for field operations east, working out of ICE headquarters in Washington, D.C. and overseeing 10 ICE field offices on the East Coast.

Liggins gave the order to his subordinates because he wanted to tie up loose ends, noted deGravelles of the Middle District of Louisiana in Baton Rouge. The ruling comes as part of Mohammed’s habeas petition case, which his counsel filed while Mohammed was first unlawfully detained in Camp 57, the immigration unit at the Louisiana State Penitentiary.

Liggins was aware that Mohammed couldn’t be re-detained without due process, but he gave the instructions anyway, Liggins confirmed in testimony last month.

That day, Liggins sent 10 agents to Mohammed’s apartment, where they barged their way in by telling Mohammed that his ankle monitor was malfunctioning, a lie.

At Wednesday’s ruling, deGravelles scolded Liggins for ordering re-detention because it would speed up deportation proceedings for Mohammed. That is no justification, deGravelles said.

Counsel for ICE from the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Baton Rouge acknowledged that ICE had violated those orders, but argued that a contempt charge wasn’t warranted.

Due process is required for everyone in United States

Due process in this case required that if ICE re-detained Mohammed, they must give him notice of specific reasons for his re-detention, conduct an informal interview with him promptly after re-detention, and have a significant likelihood of removing him in the foreseeable future.

None of that happened.

An immigration judge previously ruled in 2024 that Mohammed cannot be deported back to Ethiopia, because he would face torture and persecution there due to his ethnicity.

So ICE has been trying for months to deport Mohammed to a third country — Eswatini, Equatorial Guinea, or the Central African Republic.

But deGravelles’ April order made clear that ICE cannot deport Mohammed to a third country without first re-opening his immigration case and giving him the opportunity, in front of an immigration judge, to raise any credible fears he might have about being deported to that country. ICE also needed to first ensure that he would be accepted into the designated third country.

None of that happened.

ICE re-detained Mohammed before even nailing down which country he’d be deported to. That alone was enough to violate the court order, deGravelles said.

Without the protection of deGravelles’s court orders, Mohammed could have remained detained months or years while his immigration case proceeded. It’s also possible that an immigration judge would ultimately rule ICE can’t deport Mohammed to any of those three countries, deGravelles pointed out. That would mean Mohammed suffered “the unlawful deprivation of liberty this court sought to remedy,” the judge said.

After deGravelles issued an emergency order, ICE released Mohammed later on the same day, July 28. On Wednesday, the judge ordered ICE to pay Mohammed’s attorney’s fees and $180 for the time he lost while detained.

After repeated unlawful arrests, man has nightmares of ICE officers

The repeated unlawful detentions have affected Mohammed badly, he testified at the contempt hearing. His landlord, who was “petrified” by ICE officers showing up at the building and acting aggressively, told him he had to move out, Mohammed said.

“I’m really petrified,” he said in testimony. “I have nightmares, especially when I see the black cars.”

“Today’s decision makes it clear that ICE, like all law enforcement agencies, must follow the law,” Bridget Pranzatelli, Mohammed’s counsel with the National Immigration Project, wrote in a text. “By repeatedly detaining Mr. Mohammed in violation of clear court orders, due process, and federal law, ICE acted unlawfully,”

As the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign reaches its 20th month, fed-up federal judges appear increasingly ready to hand down sanctions over ICE’s repeated violations of court orders. Last year, a Boston judge held an individual ICE agent in contempt. In March, a Minnesota judge held five people, including then-DHS secretary Kristi Noem and three ICE officials, in civil contempt, but noted the court did not know who was directly responsible for the violation. Earlier this month, a judge in California gave contempt citations to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which has authority over ICE, while a Maryland judge held ICE in contempt.

DeGravelles concluded the hearing by warning that he was ready to escalate sanctions if needed.

“Respondents are reminded of their obligations to abide fully and strictly by this court’s orders,” the judge said. “Should there be any further violations, additional and more serious sanctions will be issued by this court.”

text:
Legal aid groups for asylum seekers and refugees are suing to stop a new policy at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) that they say changes a key part of the asylum process.

The new policy took effect almost a month ago, and allows USCIS personnel to bypass what’s called the affirmative asylum interview.

It’s a interview that for years has been conducted by a USCIS asylum officer when a person in the U.S. is seeking protection because of a threat in their home country. The process is not available to those already in deportation proceedings.

Melissa Crow is the director of litigation with the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies — one of the groups part of the suit. She says asylum officers are supposed to serve as neutral fact finders.

“Asylum officers are trained in trauma-informed interview techniques, the process before the asylum officer is not adversarial,” she said. “The government's own training materials state that it is well-established that a non-adversarial approach, where the interviewer builds rapport, is the most effective interview style to elicit credible information from an applicant.”

Crow says unlike defensive asylum applications, which are done when someone is in deportation proceedings, affirmative asylum interviewees can be granted asylum without needing to go through immigration court.

But under the new policy, called an interim final rule, asylum officers can skip the interview and refer cases directly to court — where the applicant will face removal proceedings. Crow’s suit argues the new policy was enacted without the proper procedural steps and asks the court to block it.

In an email, USCIS Spokesman Zach Kahler said the U.S. asylum system exists to protect people who genuinely fear persecution and said the new rule will help ensure agency resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims “instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole."

The Trump administration says the new rule will shorten the amount of time it takes asylum officers and immigration judges to adjudicate applications, and reduce the asylum backlog. But Crow says, the rule will likely further strain the court system.

“The rule admits that in some cases, they're going to refer people [to court] who could have easily been granted asylum and taken out of the system quickly,” Crow said. “But the larger problem, I think, is that it is only going to increase the horrendous backlogs that have plagued the immigration court system for so long — because they're going to have so many more cases in front of them.”

Michael Knowles is the executive vice president for the American Federation of Government Employees’ National Citizenship and Immigration Services Council 119 — a coalition of local unions representing more than 13,800 USCIS employees.

He says regardless of immigration status, anyone in the U.S. or arriving in the U.S. has the right to apply for asylum and have an interview with an asylum officer, who determines whether the person meets the definition of a refugee under U.S. and international law.

“Someone who is fleeing persecution on account of their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or their political opinion,” Knowles said. “The U.S. is required to protect refugees, and asylum officers are the officials who are tasked to decide whether the person is a refugee or not.”

To do that, he says, asylum officers must conduct the interview.

Knowles worked as an asylum officer for 34 years before retiring in October, and he also heads his union’s local chapter. He says officers do an average of two affirmative asylum interviews every day, and the process is extensive.

“People need to have a fair shot before they end up going to the court, because in the court, they’re in an adversarial hearing where the government is trying to deport them, rather than determine whether they should be protected,” he said.

text:
In the height of the 2025 hurricane season, an immigration detention center opened in the heart of the Everglades and Big Cypress National Preserve. State officials nicknamed the facility "Alligator Alcatraz."

Environmental groups like the Center for Biological Diversity and Friends of the Everglades filed suit in federal court before it opened, aiming to halt operations.

ALSO READ: How a detention center awoke a decades-old environmental fight

In late June, officials relocated detainees housed there, took down the large white tents, and removed generators — effectively shutting it down.

Lead attorney for the Center, Elise Bennett, has been arguing the case since last year. After an order to close it down, a reversal of that decision and back-and-forth with an appellate panel, the case will soon return to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams in Miami.

Attorneys filed an amended lawsuit Aug. 12 to update evidence they'd gotten in the past year. It was ahead of a court hearing with the judge and attorneys involved in the case.

"The most important facts have not changed, and the important facts are that no National Environmental Policy Act analysis has been done," Bennett said. "No formal consultation process with a biological opinion and safeguards for species has been completed. Those things haven't changed."

What has changed from the original lawsuit is the evidence on who is paying for it. The appellate court reversed an order to wind down the facility last year after saying there wasn't enough evidence to prove the federal government was reimbursing the state.

"We have all of that now," Bennett said. "The state of Florida had submitted an application, FEMA has processed it, awarded the money, and now disbursed grants."

ALSO READ: Trump admin pays Florida first $58 million in 'Alligator Alcatraz' reimbursements, state says

The amended suit also adds a new claim against the Endangered Species Act.

"[At the facility site], we had both the existence of very endangered species, like the Florida bonneted bat and the Florida panther, and we also had what's called critical habitat on the site that, unquestionably, was impacted by the project," Bennett said.

She said she'd hoped the original case would have prevented damage to the site.

"And now we're at a point where we're just trying to do our best to fix what has already been done," Bennett said.

She said the goal of the case is to get more information to the public and right the wrongs of the detention center.

"It's to get the environmental analyses that were required," Bennett said. "And through those federal laws to get conservation on the ground that will at this point remediate the harms that have been done."

She said another goal is to deter "bad acts" like the detention center in the future without environmental analyses in place.

Attorneys will head back to court in the next few months. Bennett said the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians indicated during last week's court hearing it would soon file an amended claim, and that attorneys representing the state and federal government would move to dismiss.

"These claims are meritless, and we look forward to presenting our arguments in court," a FEMA spokesperson told WUSF.

text:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — A five-year-old boy and his father were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Austin on Sunday, Aug. 16, according to a GoFundMe post from the family.

“My son is only five years old; he was supposed to start kindergarten this week, and instead he is being held in an immigration detention center. He should be in school, playing soccer and at home with his family. I am asking ICE to release Liam and his father immediately so that our family can be together again,” Liam’s mother said in a statement posted by FWD.us.

Patricia Resendiz said in the GoFundMe that she is the aunt of Liam and sister-in-law of the father. She wrote the boy, five-year-old Liam Tadeo, is being held at the Dilley processing center with his father.

That facility is near San Antonio, and advocates have previously called for its closure. It’s the same location where another five-year-old boy, also named Liam (Conejo Ramos), was sent after he and his father were detained in Minnesota. That case sparked significant outcry nationwide.

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson confirmed ICE arrested Victor Martinez Nieto, the father, during a traffic stop in Austin. He is an undocumented immigrant from Mexico.

DHS said ICE has arrested the man before, in late 2025 in Hutto.

“He accepted voluntary departure and was removed from the country on February 12, 2026. Martinez Nieto illegally reentered the country at an unknown time and place after being removed,” the DHS spokesperson said.

DHS said Martinez Nieto and his son will remain together in ICE custody “pending removal.” The spokesperson also added:

“Parents have a choice if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates. This is consistent with past administrations’ immigration enforcement.

The Dilley Detention Center is retrofitted for families. Children have access to teachers, classrooms, and curriculum booklets for math, reading, and spelling. All of this is generously funded by the U.S. taxpayer. Adults with children are housed in facilities that provide for their safety, security, and medical needs.

Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.“

KXAN has also reached out to sources at the city of Austin and Texas Department of Public Safety. Those sources told KXAN this appears to have only been ICE and not involved local or state law enforcement agencies.

State leaders react

“He should be in kindergarten this week,” Austin Rep. Greg Casar said in an Instagram post about the most recent detention in Austin. “Instead he’s in a trailer prison in the desert.”

Casar drew comparisons to the Minnesota case.

“Release Liam. Release these kids. Close the Dilley children’s prison,” Casar wrote.

Meanwhile Lauren B. Peña, Republican candidate for U.S. House District 37, said this:

“Are we hearing this right? My opponent Greg Casar wants to split up a family allegedly detained by ICE? This boy named Liam was not ‘detained’ — rather he was kept with his father. Kudos to ICE for keeping families together during this difficult time of reversing the Biden Administration’s terrible polices which allowed over 10 million immigrants to illegally cross our border.”

Investigative producer Dalton Huey contributed to this report.

text:
SILVER SPRING, Maryland — Nearly 100 transnational, national, state, and local organizations and over 170 faith leaders urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for El Salvador. Salvadoran TPS holders remain in need of TPS humanitarian protection. A termination at this time would result in sending hundreds of thousands of Salvadoran TPS holders back into unstable condition. The humanitarian protection for Salvadoran TPS holders is scheduled to expire on Sept. 9, 2026. Given the current conditions in El Salvador, extending the designation is the right thing to do.

"TPS holders from El Salvador are our neighbors, friends, colleagues, faith leaders, highly-skilled workers, and small business owners who have built their lives in the United States for more than 25 years. Alianza Americas joins hundreds of faith leaders and communities in urging the Secretary of Homeland Security to extend TPS for El Salvador and protect more than 170,000 Salvadorans from being uprooted from the lives and families they have built here. At a moment when immigrant communities face tremendous uncertainty and fear, our faith and shared humanity call us to choose compassion, uphold human dignity, and love our neighbors without distinction. Extending TPS is an urgent act of justice and solidarity that can provide immediate relief. We will continue standing with Salvadoran communities and fighting for the permanent protections they and their families deserve," said Dulce Guzmán, Executive Director of Alianza Americas.

"Sending Salvadoran TPS holders back into unsafe conditions at a time where deportees in El Salvador are being detained without adequate representation, kidnapped, or potentially face some other harm, is cruel and can have a long-lasting harmful impact on those forced to return," said Elnora Bassey, a policy attorney at CLINIC. "At a time where immigrants are being targeted and lawful protections are becoming less available to those who need it, the administration has an opportunity to make a choice that demonstrates its ability to protect vulnerable populations and that we are a nation that demonstrates compassion for all people regardless of status."

As we wait on the administration to decide, CLINIC and Alianza Americas will continue to fight for the rights of our immigrant brothers and sisters and advocate that dignity and access to humanitarian protection must be available to those who need it.

text:
The Trump administration has appealed a federal judge’s dismissal of its challenge to policies in four New Jersey cities that limit how local law enforcement can cooperate with federal civil immigration enforcement.

In June, U.S. District Court Judge Evelyn Padin tossed the feds’ lawsuit that sought to overturn sanctuary policies for immigrants in Hoboken, Jersey City, Newark, and Paterson, saying an existing state directive already barred local authorities from supporting federal immigration enforcement and the local policies merely underscored that state prohibition.

In a one-page notice filed Friday, U.S. Department of Justice attorneys asked the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals to reconsider Padin’s dismissal. The feds have argued that the cities’ policies seek to regulate the actions of federal officials and so should be struck down.

The local policies and the state directive, though, only apply to the actions of local law enforcement, Padin noted.

The cities’ policies largely repeat the state directive, which forbids state and local authorities from initiating stops based on someone’s suspected immigration status or for violations of civil immigration law and bars officers from asking about a person’s immigration status unless it pertains to an ongoing felony investigation.

name: Human Rights
title: Europe: a race to the bottom on migrants' rights - CIVICUS LENS
description:
Progressive forces need to speak to genuine economic and social concerns while holding the line on migrants’ rights.
Because Spain depends on Morocco’s cooperation to run a militarised border, Morocco has leverage, making migrants pawns in a geopolitical game.
What’s urgently needed are safe, regular pathways for migrants to seek work or protection in Europe.
EU turns for the worse Events in Ceuta have come as migrants’ rights are experiencing regression at the EU level, with racism and hostility towards migrants increasingly normalised.
In June, Swiss voters rejected a proposal by a far-right party to cap the country’s population at 10 million.
text:
A mass crossing from Morocco to Spain’s exclave of Ceuta on 30 July triggered a political and social media storm that overshadowed the deaths of over a hundred people. Other European governments and right-wing politicians hurried to attack Spain for supposedly being soft on migration. This reflects a Europe-wide normalisation of racism, with states competing to look toughest on keeping out and removing migrants, endorsed by the European Union in a harsh new regulation. Far-right forces are driving the discourse, mainstreaming extremism by scapegoating migrants for crime and economic hardship. Progressive forces need to speak to genuine economic and social concerns while holding the line on migrants’ rights.

On 30 July, an estimated 78,000 people attempted to cross from Morocco into Spain’s exclave of Ceuta. Over 100 died, most while trying to swim across. Their deaths, the most visible human cost of Europe’s intensifying hostility towards migrants and refugees, have been largely overlooked in the ensuing anti-immigrant furore, stoked via social media and capitalised on by politicians.

Members of the Spanish Army's infantry forces watch a group of migrants near the border post of the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on 2 August 2026. Photo by Henry Nicholls/AFP.

Hate speech and disinformation

The mass crossing appears to have been triggered by a wave of social media disinformation. Dozens of Instagram videos circulated claiming ‘Spain was open’, showing migrants strolling freely around Ceuta and promoting the sea route as safe. Some social media channels offered to sell tips on navigating the route safely. Many of the accounts spreading these claims appeared to be based in Morocco.

The disinformation spread in the wake of a Spanish Supreme Court ruling barring authorities from summarily expelling migrants who swim to Ceuta or Melilla, Spain’s other North African exclave. It hasn’t stopped, and a second mass crossing attempt on 15 August was thwarted by strengthened security.

Ceuta and Melilla provide the European Union’s (EU) only land border with Africa and have long strained relations between Morocco and Spain. Spain, a former colonial power over parts of Morocco, insists the two cities are integral parts of its territory, although special migration rules make it hard for migrants to use them as a gateway to the EU. Morocco considers them occupied territory and claims sovereignty. Because Spain depends on Morocco’s cooperation to run a militarised border, Morocco has leverage, making migrants pawns in a geopolitical game.

Tensions spike further over Spain’s relations with Morocco’s rival Algeria, which Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez recently visited, and over the disputed territory of Western Sahara, which Morocco invaded in 1975 and largely controls. In 2021, Spain allowed the leader of the Polisario Front, Western Sahara’s independence movement, to travel to the country for COVID-19 treatment. Morocco retaliated by loosening border controls, letting more migrants cross. A mass crossing into Melilla followed in June 2022, leaving at least 23 people dead. Spain has since backed Morocco’s plan to incorporate Western Sahara as an autonomous region, but some believe the Moroccan government, which has cultivated close ties with the Trump administration, let the latest events happen to further pressure Spain. Spain notably avoided criticising Moroccan border guards for failing to stop people.

Most of those who crossed returned quickly once they realised there was no chance of getting to mainland Europe and food and shelter were scarce. The few thousand who stayed, among them children, were left sleeping on the beach in appalling conditions, with civil society groups scrambling to provide humanitarian help. On 16 August, they protested to draw attention to their plight. The Spanish government has recently relented and said it will allow 500 children stranded in Ceuta to come to the mainland.

While civil society mobilised out of compassion, Spain’s far-right Vox party and right-wingers across Europe seized on events to attack Spain’s centre-left government and others deemed too soft on migration. On 31 July, hundreds took part in an anti-migrant protest outside Morocco’s embassy in Madrid, some making Nazi salutes and carrying far-right flags. Right-wing influencers rushed to the region to file breathless reports of ‘invasion’, amplified by figures such as Elon Musk. The flames of online hatred were fanned by an apparently coordinated and rapid campaign by Russian military-linked accounts. Russia benefits from political chaos in Europe and far-right politicians tend to support Russia.

Italy’s right-wing government led the charge. With Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni facing a threat from an even more anti-migrant party, National Future, in next year’s election, her Brothers of Italy party seized the opportunity to attack the Spanish government on social media. Italy suspended the Schengen Agreement – a free-movement treaty that covers much of Europe – for Spanish citizens. Several EU states backed Italy’s call to suspend Spain from the Schengen Agreement and most signed its letter demanding an urgent meeting of interior ministers to address what it called ‘pull factors’ drawing people to the EU. Donald Trump and the Israeli government joined the attacks, seeing an opportunity to repay Spain for condemning Israel’s genocide in Gaza and opposing the war in Iran. Spain retaliated with new border checks on visitors from Italy.

Voices from the frontline

Chiara Catelli is Project and Advocacy Officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a civil society network of over 160 organisations that works to ensure human rights and justice for undocumented migrants.

Politicians have framed recent events in Ceuta in a way that misses the point entirely. What’s urgently needed are safe, regular pathways for migrants to seek work or protection in Europe.

That would mean people aren’t forced into desperate, dangerous journeys, even when, as in Ceuta, they’re driven by disinformation or false promises.

Instead, governments are using any excuse to increase sanctions and repression, without questioning the EU’s model of paying countries such as Libya, Morocco and Turkey to intercept migrants. This leaves Europe diplomatically and politically exposed and, more importantly, does nothing to address why people move in the first place.

An issue that could be resolved more easily ends up being driven by political competition over who can look toughest on migration, rather than by evidence of what works or approaches that protect everyone’s fundamental rights.

The answer shouldn’t be more repression or more externalisation. Outsourcing migration responsibilities to non-EU countries doesn’t solve the problem. Ceuta shows the opposite is true. For us, the answer needs to be more regular and safe pathways into the EU to seek both protection and work.

This is an edited extract from our conversation with Chiara. Read the full interview here.

EU turns for the worse

Events in Ceuta have come as migrants’ rights are experiencing regression at the EU level, with racism and hostility towards migrants increasingly normalised. In June, when the European Parliament approved a new return regulation that gives states enhanced powers to deport migrants, its usual polite, procedural manner gave way to something ugly. Right-wing parliament members celebrated the vote with chants of ‘send them back’. Language once confined to racist fringe groups was now heard at the heart of a democracy of some 452 million people.

The regulation, expected to become law in September, implements aspects of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which entered into force in June. It will let EU states detain migrants for up to two years and send them to deportation centres outside the EU, extending the trend of wealthy states subcontracting poorer ones to manage migration. Civil society groups have warned it could bring routine US-style immigration raids, increased surveillance and racial profiling, while United Nations human rights experts have stated that the regulation may breach several international human rights commitments EU states have made.

These changes reflect the European Parliament’s rightwards shift. At the last election in June 2024, far-right parties from Austria, France and Germany made significant gains and established centre-right parties did better than centrist and green ones. Across Europe, mainstream centre-right and centre-left parties have hardened their line on immigration in response to the successes of right-wing parties that have relentlessly focused on the issue. Firewalls that once kept established parties from cooperating with extremist ones haven’t survived calculations of political convenience. The mainstream centre-right European People’s Party group, parliament’s largest, voted alongside far-right parties to push the return regulation through.

Further regression lies ahead. When EU ministers met following the events in Ceuta, they agreed to improve early warning systems, including through stronger social media monitoring. Migration control and surveillance go hand in hand.

The EU’s preoccupation with looking tough on migration is eroding its human rights principles, including when it pays repressive states to help control migration, granting them political leverage. Another troubling development came in June, when EU officials held an unprecedented meeting with Taliban representatives to discuss deporting Afghan migrants with rejected asylum claims. The Taliban have never been recognised as Afghanistan’s government, but the meeting risks normalising their rule even as they pass further laws erasing women’s rights. To deport asylum seekers who’ll likely face danger, the EU is downplaying systematic violations of women’s fundamental rights.

Voices from the frontline

We spoke with an anonymous member of the Afghan section of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom, a global membership-based feminist peacebuilding organisation.

The meeting came as shocking news for women’s rights defenders inside and outside Afghanistan. With Afghan women’s rights deteriorating under Taliban rule, it’s hard to understand why European and regional governments would deepen ties with them. It’s particularly troubling that governments with human rights and feminist foreign policies are sidelining Afghan women and handing the Taliban international platforms.

Together with others, we have documented the failings of Taliban laws, including the recently introduced Criminal Procedure Code and the Code on Judicial Separation of Spouses, drawing on consultations with women on the ground and religious scholars inside and outside Afghanistan. We shared our findings with EU governments to raise concerns about the meeting and used social media to voice our opposition.

As a result of this mobilisation, the EU said the meeting would focus only on asylum seekers. Yet political considerations must not take precedence over women’s rights. Taliban policies, including the latest marriage and divorce decree, should serve as a warning to the international community.

This is an edited extract from our conversation. Read the full interview here.

National-level regression

Some EU states are leading this race to the bottom. If it seems cruel, that’s the point. Even though irregular migration numbers are falling, performative toughness is the intention, communicating to voters that governments are acting on an issue relentlessly pushed by extremist politicians and social media accounts. For migrants and refugees, the result is a denial of rights. As legal routes close, they take more dangerous ones, risking criminalisation, violence and, as seen in Ceuta, death.

In June, Sweden’s parliament approved laws that remove any path to permanent residency for people granted asylum, allow authorities to cancel residency permits on broadly defined grounds of ‘bad behaviour’ and require many public sector employees to report suspected undocumented migrants. The bad behaviour provisions apply retroactively, potentially leaving many migrants at risk of deportation for minor past offences. The reporting requirement could lead to de facto racial profiling, subjecting Black and Brown people to suspicion white people don’t face and turning public servants who joined their profession to help people into unofficial border police. As a result, migrants may stop using vital services, such as healthcare, to avoid suspicion, or opt out of protests for fear of being arrested. The result will be a two-tier system, including for civic freedoms.

Sweden says it wants to have the most restrictive asylum laws in the EU, and it’s no coincidence that the latest changes have come ahead of a September election in which migration is a key issue. The centre-right government relies on the far-right Sweden Democrats party, which is hoping for further gains. This brings the risk of a contagion effect. Other EU governments are watching how Sweden’s new laws are applied with a view to copying them.

Neighbouring Denmark, which stood squarely beside Italy in condemning Spain, offers another grim example. The coalition led by the centre-left Social Democrats stayed in power following the March election, having adopted increasingly strict asylum restrictions and dismantled protections for migrants and refugees, framing its decisions as a defence of the welfare state. Its policies now closely mirror those of the far-right Danish People’s Party.

Time and again, the strategy fails. When mainstream parties adopt far-right positions, they don’t win back voters, but legitimise far-right narratives, and many voters trust a party that has always championed anti-migrant policies over one that has opportunistically adopted them. Denmark’s Social Democrats hung onto power, but with their worst result in over 120 years, while the Danish People’s Party tripled its seats.

Voices from the frontline

John Stauffer is legal director and deputy executive director of Civil Rights Defenders, a Swedish civil society organisation that acts as a civil rights watchdog at home and supports human rights defenders in repressive contexts worldwide.

The good behaviour law means we are no longer all equal before the law. Something a Swedish citizen can say or do without any legal consequence can cost a residence permit holder their right to stay.

What makes this worse is that nobody knows exactly where the line falls. Legal scholars have described these laws as very broad, vague and difficult to apply in practice, so people have no way of telling in advance what might be used against them.

That uncertainty produces a chilling effect on people’s willingness to use their rights. Permit holders who are not citizens are withdrawing from public debate. They stop voicing their views and stay away from protests, because they fear that joining a pro-Palestine march or climate action, for example, might cost them their permit. We are, in fact, creating a two-tier system where the lives of non-citizens will be characterised by uncertainty and limited access to rights, while citizens enjoy full rights.

The government has been building a narrative that connects migration to rising rates of violent crime. Using that as a justification, it has tried to build strong support for stricter migration policies and at the same time has pushed more repressive policies to combat crime, including greater possibilities to revoke residency permits for migrants who have committed crimes, including less serious crimes.

As we approach the September election, it remains to be seen whether people truly support this model. The largest opposition party, the Social Democrats, have, however, supported many of the new immigration policies.

This is an edited extract from our conversation with John. Read the full interview here.

Brighter moments

The trend isn’t in one direction. Civil society continues to mount coordinated resistance, including by physically obstructing deportations, providing essential services and taking legal action against regressive policies. Many of its successes are defensive, holding the line on rights that are under attack, including by winning case-by-case reversals of deportation orders.

Some victories have wider implications. Following a campaign supported by over 700,000 signatures, last year the Spanish government opened a scheme to grant residence and work permits to many undocumented migrants. Over a million people applied. But the move has helped fuel the backlash against Spain. Even though the application period has closed, EU states and the bloc’s migration commissioner criticised the scheme in the wake of events in Ceuta, identifying it as one of the ‘pull factors’ Europe should eliminate.

In June, Swiss voters rejected a proposal by a far-right party to cap the country’s population at 10 million. Borrowing the language of sustainability, the anti-migrant Swiss People’s Party claimed the measure was needed to protect housing, infrastructure, the natural environment and social support programmes. Such narratives are increasingly being used to justify anti-migrant policies. Had it passed, the measure would have meant strict limits on asylum places, residency permits and family reunification.

In Switzerland, such proposals must go to a referendum. While 45.2 per cent of voters backed the move, 54.8 per cent were against it. This doesn’t necessarily mean a ringing endorsement of migration. Voters may have feared for non-EU member Switzerland’s economically crucial access to the single market, had it ended its free movement agreement with the EU. Nonetheless, it shows normalisation of far-right anti-migrant discourse can be checked.

That discourse is pushing still further, normalising the prospects of forced removal under the banner of ‘remigration’. In response, progressive forces need to find new ways to separate genuine public concerns about rising costs, crime and deteriorating public services from the migration framing currently attached to them. Politicians offer cruel migration policies as deceptively simple solutions to complex problems, but the real answers lie in rebalancing economies: intervening when companies profiteer, housing markets fail and the super-rich dodge their contributions to the public finances. That path is harder, but the alternative is a race to the bottom with no floor.

OUR CALLS FOR ACTION

The European Union and its member states must commit to respecting the rights of migrants and refugees and reverse hostile policies, including harsh removal policies and the establishment of deportation centres in other countries.

The Spanish government must allow an independent inquiry into migrant deaths in Ceuta and act on its findings.

Progressive political parties and civil society groups should develop policies that speak to public anger about problems such as cost increases, crime and poor public services without normalising anti-migrant discourse.

For interviews or more information, please contact research@civicus.org

text:
A federal judge in Baton Rouge has ordered that an ICE official overseeing offices across the East Coast be held in contempt for repeatedly violating court orders to respect due process.

It appears to be the first time an individual ICE official in a leadership position has been cited in contempt of court.

“The Court finds Respondents’ agent-then-Acting Field Office Director Vernon Liggins in contempt for violating the Court’s Orders,” reads the order that U.S. District Judge John deGravelles handed down on Wednesday, in a ruling that indicates the judicial branch is increasingly ready to sanction ICE and its employees for violating court orders.

On July 28, Liggins, on his last day as acting field officer in Baltimore, personally instructed his agents to detain Ibrahim Mohammed, an Ethiopian man living in Maryland. Liggins was being promoted to ICE’s acting deputy assistant director for field operations east, working out of ICE headquarters in Washington, D.C. and overseeing 10 ICE field offices on the East Coast.

Liggins gave the order to his subordinates because he wanted to tie up loose ends, noted deGravelles of the Middle District of Louisiana in Baton Rouge. The ruling comes as part of Mohammed’s habeas petition case, which his counsel filed while Mohammed was first unlawfully detained in Camp 57, the immigration unit at the Louisiana State Penitentiary.

Liggins was aware that Mohammed couldn’t be re-detained without due process, but he gave the instructions anyway, Liggins confirmed in testimony last month.

That day, Liggins sent 10 agents to Mohammed’s apartment, where they barged their way in by telling Mohammed that his ankle monitor was malfunctioning, a lie.

At Wednesday’s ruling, deGravelles scolded Liggins for ordering re-detention because it would speed up deportation proceedings for Mohammed. That is no justification, deGravelles said.

Counsel for ICE from the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Baton Rouge acknowledged that ICE had violated those orders, but argued that a contempt charge wasn’t warranted.

Due process required for everyone in US

Due process in this case required that if ICE re-detained Mohammed, they must give him notice of specific reasons for his re-detention, conduct an informal interview with him promptly after re-detention, and have a significant likelihood of removing him in the foreseeable future.

None of that happened.

An immigration judge previously ruled in 2024 that Mohammed cannot be deported back to Ethiopia, because he would face torture and persecution there due to his ethnicity.

So ICE has been trying for months to deport Mohammed to a third country — Eswatini, Equatorial Guinea, or the Central African Republic.

But deGravelles’ April order made clear that ICE cannot deport Mohammed to a third country without first re-opening his immigration case and giving him the opportunity, in front of an immigration judge, to raise any credible fears he might have about being deported to that country. ICE also needed to first ensure that he would be accepted into the designated third country.

None of that happened.

ICE re-detained Mohammed before even nailing down which country he’d be deported to. That alone was enough to violate the court order, deGravelles said.

Without the protection of deGravelles’s court orders, Mohammed could have remained detained months or years while his immigration case proceeded. It’s also possible that an immigration judge would ultimately rule ICE can’t deport Mohammed to any of those three countries, deGravelles pointed out. That would mean Mohammed suffered “the unlawful deprivation of liberty this court sought to remedy,” the judge said.

After deGravelles issued an emergency order, ICE released Mohammed later on the same day, July 28. On Wednesday, the judge ordered ICE to pay Mohammed’s attorney’s fees and $180 for the time he lost while detained.

Man has nightmares of ICE officers

The repeated unlawful detentions have affected Mohammed badly, he testified at the contempt hearing. His landlord, who was “petrified” by ICE officers showing up at the building and acting aggressively, told him he had to move out, Mohammed said.

“I’m really petrified,” he said in testimony. “I have nightmares, especially when I see the black cars.”

“Today’s decision makes it clear that ICE, like all law enforcement agencies, must follow the law,” Bridget Pranzatelli, Mohammed’s counsel with the National Immigration Project, wrote in a text. “By repeatedly detaining Mr. Mohammed in violation of clear court orders, due process, and federal law, ICE acted unlawfully,”

As the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign reaches its 20th month, fed-up federal judges appear increasingly ready to hand down sanctions over ICE’s repeated violations of court orders. Last year, a Boston judge held an individual ICE agent in contempt. In March, a Minnesota judge held five people, including then-DHS secretary Kristi Noem and three ICE officials, in civil contempt, but noted the court did not know who was directly responsible for the violation. Earlier this month, a judge in California gave contempt citations to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which has authority over ICE, while a Maryland judge held ICE in contempt.

DeGravelles concluded the hearing by warning that he was ready to escalate sanctions if needed.

“Respondents are reminded of their obligations to abide fully and strictly by this court’s orders,” the judge said. “Should there be any further violations, additional and more serious sanctions will be issued by this court.”

text:
Days before he was due to start kindergarten, a 5-year-old Texas boy was taken to an immigration detention center with his father after federal agents stopped them as they traveled to a soccer game, according to his family and Spanish-language news reports.

Liam Tadeo and his father were detained following a traffic stop in Austin on Sunday, August 16, and later taken to the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, the boy’s mother told N+ Univision. Video circulating online appears to show Liam crying before his father is arrested as officers escort them into a car. He was due to start kindergarten this week, his aunt Patricia Resendiz said in a GoFundMe.

Read More on News

In a statement to Newsweek on Friday, a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson identified Liam's father as Victor Martinez Nieto, a Mexican national whom ICE arrested on August 16 during a vehicle stop in Austin. According to DHS, Martinez Nieto first entered the United States illegally around March 10, 2022, near Laredo, Texas.

DHS said ICE previously arrested Martinez Nieto in Hutto, Texas, on November 15, 2025. The agency said he accepted voluntary departure and was removed from the United States on February 12, 2026, before later reentering the country at an unknown time and place, according to DHS.

DHS said Martinez Nieto and his son remain together at the Dilley facility pending his removal. Responding to criticism of the case, the agency told Newsweek that parents can either be removed with their children or designate a safe caregiver, describing the policy as consistent with immigration enforcement practices under previous administrations.

During N+ Univision’s interview with Tadeo's mother, who asked not to be named, Tadeo called her from the detention center, telling her that he loved and missed her, the Spanish network reported.

Resendiz said in the family’s GoFundMe: "The detention of Liam and my brother-in-law was cruel; they are not criminals—they were simply on their way to a soccer match. Liam is a beautiful, intelligent, and big-hearted little boy. My sister is devastated, and so are we."

Texas Democratic Representative Greg Casar has spoken out in support of the family, saying in a post on X: "ICE just arrested a 5-year-old on his way to a soccer game in Austin. His name is Liam, just like the little boy from Minnesota. He should be in kindergarten this week. Instead he's in a trailer prison in the desert. Release Liam. Release these kids. Close the Dilley children’s prison."

Democrats Warn of Increased ICE Activity in Austin

Liam Tadeo’s reported detention comes as Democratic officials and community leaders warn that immigration enforcement has increased in Austin, although ICE has not publicly released data confirming the scale of any recent rise.

Representative Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who represents the state’s 35th Congressional District, last week told local media that ICE arrests in the city had risen to three or four times their usual level over several days in August. He said activity had been reported in north-central, south and southeast Austin and that his office had asked the Department of Homeland Security for information about the operations.

Casar spoke alongside community leaders after witnesses reported seeing ICE officers handcuffing people outside a Seventh-day Adventist church in Austin’s Rundberg neighborhood. The church operates a free food distribution program near an elementary school. Casar argued that the location of the reported arrests undermined the administration’s claim that its enforcement efforts were focused on people with serious criminal records.

DHS defended its enforcement activity in Austin and told the broadcaster FOX 7 Austin that ICE would not slow down its operations. It identified two Mexican nationals arrested on August 13—Juan Alvarado-Olmedo, "criminal history includes DUIs, assault, contempt of court, larceny, and damage to private property as well as illegal entry and illegal reentry—a felony" and Luis Garcia Fernandez, who had "completed approximately five months of incarceration related to a felony sexual assault offense."

"Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App," the DHS said. "The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70 percent of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S.," the DHS added. "Our message is clear: if you come into our country illegally and break our laws, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you."

Echoes of Liam Conejo Ramos’ Detention

Liam Tadeo’s case has drawn comparisons to that of Liam Conejo Ramos, another 5-year-old boy who was taken into federal custody with his father and held at the same family detention center in Dilley, Texas.

Conejo Ramos and his father, Adrian Conejo Arias, were apprehended by immigration officers in Minnesota on January 20 after the boy returned home from preschool. Images of the child wearing a blue knitted bunny hat and carrying a Spider-Man backpack spread widely online, turning his case into a focal point of opposition to the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement campaign.

The DHS said agents were targeting Conejo Arias, not his son, and alleged that the father ran from officers, leaving the child behind. School officials and the family’s representatives disputed the government’s account, saying another adult offered to take the boy but agents declined.

Conejo Ramos and his father were transferred to Dilley before a federal judge ordered their release. The images of the boy continued to feature in the wider backlash against the administration’s immigration operations, which included demonstrations in Minnesota and anti-ICE activism surrounding Super Bowl LX.

Administration’s Position on ICE Enforcement

The Trump administration has described ICE detentions as necessary to enforce federal immigration law and protect public safety. White House border czar Tom Homan previously said the administration’s priorities were "criminal aliens, public safety threats, and national security threats," adding: "If you’re in the country illegally, you’re never off the table."

Officials have also disputed longstanding criticism of conditions at Dilley. In February, ICE Director Todd Lyons called it "a family residential center designed specifically to house family units in a safe, structured and appropriate environment." In its statement to Newsweek, DHS said the facility is "retrofitted for families" and that children have access to teachers, classrooms and curriculum materials covering subjects including math, reading and spelling, alongside medical care and recreation areas.

Addressing the detention of Liam Conejo Ramos and his father, Vice President JD Vance asked: "What are they supposed to do?" He argued that having a child could not prevent officers from arresting a parent they believed was subject to immigration enforcement.

As federal immigration enforcement activity increases across the region, King County’s Office of Law Enforcement Oversight has delivered a new set of community-driven recommendations aimed at changing how the King County Sheriff’s Office responds when federal immigration agents operate in the county.

Last week, the Office of Law Enforcement Oversight, known as OLEO, provided the King County Sheriff’s Office with seven community-informed recommendations in a report focused on responding to increased federal immigration enforcement within the county.

SEE ALSO | King County Council passes 1-year emergency ban on new ICE detention centers

OLEO said the recommendations are intended to strengthen the Sheriff’s Office’s current policy to be more responsive to community needs, expand community education and outreach, and promote understanding by clarifying existing policy language.

OLEO’s report comes as Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests at community sites, including schools and workplaces, have “dramatically increased since 2025,” according to the oversight office. OLEO said that as ICE arrests have intensified, community members have formed coalitions to protect immigrants and refugees, but confusion remains about the role of local law enforcement in responding to federal immigration enforcement.

“It’s important for the Sheriff’s Office’s policies to reflect what communities need in the face of increasingly aggressive immigration enforcement,” said Angela Ngiangi Diansasila of the Congolese Integration Network. “These recommendations help the Sheriff’s Office achieve more with their immigration policies and better protect vulnerable immigrant and refugee groups.”

OLEO said its outreach included an online survey and multiple listening sessions, and that the recommendations were also informed by research into emerging practices in peer jurisdictions.

Among the report’s key takeaways, OLEO said 56% of survey respondents reported that fears of immigration enforcement have affected school attendance, health care access and other activities. OLEO also reported that 41% of respondents said they are less willing to call police for help, 37% said they are less willing to report a crime, and 70% said they feel more worried about racial profiling by law enforcement.

SEE ALSO | King County Council bars ICE, DHS from using non-public county property for operations

“Through our outreach, community members and advocates shared with us how intensified immigration enforcement has made them fearful of contacting law enforcement or other public agencies for assistance, making it crucial for the King County Sheriff’s Office to expand its outreach to address community fears in accessible ways,” said Angelica Maria Gonzalez Graham from Eastside For All. “The report includes recommendations for how the Sheriff’s Office can share information with communities that need it and clarify the Sheriff’s Office’s role in supporting communities targeted by harmful immigration enforcement practices.”

The seven recommendations include:

Creating a policy, in consultation with legal advisers and community members, directing deputies to intervene when they observe federal law enforcement agents engaging in unlawful excessive force

Expanding outreach to meet community needs and answer questions about immigration enforcement practices

Completing and publishing audits of technology and data software contracts to ensure policy compliance and share contract details with OLEO

Partnering with immigrant service networks to create a protocol for moving abandoned vehicles from roads when there are verified reports that a federal immigration enforcement agency detained the driver

Tracking and regularly publishing readily available information on federal immigration enforcement activity in King County without increasing communication with federal immigration authorities

Clarifying supervisor responsibilities and requiring additional deputies to be present when responding to federal immigration enforcement activities to ensure full documentation

Removing the term “criminal immigration enforcement” from Sheriff’s Office policy and replacing it with language OLEO says better captures when the Sheriff’s Office may engage with federal law enforcement agencies.

OLEO noted that in April 2026, the Sheriff’s Office updated its policies restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities and requiring the Sheriff’s Office to document federal immigration enforcement activity in King County.

OLEO said the Sheriff’s Office has received the report and stated in an initial response that it will engage with subject matter experts to thoroughly review and respond to the recommendations. OLEO said the Sheriff’s Office’s full response will be published on OLEO’s webpage when it becomes available.
