text:
The Department of Homeland Security launched in 2025 a “worst of the worst” list of "illegal aliens" arrested for alleged gruesome offenses, including “homicide-burglary,” “sex assault-carnal abuse” and “aggravated assault-strangulation.”

DHS General Counsel James Percival on July 23 launched his own "worst of the worst" list. What's remarkable is that the four people on it are as law-abiding as anyone you'll ever meet. Each is a sitting federal judge.

They made the list because they had ruled against the Trump administration on immigration cases. Percival claimed that the four judges engaged in "naked politics” cloaked "in the thin veneer of legalese."

That's what lawyers call an ipse dixit: an unsupported assertion the speaker claims is true simply "because I say so."

DHS and Percival are doing something reckless – and even if they don't intend harm, they could get someone killed.

Threats against federal judges who rule against Trump are increasing

The U.S. Marshals Service is responsible for protecting federal judges, and its threat board was blinking red even before Percival's post. There were 564 threats against federal judges in the 2025 fiscal year, up 11% from the year before. As of Aug. 17, that number for this fiscal year is already 415 threats.

Family members of at least 11 judges who ruled against the administration have faced threats or harassment.

The threats aren't confined to immigration rulings. In 2025, U.S. District Judge John McConnell, an Obama appointee, temporarily blocked the administration's freeze on trillions of dollars in federal funding. He received at least six credible death threats and hundreds more threatening messages.

One caller left this message: "I wish somebody would f---ing assassinate your a--."

Conservative jurists are at risk, too. Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett has a reliably conservative voting record, but she's infuriated some MAGA figures by breaking with the administration in key cases.

In urging Congress to appropriate more funds for judicial protection, Barrett described trying to explain to her 12-year-old son why she had brought home a bulletproof vest: "He wanted to know what it was and why I had it, and I didn't know how to respond."

To be sure, Democrats have made their own contribution to this threatening climate. In 2020, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer warned Supreme Court Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch that they would "pay the price" if their votes restricted abortion rights.

Schumer apologized the next day, but two years later a man attempted to assassinate Kavanaugh at his home. (There's no direct evidence Schumer's comment motivated the attack.)

A judge's son was killed. DHS is ignoring her warning.

After Percival posted the list, alarmed bar associations and federal judges pleaded with him to take it down. None had more moral authority to make that plea than Judge Esther Salas of the U.S. District Court in New Jersey. The judge's son was killed in their home in 2020 by an anti-feminist attorney posing as a delivery driver, intent on killing her.

“I just ask our political leaders to tone it down,” Salas said. "Criticize us on the merits, appeal us, but stop villainizing and demonizing my colleagues please."

Percival ignored the pleas, with every reason to count on the Trump administration's unwavering support.

President Donald Trump has viciously attacked Supreme Court justices who ruled against him (even those he appointed), calling them "fools," "disloyal to our Constitution" and a "disgrace to our nation."

At The Federalist Society conference in November, then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche declared that the Trump administration was at “war" with "activist judges," which apparently means any judge who rules against it.

After his Senate confirmation as attorney general, Blanche insisted the Justice Department does "respect the role of the judiciary,” a claim that should be taken with a grain of salt the size of a cantaloupe. The administration's war on federal judges goes on, and DHS is helping wage it.

In his first interview since Chad and Venezuela announced their withdrawals, and since the United States began its campaign against the ICC, Osvaldo Zavala, the Court’s registrar, told EL PAÍS that the institution believes that “defending justice is even more important when doing so is difficult.” “We feel that we are taking blows that are fundamentally aimed at multilateralism and the international rule of law,” he added. To make his point clear, Zavala stressed that the Court’s work “will always be seen from a political perspective, but it is a judicial organization.”

text:
A federal judge in Denver has blocked parts of a new Colorado state law requiring health and safety inspections of centers that detain immigrants.

The GEO Group, which operates the immigrant processing center in Aurora for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, filed a lawsuit seeking to block implementation of HB26-1276, signed into law in June.

Judge Daniel Domenico found that the law singled The GEO Group out as a federal contractor and required it "to violate its contract with the federal government, both grounds for preemption," stating, "Here, GEO has shown that it is singled out for a special bill that applies to no other facility. That other facilities might have some similar regulatory burdens does not change the fact that none of them are required to comply with HB 1276."

"At least some of the burdens of this bill are unique. The requirement of a certain number of unannounced visits, for example, does not appear elsewhere," Domenico wrote. "And the state acknowledges that the penalty scheme is not imposed on other facilities."

State Rep. Lorena Garcia, who represents parts of Adams County, co-sponsored the Colorado law. In July she told CBS Colorado, "We have seen over and over and over again a lack of care of the people who are being held in GEO centers. We have seen repeated attempts from our departments of health to go and investigate, and they're being refused entry."

On Wednesday Attorney General Phil Weiser filed a lawsuit in Adams County District Court asking a judge to compel GEO to comply with a public health order, after tuberculosis was found at the facility in June.

Thursday, Weiser said, "Today's ruling granted the GEO Group a narrow, temporary injunction against one provision of a new 2026 law-not the broad relief it sought-and leaves Colorado's existing public health and safety authority intact. Separately, our lawsuit filed yesterday seeks to enforce that existing authority and require GEO to cooperate with the state's investigation into tuberculosis at the Aurora facility, and we will continue using every available tool to protect the health and safety of Coloradans."

CBS Colorado has reached out to GEO Group for a response and will update this story as soon as one is received.

text:
Minnesota's Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge of the winter and early spring might be over, but a Twin Cities man hasn't stopped tracking deportation flights out of the airport.

By his count, he's documented 5,000 detainees flown out from Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport since November.

"These are mothers who aren't going to be home tonight for bedtime snuggles with their kids," said Nick Benson.

For months, he's spent his afternoons at the airport.

"They're fathers who aren't there to support their families anymore. I've seen men and women who are old enough to be grandparents getting on these flights," he said. "Public attention may have moved on. ICE is still here taking people out of our communities."

Tuesday marked a milestone. Benson says he witnessed the 5,000th detainee boarding a flight to Louisiana.

"That 5,000 doesn't include the thousands loaded onto these flights before we started watching in November," he said.

He and a team of observers built an independent database using publicly available flight information, using known flights to count the number of people boarding these planes.

"We set up the camera, we record them loading and then we head home and put that information in a database. We use that to keep track of people that are loaded and unloaded from each flight," he said.

Benson says he tracks these numbers in person but also uses data from the Department of Homeland Security to confirm his numbers are accurate.

"Our margin of error was at least 1 person per flight," he said.

Benson says families of detained immigrants have reached out to him on the work he is doing.

"This is the only transparency that's available to these families. I've heard from families who have loved ones being put on these flights and they'll say thank you for being there because it shows someone cares about my loved one," Benson said.

Benson says he wants state lawmakers to force the airport to install cameras to document the flights.

Until then, he'll keep taking pictures.

title: ICE agents near Tacoma arrested the wrong guy. They put him in detention anyway
description:
After they pressed him to the ground and handcuffed Velasquez while onlookers recorded video, the ICE agents discovered they had the wrong guy.
Velasquez said he realized the officers were ICE agents when he saw their uniforms, but he said they never identified themselves to him.
Attorney says ICE agents lied in arrest report Klein, 73, has filed hundreds immigration-related cases in Western Washington.
He described the video of his client’s arrest as “horrific” and referred to the ICE agents as fascists.
Lopez said it is obvious to her that ICE agents racially profiled Velasquez.
text:
Outside a Lakewood barber shop last month, a 23-year-old man was sitting in his car before his work shift when he was surrounded by other vehicles. ICE agents — some masked and some not — descended upon his car and yelled commands at him that he didn’t understand, then smashed his window and pulled him out.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were on the hunt the morning of July 17 for a Mexican citizen who drove a gray Volkswagen GTI and had a final order for his removal from the country, according to an arrest report. The man they’d approached, Moises Velasquez, was sitting in the same kind of car and allegedly matched their target’s description.

After they pressed him to the ground and handcuffed Velasquez while onlookers recorded video, the ICE agents discovered they had the wrong guy. Velasquez was Venezuelan, and contrary to what the agents wrote in their arrest report, he had employment authorization and an immigration hearing scheduled for December.

“I told them that I was not violating any laws here in this country, and I was just waiting for my hearing to come,” Velasquez said in an interview Thursday, through an interpreter. “I saw that they didn’t care.”

The officers arrested Velasquez, took him to Tukwila to be processed at ICE’s Seattle Field Office and then detained him at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

Velasquez was released Wednesday on the order of U.S. Magistrate Judge S. Kate Vaughan, who found his arrest unlawful and said the facts of his case indicated an “egregious” level of carelessness by the officers.

Vaughan wrote that Velasquez was approached merely because of his “alleged resemblance” to the officers’ actual target while he sat in a vehicle of the same make and model of the car they were looking for. There was no indication they took basic measures like running his license plate to see if it matched the target’s vehicle.

“Upon discovering Petitioner was Venezuelan, and not their intended Mexican target, officers nonetheless proceeded to detain him based only on records pulled while in the field,” Vaughan wrote. “The officers appear to have drawn a legal conclusion from their review of those records, which turned out to be factually baseless.”

Attorneys representing the government in Velasquez’s habeas corpus case did not respond to a request for comment Thursday.

Tacoma man recounts unlawful arrest by ICE agents

Through the interpreter, Velasquez told The News Tribune in an interview that the morning of his arrest started out as an ordinary day. He arrived to work at the barber shop early, and he was on a call with his wife.

“As I am trying to just get out of my car, I notice a car blocked my door, and an agent got out aggressively, coming towards me and yelling,” Velasquez said. “I closed my door, and I locked it.”

Velasquez said the agent asked him to open the door, and he asked if there was a reason.

“He didn’t give me a reason, so I just stayed there, and he continued to demand that I open the door, but I didn’t, and then he broke it,” Velasquez said.

Velasquez said he moved to the passenger seat, and the agent reached through the broken window to unlock the door. He said the agent grabbed him. Video taken by a bystander that was shared with The News Tribune showed four officers on the passenger side of Velasquez’s car yanking on him. More officers were at the driver’s side and rear of the vehicle.

“They all started pulling me,” Velasquez said. “Some of them grabbed my feet, my hands, my head. They were just, you know, pulling, trying to pull me out of that vehicle.”

Video showed the ICE agents immediately pull Velasquez to the ground on his stomach, where two officers got on top of him. Velasquez said they had their legs behind his head and on his back. He said being pushed down busted his lip, and he had blood in his mouth.

Velasquez said he realized the officers were ICE agents when he saw their uniforms, but he said they never identified themselves to him.

In an 11-second video of Velasquez’s arrest shared with The News Tribune by his attorney, Bart Klein, Velasquez can be heard screaming over and over. Velasquez said Thursday that he was asking for help in Spanish and English. He can also be heard yelling, “familia.”

“I had told them … ‘Hey, brother, my wife is about to give birth. I have family,’ but they didn’t care,” Velasquez said through the interpreter.

Attorney says ICE agents lied in arrest report

Klein, 73, has filed hundreds immigration-related cases in Western Washington. He described the video of his client’s arrest as “horrific” and referred to the ICE agents as fascists. He said he didn’t know what else to call them.

“I don’t think they even cared,” Klein said. “These are like wolf packs. They’re picking up every Venezuelan out there.”

Klein said ICE’s claim that his client matched their target’s description was a lie meant to justify their “attack.” The arrest report said that Velasquez “freely admitted” to being in the country illegally. Velasquez disputed that.

“On the contrary, I told him, ‘Hey brother, I am here, I have my Social Security card, I have my work permit and my driver’s license. You can check if you’d like to verify.’”

The arrest report also claimed that Velasquez had never advised the government of a change of his address “in violation of his conditions of release.”

According to Vaughan’s Aug. 19 order, the government later conceded that it had no evidence that specific conditions were imposed on Velasquez’s release.

Velasquez applied for admission to the United States in September 2023 in Brownsville, Texas, according to court documents in his habeas corpus case. He had secured an appointment through CBP One, a Biden-era government app that helped migrants legally enter the country, and was granted parole. According to Vaughan’s order, he has no known criminal history.

ICE’s arrest report also claimed that based on its findings that Velasquez was in violation of his conditions of release, an Enforcement Removal Operations supervisor issued an arrest warrant.

Klein said the document was created after Velasquez’s arrest. He said Department of Homeland Security regulations require ICE to have lawful authority at the moment of the arrest, and a warrant created after the fact can’t retroactively justify it.

Velasquez came to the U.S. with his wife. He had a friend in Seattle, and with the help of some volunteers at the southern border, he took a bus to California and then a plane to Seattle. He moved to Tacoma and later pursued an asylum claim and work authorization.

Being a barber is his dream, Velasquez said, and that was what he hoped to do in Tacoma. Although he missed nearly a month of work due to his detention, Velasquez said he expected to return to work Monday.

Velasquez provides for both his mother, who lives in Venezuela, and his wife. He said his arrest and detention made him fearful that he would not be able to support them.

His wife was eight months pregnant at the time of his arrest. He shared a photo with The News Tribune that shows he and his wife looking at images from an ultrasound of the boy when his wife was four or five months pregnant. Sitting in a car with their backs to the camera, baseball caps on each of their heads read, “Dad” and “Mom.”

“I didn’t want to leave behind my son, his mom,” Velasquez said. “You know, if I was taken from this country, especially because I was the main breadwinner of the home, I didn’t want to just leave them hanging.”

Velasquez did not miss the birth of his child, but Vaughan said his client’s detention caused him to miss the opportunity to support his partner, and that his “baseless and unlawful deprivation of liberty” was an irreparable injury that was not compensable with money damages.

During his detention at the Northwest ICE Processing Center, Velasquez said, the facility added bunk beds outside the cells that doubled the capacity of the area he was in from 60 to 120. He said it felt overcrowded.

Velasquez said there was no privacy in the facility, his laundry sometimes came back still smelling bad, and his mattress felt like he was sleeping on the metal below it. Some of the food — particularly when the facility served chicken, he said — was inedible or flavorless.

“They had it there stored for about three weeks, and they tried to reheat it, and we tried to eat it, but it was so dehydrated that it was very hard to eat,” Velasquez said.

On Wednesday, Velasquez said a guard informed him that he was being released. He said it caught him by surprise, and he asked why he was getting out.

“He looked at me, he said, ‘I don’t know,’” Velasquez said. “Gave me a bag, and then I kind of gathered a little bit of items that I had there, and then I just went out. I was in shock. I couldn’t believe it.”

Velasquez said a volunteer outside the facility offered to give him a ride home, and he accepted. He said he called his wife about his release.

“It was just very emotional because, you know, she couldn’t believe me, and I was so happy,” Velasquez said. “And that I was going to be able to see her again and to be there for my baby.”

‘Driving while Hispanic’

Klein bemoaned what he believes is an increasing lawlessness in immigration enforcement.

“There’s a rule of law, and that’s our society, so everybody feels safe,” Klein said. “But there’s no reason if you’re a person that got naturalized or a certificate of citizenship that you should feel safe at all.”

Klein was connected to Velasquez through Karla Lopez, a court-certified interpreter who works in Pierce and King counties. She volunteered to assist The News Tribune with interviewing Velasquez on her own time. Her daughter, whose husband works with Velasquez at the Lakewood barber shop, called her the morning of the arrest.

“You can see in one of the videos that they’re going through all his documents from his wallet, and you know, just going through it, and he’s screaming for dear life,” she said.

Lopez said it is obvious to her that ICE agents racially profiled Velasquez.

In September 2025, the Supreme Court’s issued a temporary decision issued that gave federal agents authority to stop people based on apparent race or ethnicity, their accent or the type of work they do. According to The New York Times, the lawsuit that led to the decision and similar cases are working their way through lower courts.

“There’s so many videos out there of people that are U.S. citizens are getting pulled over,” Lopez said. “They get pulled over driving while Hispanic, right?”

Velasquez said dealing with an ICE officer is a difficult situation, but he said he guessed that he was fortunate. He said the video of his arrest showed him trying to not let the officers get to him. Some videos he’s seen show ICE officers shooting people.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday carried out its first deportation flight to Haiti since the Trump administration terminated deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians earlier this year.

The plane, which carried more than 160 people, arrived in the northern Haitian city of Cap-Haïtien, The Associated Press reported. The U.S. has a ban in place on flights in and out of the country’s main airport in the capital city of Port-au-Prince due to ongoing gang violence.

The deportees on this flight included those previously covered under Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a U.S. program that protects from deportation foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country and offers them a pathway to work authorization.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that the Trump administration could end this protection for the around 330,000 Haitians and more than 6,000 Syrians covered by this program.

The administration has looked to terminate deportation protections for migrants from 13 of the 17 countries covered by TPS, arguing that these countries no longer meet the required criteria.

The State Department still lists Haiti as a “Level 4: Do Not Travel” country on its travel advisory website, citing gang-related crime, terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare services in the nation. The department also notes Haiti has been under a national state of emergency since 2024.

Immigration activist groups have warned that people deported to Haiti could face dangerous conditions. The U.N. reported that more than 3,100 people were reported killed and 1,189 others were injured in Haiti from January to June.

Haiti’s Group Supporting Refugees and Returnees warned in a Thursday statement the country was “not ready to receive this number of migrants who were in the TPS program.”

text:
SANTA FE, N.M. — Santa Fe neighbors said they’re on edge after back-to-back days of immigration law enforcement agents preparing for a raid and conducting raids in our capital city.

“It was horrible,” Ray Lievens said. “They shouldn’t take the parents away from the child and just leave the child abandoned.”

“That’s pretty scary,” Louise Garcia said. “Just knowing, you know, they’re around and it’s hitting closer to home.”

Wednesday, at least eight people were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) according to Congresswoman Theresa Leger Fernández (D-NM). Thursday, she confirmed ICE was seen staging at the Food King on St. Michaels Drive.

What we know about Thursday’s ICE presence

The area next to the Food King used to be a K-Mart. Now, it’s believed to be a FEMA headquarters, with the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon claims office right next to it. Signs posted on the door say it’s a government building that isn’t open to the public.

KOB 4 crews saw agents there, but no specific Department of Homeland Security (DHS) or ICE lettering. KOB 4 attempted to confirm if ICE was in Santa Fe Thursday but the agency did not respond to that specific inquiry.

Leger Fernández said she met with impacted families Thursday to learn more because she’s not getting much information from the feds.

She said, to her knowledge, everyone who has been recently arrested is still in New Mexico.

“Do not take them out of New Mexico. Don’t send them away so that they end up in Minnesota and Michigan, somewhere far away, where the family cannot reach them,” Leger Fernández said.

Her team does believe they could be transferred out of New Mexico soon.

Leger Fernández visited the ICE detention facility in Torrance County, a place she says is practically a jail. She said she was denied any ability to talk to detainees there.

What happened Wednesday?

Leger Fernandez says there were eight arrests. Thursday, DHS confirmed only one: Edgar Chacon-Miranda in the La Familia Clinic parking lot.

Witnesses said he was separated from his 11-year-old daughter. His niece, said Chacon-Miranda and his daughter were at the clinic to get vaccines when the girl was interrogated by agents.

“La niña inocentemente contestó y se alteró llorando; luego, los agentes le empezaron a decir ‘Señor Edgar Chacón que se baje o le quebrarános los vidrios,'” Madelione Pernillo said. (The girl innocently answered and then cried as agents began to say ‘Edgar Chacon come out or we’ll break the windows.’)

“Mi prima de once años quedó traumatizada; por las noches se levanta llorando por mi tío,” Pernillo said.

In a statement, Homeland Security said the following:

“On August 19, ICE conducted a targeted enforcement operation and arrested Edgar Chacon-Miranda, a criminal illegal alien. He was arrested inside the parking lot of the La Familia Medical Center Pharmacy after officers observed him park there. Chacon-Miranda’s extensive criminal history includes arrests for battery against a household member, criminal sexual penetration in the second degree, child abuse, and abandonment of a child.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S.”

KOB 4 pulled a criminal complaint from Sante Fe County for Edgar Chacon-Miranda. He was charged with rape, battery and child abuse but all of those charges were apparently dropped.

City officials also said Santa Fe police did not participate in Wednesday’s enforcement activity and reiterated that city resources are not used to identify or apprehend people solely based on immigration status unless required by law.

Another impacted family shares their story

“We are not safe when we have ICE agents surrounding a car with a baby on oxygen in the back seat, and then they take one of the women in the car. That makes our communities less safe,” Leger Fernández said.

The congresswoman said that’s what happened in Santa Fe when ICE agents reportedly arrested a woman. Thursday, a family member said agents gave false information.

“Nos dijeron que iban a quebrar las ventanas, que no importaba lo que hiciéramos; de todos modos, se iban a llevar a mi suegra,” Yajaira Gutierrez said. (They told us they were going to break our windows, that no matter what we did they were going to do it anyway and take my mother-in-law.)

“Todos tienen derechos, pero al parecer en este país no los tienen. Así que lo único que pudimos hacer fue ver cómo se llevaban a un familiar,” Gutierrez said. (Everyone has rights, but apparently in this country they don’t, so the only thing we could do was watch as a family member was taken away.)

Leger Fernández said she has co-sponsored legislation to keep ICE away from churches, health clinics, schools and more.

Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia said the city is pursuing legislation that would prohibit ICE from staging or conducting immigration enforcement operations on city property.

text:
Washington D.C.—Over the last 24 hours, ICE Flight Monitor, housed at Human Rights First, has tracked multiple forced third country transfers from the United States to Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon, Paraguay, as well as flights deporting Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras, and Costa Rica. This represents an alarming escalation of the Trump administration’s cruel and unlawful mass deportation campaign.

On August 20, ICE Flight Monitor tracked an ICE Air Flight that arrived in Monrovia, Liberia, at 12:45 pm local time. This flight, which originated in Alexandria, Louisiana, with a refueling stop in Dakar, Senegal, marks the first forced third country transfer to Liberia under a bilateral agreement with the United States. The flight arrived in Liberia with the first group of 15 third country nationals from the United States, including people from Latin American and Caribbean countries.

After stopping in Liberia, the deportation flight continued on to forcibly transfer third country nationals to Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon, arriving at 8:50pm local time and just after midnight local time on August 21st. More than 60 non-Equatoguinean refugees and torture survivors have been forcibly sent to Equatorial Guinea since November 2025 – upon arrival, they are detained in a decommissioned hotel, where they have been subjected to abuse by guards. Many of those removed to Equatorial Guinea have been sent onward to the very places from which they fled, despite having a grant of protection from a U.S. immigration judge protecting them from removal to their home country.

“Since 2025, ICE Flight Monitor has tracked over 100 flights carrying third country nationals to countries other than their own, and we have witnessed the horrific abuses to which people are subjected upon arrival. In recent months, we have tracked first-time flights to the Central African Republic, Sierra Leone, Dominica and now Liberia,” said Savi Arvey, Director of Policy, Refugee & Immigrant Rights at Human Rights First. “We are extremely concerned about the egregious violations of people’s due process rights when they are summarily removed to a third country; the conditions to which people are subjected upon arrival; and the very real risk people face of being sent onward from those countries to the very places from which they fled.”

###

To speak with Savi Arvey, please contact press@humanrightsfirst.org.

For more information on flight tracking, visit ICE Flight Monitor, which uses publicly available aviation data to track U.S. immigration enforcement flights operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and partner agencies. Founded on the methodology pioneered by researcher Tom Cartwright, the project provides transparent, data-driven reporting to strengthen accountability and inform the public about the human and democratic costs of mass deportation policies.

text:
More than 140 people detained at the ICE facility in Tacoma have ended a nearly weeklong hunger strike over food and medical care.

The hunger strike occurred at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. This most recent hunger strike — the 20th hunger strike that transpired at that facility this year — was spurred by the detainees allegedly being served inedible food, having irregular meal schedules, and being neglected from medical services.

According to The Seattle Times, GEO Group, which owns and operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center, promised new food options and larger portions to end the strike.

At the start of the hunger strike, The Seattle Times reported those in custody suffered from being served food that contained “burned plastic, metal string, rope, splinters, hair, and worms” in addition to inadequate medical care. Additional complaints included unsafe drinking water, black mold, and improperly cleaned laundry.

The hunger strike caused two members of Congress to visit the detention center to see the conditions firsthand. The congresswomen arrived unannounced Saturday, at the same time a protest was happening outside the facility in solidarity with the detainees. The representatives shared that they were allowed to see the kitchen, but not the area where detainees receive medical care.

“They misled us about who was on a hunger strike and what the status of that was,” one representative, Maxine Dexter of Oregon, said, according to KIRO 7.

“It makes it very hard to parse what is actually happening in these facilities when we are hearing separate accounts,” the other representative, Emily Randall of Washington, said.

La Resistencia, a grassroots immigrant-rights organization based in Washington that originated in Tacoma, has been heavily involved in supporting the hunger strike.

“We have been an organization for over 12 years. We have supported, on average, a dozen hunger strikes a year,” Josefina Mora-Cheung, the director of organizing for La Resistencia, said. “This year, this is the 20th hunger strike we are supporting.”

In June, Washington Attorney General Nick Brown joined a coalition of 22 other attorneys general in urging the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE to reverse a policy that ends investigations and public reporting of deaths that occur shortly after people are released from ICE custody. Brown argued the policy that stops investigating and reporting ICE facility-related deaths “reduces the federal government’s accountability for conditions in ICE and its contractors’ facilities and jeopardizes the safety of detainees.”

There are 1,458 people currently detained at the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

This is a developing story, check back for updates

title: Coalition pushes for ICE entrance policy passage in metro Atlanta schools - AJC.com
description:
Amid the start of a new school year and reports of more ICE arrests in Georgia, some community groups are advocating for rules in a few metro Atlanta school districts that would make it tougher for the federal agents to remove a student from a public school.
Jessica Stern, an immigration attorney, parent and policy lead for the Safe Space to Learn Coalition, has been advocating for policies that would require a judicial warrant or court order for agents to enter private areas of a school (such as a classroom or administrative office), question a student or remove them from campus.
It would also require district legal review before access is granted and reaffirms protection of student records under FERPA, the federal student privacy act.

text:
Italy’s operation of migration facilities in Albania has exposed refugees and migrants to arbitrary detention, inadequate healthcare, obstructed legal assistance and possible unlawful deportation, alleges a report by human rights organization Amnesty International released on Thursday, August 20.

The 34-page report utilized desk research conducted from January 2024 to June 2026 to draw its findings. Researchers reviewed official documents, court judgments, parliamentary and ombudsman inspection reports, and material published by NGOs and news organizations. Amnesty also corresponded with the Interior Ministry and interviewed Italian detention ombudsmen, representatives of UNHCR and the International Organization for Migration, and two lawyers representing Gjader detainees. Amnesty did not interview detainees directly because the ministry denied its requests to enter the centers.

Under an agreement signed in 2024, some people rescued at sea by Italian ships are to be taken directly to Albania, where their asylum claims will be processed. Two centers were constructed in Albania for asylum seekers to be processed and detained prior to deportation or sent on to Italy.

Between October 2024 and January 2025, Italian authorities transported 74 people from international waters to Albania in three operations. Twelve people, translating to about 16 percent, were later identified as minors or otherwise vulnerable and sent to Italy. Italian courts declined to validate the detention of the remaining men, bringing the initial transfers to a halt.

October 2024: The Italian navy ship Cassiopea transported to Albania 16 male foreign nationals (10 from Bangladesh and 6 from Egypt),

November 2024: The Italian navy ship Libra transported 9 people (7 of them from Bangladesh and 1 from Egypt)

January 2025: The Italian navy ship Cassiopea transported to Albania 49 male foreign nationals (38 from Bangladesh, 8 from Egypt, 2 from Gambia and 1 from Ivory Coast)

Read Also

EU states press Commission to fund 'return hubs' outside the bloc

Violation of human rights and international law

The report detailed what Amnesty International described as practices that violated the human rights of people intercepted at sea and were inconsistent with international legal obligations.

Endangering people at sea

According to the report, the arrangement of intercepting people in distress at sea and transporting them to Albania placed rescued migrants at additional risk. The voyage required two or three additional days to Shengjin, more than 500 nautical miles from common rescue areas. The organization said such delays prolong survivors’ distress, keep rescue vessels away from the central Mediterranean and conflict with obligations to disembark rescued people promptly in a place of safety.

Gaps in identifying vulnerabilities during the pre-screening process

Amnesty states that screening conducted aboard ships failed to identify some children and people with medical or other special needs. Amnesty said survivors of torture or trafficking and people with mental-health conditions require confidential assessments by specialists, which cannot reliably be provided in the chaos following a rescue onboard crowded vessels surrounded by security personnel.

De facto detention

According to Amnesty International, people rescued at sea and selected for transfer to Albania were effectively confined from the moment they boarded Italian "hub ships," in some cases for up to four days before reaching Gjader. The organization characterized this as "de facto detention" without a sufficient legal basis. Amnesty further argued that, once in Albania, detention was applied routinely rather than after an individualized assessment of whether it was necessary and proportionate.

Weakened access to asylum and legal representation

Amnesty International also argued that the accelerated procedure limited access to asylum and legal representation. According to the report, lawyers were sometimes appointed only hours before hearings and were unable to meet their clients beforehand. Detainees participated remotely from Albania while their lawyers and judges sat in Italy. One lawyer told Amnesty that the video connection showed only the upper half of his client’s body, preventing an assessment of possible injuries or ill-treatment.

Deplorable conditions at detention centers

Amnesty International said monitoring reports described what it called a "security-focused environment" that hindered communication with family members and lawyers and made access to healthcare more difficult. Records cited in the briefing documented dozens of critical health incidents, including self-harm and suicide attempts. Additionally, the report highlighted that the distance from medical services in Italy could worsen psychological and physical conditions.

Deportations as a violation of non-refoulement principle

Amnesty International also raised concerns about deportations carried out directly from Albania. Detainees were allegedly moved from Gjader through Albanian territory to an airport under procedures not regulated by the agreement or its implementing legislation. Limited access to lawyers prevented detainees from raising claims that return would expose them to persecution, torture or other serious abuse, according to the report.

Read Also

'Not our problem…ask the Italians': Albanian PM Edi Rama says of Italian migrant hubs

Lack of transparency

Amnesty International also emphasized how independent monitoring of the operations at the Albanian detention centers has also been restricted. Parliamentary visitors, ombudsmen and civil-society representatives reported difficulties accessing cells, official data and confidential conversations with detainees. Italy’s Interior Ministry repeatedly rejected Amnesty’s requests to visit Gjader, citing security and public-order concerns.

Last month, a delegation of Green politicians from the European Parliament was denied entry to the Italian-run migrant detention center in Gjadër, northwest Albania. It was an unplanned visit made on the sidelines of parliamentarians meeting with environmentalists and civil society leaders protesting the construction of a mega-luxury resort on Sazan Island in the Adriatic Sea off the southwestern coast of Albania.

Amnesty called on Italy to terminate the agreement, return Gjader detainees to Italy and use detention only as a last resort. It also urged other European governments not to reproduce the "return hubs" model.

Under the overhauled European Union Migration Pact, which came into force in June, several countries have expressed their intention to explore outsourcing asylum procedures to third countries outside the EU.

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — A federal contract for an Immigration and Customs Enforcement support center that was previously planned for Adams, Tennessee, now appears to be headed to the Nashville area, though federal officials are not disclosing exactly where the operation will be located.

Federal contract records show the U.S. Dept. of Homeland Security and ICE awarded Alaska-based company Koniag a contract worth up to $63 million to operate a 24-hour support center for local law enforcement agencies that partner with ICE through 287(g) agreements.

The contract lists the facility in the 37214-3749 ZIP code, which includes much of Donelson and the area around Airport Center Drive near Nashville International Airport. However, the exact location remains unclear.

Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell told News 2 the city is aware of the planned support center but has not been given details about where it will be located.

An ICE spokesperson also declined to provide a location, issuing the following statement to News 2:

“ICE will not confirm new or current office locations, as our officers are facing a coordinated campaign of violence against them — including an 8,000% increase in death threats against them and a 1,300% increase in assaults against them. Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests and ensuring we have resources to carry out President Trump’s mission.”

The Nashville-area ZIP code appears to be a recent change.

As recently as last week, the same federal contract listed a ZIP code in Adams, a small community in Robertson and Montgomery Counties near the Kentucky state line.

Local leaders there said they were also surprised by the plans. On Thursday, the legislative office for State Rep. Ronnie Glynn (D-Clarksville) told News 2 Adams, TN was a “misprint on the contract,” and the zip code 37010 is not in consideration.

This support center is the latest example of confusion surrounding ICE operations in TN.

Earlier this year, ICE confirmed plans for a detention facility in Lebanon through an email to News 2. However, several elected officials said they had not been informed of the proposal, and some questioned whether the project was actually moving forward.

At that time, Sen. Mark Pody (R-Lebanon) called the plans “misinformation.”

“I am not going to do a confirmation just on one email,” Pody said in a February 2026 interview with News 2. “We’ve been through this enough that there are sometimes things that are misled or it is not actually a fact.”

The Lebanon detention facility proposal was ultimately scrapped after Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) intervened.

News 2 uncovered similar situations across the country where local officials were kept in the dark, including in Hanover, Virginia; Surprise, Arizona; and Durant, Oklahoma, where News 2 interviewed Mayor Martin Tucker.

“No one ever approached the city directly and still haven’t,” Tucker said in a February 2026 interview with News 2. “We’re just responding to that along with the rest of the community to say that we didn’t think this was a good idea to have within our city limits, and the Choctaw Nation especially didn’t want to have it on their campus, where we’re trying to operate our federal government and carry out the business that we carry out.”

Metro Councilmember Jeff Gregg, who represents much of the Donelson area, said, “Local leaders have been kept in the dark” regarding the announcement.

“I’m working my sphere of contacts to learn the exact location within the 37217 [ZIP] code,” he said in a Facebook post.

News 2 has reached out to Sen. Mark Pody, U.S. Rep. John Rose and Koniag for additional information but had not received responses by the time this article was published.

text:
The ICE officer looked familiar.

As Simin Aroum Shaw sat handcuffed in the back of a gray sedan, she recognized a man in the front seat as one of the hundreds of ICE agents staying at the Marriott hotel she managed in Louisiana.

The 45-year-old Iranian woman had been driving to work that morning in July 2025 when she was stopped by police and detained by three ICE agents. Her son was home with a babysitter.

“I was devastated,” said Shaw, who was among hundreds of Iranians ICE arrested in the weeks after the US bombed Iranian nuclear sites.

She was still languishing in detention when the US launched a full-scale war with the country in February.

The conflict has since provided an unexpected result for some undocumented Iranians: temporary freedom. Federal judges in Louisiana and elsewhere have forced ICE to release detainees from Iran and other regions affected by the hostilities, according to a Bloomberg Law review of habeas corpus petitions filed in recent months.

Judges said that holding detainees with final removal orders more than six months is unconstitutional if ICE can’t deport them anytime soon. They’ve released at least 10 people because of the conflict, including Shaw.

“Given the current war, it is not significantly likely that Petitioner will be removed to Iran in the reasonably foreseeable future,” Kayla Dye McClusky, a magistrate judge in the Western District of Louisiana, wrote in March. She recommended the court release a 58-year-old Iranian who’d been living in the US for more than 26 years, helping raise two stepdaughters with his American wife. “In fact, removal is not even remotely likely.”

The push to release detainees is good, even if temporary, said Ryan Costello, policy director for the National Iranian American Council. The deportation orders are still in place, he said, so the Trump administration could keep targeting Iranians as the war drags on.

“The legal architecture has really eroded here. And so these Iranians are kind of left in limbo,” he said.

ICE directed questions from Bloomberg Law to the press office of the Department of Homeland Security, which didn’t respond.

Decades of Refuge

More than 40 years of severed diplomatic ties between Tehran and Washington made it nearly impossible to deport Iranians without legal immigration status. So many Iranians with deportation orders lived and worked for decades under supervised release in their communities.

Then, early on June 22, 2025, American stealth bombers dropped bunker buster explosives on Iranian nuclear facilities.

Three days after the first bomb, and 1,200 miles from Louisiana, an Iranian auto repair shop owner was arrested outside his home near Baltimore. The next day, another Iranian man living in the country for decades was arrested at his business in Louisiana.

In all, ICE arrested 300 Iranians in June and July 2025, more than triple the number arrested in the previous five months, according to data obtained by the NIAC, the Iranian-American organization.

Among them were students on international visas, Iranians seeking asylum, and those with deportation orders, like Shaw. As a child, Shaw’s family escaped Iran during the Islamic Revolution and built a life as refugees in Arkansas. An immigration judge later revoked her green card after a drug conviction. ICE tried to deport her back then, but Iran wouldn’t issue travel documents.

Shaw’s supervised release order was revoked by ICE the day the bombing started.

No one told her.

She never expected to be detained because she’d complied with the supervision order for years.

But that muggy morning in July, she drove her blue Volkswagen Jetta to work and didn’t make it home. Two of her siblings flew to Louisiana later that day to pick up her son and get her car off the road.

Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney with the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, has represented several Iranians she says were targeted because ICE views them as a security threat.

“It’s just really egregious,” she said. “Because of the nature of the war and the diplomatic issues between us and Iran, there’s a higher level of scrutiny for Iranians.”

Deals

Shaw sat on her bunk bed each night at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, listening as a detention officer read the names on the deportation list. Some women cheered when they heard their names. Others cried when they didn’t. Those leaving were handed a trash bag for their belongings.

Shaw remained locked up far past the six-month limit the Supreme Court usually considers unconstitutional for immigrants with final deportation orders.

Conditions were brutal, she said. It was nearly impossible to get medical care and basic necessities, such as tampons. They gave detainees beans for every meal and usually two slices of bread, turkey bologna, and cheese for lunch.

The facility constantly lost power and water, so everyone was always hot and sweaty. Detention officers threw her into solitary confinement nearly a dozen times for talking back or complaining about the treatment of detainees, she said.

“They treated us like we were in prison,” said Shaw, who said she spent up to two weeks at a time in isolation. “They would put us in solitary using force. They attacked detainees — like grown men that looked like they’re quarterbacks.”

The facility in Basile is a former prison that’s run by The GEO Group, a private prison company that also contracts with ICE.

The GEO Group didn’t respond to questions from Bloomberg Law.

After the surge of arrests, ICE asked Iranian officials at the Iranian interests section at the Pakistani embassy in Washington to issue travel documents to deportees. They didn’t respond to a request for Shaw’s documents.

ICE told the courts that it would soon be able to deport Iranians back to Iran, or to a third country, despite the war.

In September, a flight departed from Alexandria, Louisiana, deporting 50 to 60 people, according to a lawsuit filed by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund. It was part of a deal the US struck with Iran to accept deportations.

“Essentially the Trump administration had to figure out how to deport Iranians because there had never been a deportation flight to Iran under the Islamic Republic,” said Costello, whose organization has been tracking the arrests of Iranians.

ICE made another request to the Iranian interests section for Shaw’s travel papers. No response.

In early November, ICE had Shaw talk on the phone to Iranian officials at the Pakistani embassy to see if that would help.

“They said, ‘I have searched the system. I cannot obtain any documents for you.’ And that’s it,” Shaw recalled.

At least two more charter flights departed with detainees headed to Iran between December and January without Shaw on board.

She spent her days reading law books from the facility library with names such as “Immigration Pleading and Practice” and “Law of Asylum in the United States” to kill time.

She learned she had a good chance to be released under a 2001 Supreme Court decision known as Zadvydas v. Davis. The ruling established that holding immigrants with final deportation orders beyond six months is unconstitutional, unless the agency can show that there’s a “significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future.”

With no lawyers willing to take her case, Shaw challenged her detention by herself. In late February, she filed a habeas petition in the US District Court for the Western District of Louisiana. By then, she’d been detained for more than seven months.

A few days after filing the petition, nuclear negotiations with Iran unraveled and the US and Israel launched a full-scale war against the Islamic Republic — Operation Epic Fury.

Invasion and Release

Despite the ongoing war, and airspace closed in Iran and neighboring countries, some Justice Department lawyers representing ICE argued that the war would merely delay deportations.

But a flight scheduled for the end of March never happened, and the sustained conflict caused the government’s argument to crumble.

DOJ lawyers in California admitted that it was unlikely ICE would be able to deport an Iranian man named Mohammad Yousefi, whose bid for asylum had been rejected. The judge ordered his release.

In April, judges in California and Kentucky had another three people released for similar reasons. Among them was Alireza Anjomshoa, an Iranian man who’d been detained for roughly seven months at a Kentucky jail after an immigration judge denied his asylum application.

“Petitioner has provided good reason to believe that there is no significant likelihood that any detainee — let alone Petitioner specifically — will be removed to a country deemed ‘uncooperative’ with which the United States has no diplomatic relations and is currently engaged in a military conflict,” wrote Claria Horn Boom, US District Court Judge for the Eastern and Western districts of Kentucky. “This is not a case where the parties are simply waiting on travel documents to be issued.”

By April, federal public defenders in Western Louisiana were helping Shaw and some of the other detainees who had flooded the courts with habeas petitions. She took the public defender’s advice and left Louisiana as soon as she was released.

When she walked out of the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center on June 13, she wore the same work outfit she had on when ICE detained her. A friend picked her up and they went to Chili’s, where Shaw indulged on shrimp, steak, and chicken fajitas.

Her brother bought a plane ticket and flew Shaw to Kansas, where she now lives with her father. She checks in regularly with ICE, per the rules of her supervised release. She’s waiting to get permission to work.

“There’s just a lot of uncertainty in my life,” she said. “So they have done more damage than they think.”

Shaw may have been freed from detention, but she lost her home. Her belongings were sold in an estate sale. Gone were the baby boxes she had put together for her two sons with their foot prints and hand prints.

“I can’t ever replace those,” said Shaw, whose eldest son is also an American citizen, now 26 and engaged.

Worst of all, her youngest son is now living more than two-and-a-half hours away with her brother.

“I have never been away from my baby since the day he was born until the day they took me away,” she said, sobbing. “And now we have to think about him. We have to think about his well-being and we just don’t want to move him around anymore.”

Now 10, her son meets regularly with a therapist. Shaw can’t meet with a mental health provider because she doesn’t have health insurance. But her siblings did buy her some sewing equipment to help restart her seamstress business, which has kept her busy as she awaits a work permit.

She doesn’t want her youngest son living with her in case she gets picked up again by ICE.

“They can detain me right now. They can come to my house,” she said. “They can pick me up anywhere I go. They can be watching me right now, to pull me over when I leave.”

She still has a deportation order, after all.

Springfield city leaders say they are aware ICE agents are carrying out arrests in the community.

In a Wednesday press release, Springfield Mayor Rob Rue acknowledged U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are in the city and have told his office they are conducting field enforcement activities in the city, across Ohio and nationwide.

The federal agency also confirmed targeted enforcement activity will continue throughout Ohio.

In his latest statement, Rue said the city is focused on the well-being of all residents, ensuring city services continue to be professionally and consistently provided. Last December, he shared a similar message to hundreds of Springfield residents who gathered at St. John Missionary Baptist Church.

"Springfield, we will continue to advocate for the safety of our citizens and every individual that’s here in our community no matter how they got here," Rue said in December. "It’s a human being issue for me."

This week Rue emphasized the city does not direct nor control ICE enforcement activity. He also urged all citizens to treat each other with dignity and respect.

Springfield Police Chief Allison Elliott said her officers enforce city and state laws. Her department does have partnerships with some federal agencies, however Chief Elliot confirmed it does not have a federal partnership with DHS nor with ICE.

In response to a WYSO inquiry about the Springfield Police department's relationship with ICE, Chief Elliott said "We also do not have a 287(g) agreement with ICE, nor are we pursuing one at this time."

A number of local law enforcement departments have a 287(g) agreement with ICE.

Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act the program allows local law enforcement personnel to perform designated immigration officer functions under federal direction and oversight. Participation by local agencies is voluntary and governed by a signed memorandum of agreement.

There are three ways of participating. The lowest level is jail enforcement. This allows deputized jail and correctional officers to identify, question, and process removable noncitizens who are already in local custody facing an active local or state criminal charge.

Task force enables local police officers to exercise limited immigration enforcement authority during routine daily policing activities (such as traffic stops or checkpoints). They can also directly participate in ICE-led operations.

Finally, a warrant service officer gives trained and certified jail officers the authority to serve and execute administrative ICE warrants on individuals already housed in their detention facility.

text:
Regarding “Can California block new ICE detention centers? This Bay Area county is putting it to the test” (Bay Area, SFChronicle, Aug. 16): There’s no question this crusade has noble objectives, and the cited local concerns are understandable, but what are the consequences if detention centers are blocked?

Immigration and Customs Enforcement will continue to detain immigrants throughout our region, as sadly recounted in the story. If there are no local detention facilities, won’t detainees be sent that much farther from their homes, loved ones and potential support, to jurisdictions where immigration judges might not be as willing to consider asylum petitions?

Evidence suggests detainees do not fare as well under these circumstances, so maybe we should find ways to accommodate the fallout from the Trump administration’s reprehensible immigration policies in our own communities rather than pushing it beyond California’s borders.

Regarding “Aisha Wahab was on track for a big win. Then came the AIPAC money” (Election, SFChronicle.com, Aug 19): The Israel lobby keeps trying to choose our representatives for us. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee spends millions opposing politicians who do not give Israel unconditional support.

In recent elections, AIPAC helped unseat popular Reps. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., among others. California District 14 voters didn’t seem swayed by $6.4 million the group spent on negative ads directed at state Sen. Aisha Wahab’s campaign to replace Eric Swalwell in the House. In Thursday’s special election, Wahab beat her opponent, Melissa Hernandez, whom the Track AIPAC site ranks as the nation’s top recipient of AIPAC funding in 2026.

Ads from Israel’s lobbyists never mention the country or its wars — many Americans oppose those things. Instead, they run the attack ads about unrelated issues and try to flood the zone with money.

I don’t live in Oakland, but I have close friends there, and one of them is thinking about becoming a city police officer. Talking to him about the state of public safety has made the issue more personal for me, knowing I have friends and family there.

What he’s told me matches what’s been reported: The Oakland Police Department is leaning on overtime instead of hiring. Officers logged almost 456,000 overtime hours in 2024.

The department has only 610 sworn officers — below what’s budgeted and about 200 fewer than a study says Oakland actually needs.

My friend isn’t scared of the job. He’s scared of joining a department that’s already stretched too thin, where new officers burn out before they even get settled in.

The city should stop using overtime as a quick fix. It should cap overtime spending and use that money to hire until it hits that recommended staffing level.

If Oakland wants people like my friend to join the force, it needs to fix the job first.

Regarding “Was Palo Alto High mosque field trip proselytizing Islam or educational?” (Letters to the Editor, SFChronicle.com, Aug. 19): Political issues are often complex or multifaceted, but this one is clear-cut and straightforward.

If there is a true educational purpose in understanding another culture, that could be accomplished by visiting nonreligious venues.

A public school field trip to any religious organization is inherently an unconstitutional violation of the separation of church and state. This is simply not a debatable issue.

Regarding “We need to talk about the Bay Area’s city slogans” (Total SF, SFChronicle.com, Aug. 15): Peter Hartlaub’s column was a great read. But how could he miss my favorite city slogan for San Rafael: “The city with a mission.”

text:
FAIR shows state law is unconstitutional

WASHINGTON—The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has filed a brief in the U.S. Supreme Court urging review of a case that puts federal immigration detention in the state of Washington in jeopardy. Washington passed a law that makes immigration detention centers operating under contract with the federal government—and no other detention facilities in the state—subject to potentially-crippling state-imposed standards, inspections, and private lawsuits.

In its brief, FAIR shows that this state law is preempted under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause because it intentionally interferes with the federal program of using contractors to house immigration detainees. Indeed, by authorizing private lawsuits by detainees, the law easily could put the contractor running immigration detention in Washington out of business. And other sanctuary states could pass similar laws, crippling the federal government’s detention program across the country.

“Detention pending removal is vital to immigration law enforcement. Without it, illegal aliens will simply skip their removal hearings,” said Christopher J. Hajec, deputy executive director of FAIR. “We hope the Court sees that intentionally burdening federal enforcement violates the Constitution, reviews this case, and strikes down this attempt by a sanctuary state to hobble Trump’s deportations.”

The case is The GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson, No. 26-71 (Supreme Court).

text:
A top Department of Homeland Security attorney has repeatedly targeted sitting judges on social media over rulings against the Trump administration, according to a new ethics complaint.

Why it matters: Experts say the attacks mark a historic break from professional ethics expectations and could expose judges to violence while undermining public trust in the judiciary.

Catch up quick: Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival has repeatedly used his official government account to name district judges this summer, labeling them the "Worst of the Worst" and accusing them of "judicial sabotage."

Percival's grievances stem from rulings against the administration's push to deport millions of undocumented immigrants.

Nearly 130 former state and federal judges and two watchdog groups filed an ethics complaint with the Florida Bar on Wednesday calling for an investigation into Percival for allegedly violating professional conduct rules.

The intrigue: Attorneys regularly criticize judges for rulings they disagree with.

But they also relinquish some freedom of speech because professional conduct rules restrict them from disparaging judges, Brian Tannebaum, an attorney who represents law firms before the Florida Bar, tells Axios.

Zoom in: "You cannot make reckless statements about a judge," Tannebaum says.

"You can stand outside of the courthouse and say, 'I totally disagree with what this judge did, and we are going to appeal,' … but when you say that a judge is engaging in judicial mutiny, or judicial sabotage, … you must have a good faith basis to make those comments."

Robert Jarvis, a legal ethics expert at Nova Southeastern University, tells Axios that "if Percival really believed that these judges were unfit, he should have filed complaints with their circuit courts," adding that he also could have asked Congress to impeach them.

Threat level: The complaint alleges Percival's comments undermine judicial credibility by suggesting judges trying to do their jobs have violated the law, eroding public trust in the justice system, Jarvis says.

"It may not have been your intention to put out a kill list, but that is effectively what you did," he added, noting that disgruntled Americans upset with the legal system have threatened to attack and even killed family members of justices.

By the numbers: Federal judges have faced 415 threats in 2026 through Aug. 17, according to the U.S. Marshals Service, which provides judicial security.

About 12% of active federal judges — 307 of approximately 2,500 — have been identified as threatened in protective investigations this fiscal year.

The other side: When reached for comment about the allegations, a DHS press secretary referred Axios to a Thursday post from Percival that says he will be nominating retired Florida Supreme Court Justice Peggy Quince, who is leading the complaint, "the Justice Peggy Quince Lifetime Achievement Award for Worst of the Worst Judging."

Percival did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

What we're watching: Tannebaum says he doesn't expect the Florida Bar to open an investigation into Percival because the Bar has previously declined to investigate Trump administration officials, including a previous complaint against former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

"If you're a member of the Florida Bar, then you should be subject to the ethics rules of the Florida Bar," he says. "I'm very concerned about the disparity that's going on right now with bar discipline."

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit this week upheld a ban on immigration-related arrests outside some houses of worship. The ban is temporary, but it will remain in place while a lawsuit over immigration officers’ arrest policies makes its way through the court system. The ruling only applies to the entities named in the lawsuit: six Quaker groups, a Sikh temple in Sacramento, Calif., and the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship, a denomination with 1,400 local congregations.

The case stems from a 2025 memo for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, released just after President Donald Trump took office. The memo rescinded the guidelines of former President Joe Biden’s administration, which directed immigration officers not to arrest people in and near houses of worship unless there was no safe alternative. The appeals court ruled that for now, immigration officers must abide by the older policy.

What was the judges’ reasoning for the decision? Among other considerations, judges said that the new arrest policy already caused some immigrants to stop attending their religious gatherings. All of the congregations that brought the lawsuit argued that communal worship was an important element of their faith. That drop in attendance burdened the religious groups’ right to freely exercise their religion, the judges said.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has detained a "beloved" Springfield pastor Thursday morning, according to a local faith-based organization.

G92, which advocates for their immigrant neighbors, said in a news release that agents detained Gilbert Joubert Adrien at a South Limestone Street gas station Aug. 20.

“The community is really deeply saddened,” said G92 member Marjory Wentworth. “It makes everyone feel even more vulnerable.”

The release did not state Adrien’s church for “security reasons.”

Vilés Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center, said he speaks with Adrien all the time. They share their faith and distribute items to people in Springfield, working together as pastors and community leaders.

"If he is being deported, the congregation will be here terrified and without their leader," Dorsainvil said.

Adrien, 41, is in ICE custody at the Butler County Jail, according to a Department of Homeland Security detainee locator website. The jail also lists him as an inmate.

An estimated 15,000 Haitians living in Springfield were here legally with Temporary Protected Status, a federal designation granted to immigrants from countries facing conditions such as natural disasters or armed conflict, according to an Enquirer report. The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to end TPS in June.

Haitian residents of Springfield have been receiving letters calling them in for appointments at ICE field offices, The Enquirer previously reported. Some have been given ankle monitors, an alternative to detention used by ICE, that restrict them to a 75-mile radius from their home address.

This report may be updated.

text:
HARBEL, Liberia — The United States on Thursday carried out its first deportation under an agreement for Liberia to accept up to 1,200 people who are not from the West African country, one of the Trump administration’s largest efforts yet to deport people to countries other than their own.

The 20 deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia.

Deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean, according to Liberian Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah. Liberian Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh has said they can seek asylum in Liberia if they wish.

00:31

Judge dismisses criminal case against Kilmar Abrego Garcia

00:0000:00

The U.S. State Department declined to answer questions about the Liberia agreement, but said that implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority.” It said it was “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security.”

The U.S. Homeland Security Department declined to confirm Thursday’s deportations “for operational security reasons” and referred additional questions to the State Department.

Third-country agreements are often shrouded in secrecy. Migrants have been deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

The Trump administration struck agreements with at least 35 countries to deport people who are from other countries, including Liberia and 13 others in Africa, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a partnership of Refugees International and Human Rights First that relies on public records requests, news reports and other sources. More than 23,000 people have been deported to 26 countries under the agreements.

The U.S. State Department previously announced that Liberia agreed to accept deportees who are not from Liberia. But a six-page agreement reached in September 2025 and posted on its website does not say how many or from which countries.

In October, Liberia offered to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia of El Salvador, who was mistakenly deported to prison in the Central American country. Blocked from sending him to his native country, the Trump administration has vowed to send him to a third country, including Liberia.

Abrego Garcia has said he would agree to be deported to Costa Rica, which has said it will accept him. But the government has so far declined to send him there. Abrego Garcia is fighting deportation to Liberia in a federal lawsuit in Maryland.

title: A quiet channel between ICE and Iran shaped deportation flights, newly released emails show
authors: Safiyah Riddle, California. mailto, apnews.com, safiyah-riddle
description:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — U.S. immigration officials worked with Iran to deport Iranians in 2025, newly released emails show, revealing a working relationship between the U.S. and Iranian governments despite tensions mounting between the countries.
Iranian officials were still making requests the day the flight departed, although one official wrote that those requests were denied.
