text:
In May, a southwestern Idaho probation officer emailed immigration authorities about a man she would meet the next day for his regular check-in.

“His meeting has not changed and he is expected to be here tomorrow morning at 7:30 am,” Norma Naranjo, a senior probation officer for Canyon County’s misdemeanor probation department, wrote in a May 13 email to six Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

The following day, the man arrived a few minutes early to his appointment, and Naranjo sent another email to the agents.

“He is here are you guys on your way?” she wrote.

It is unclear from the emails, which are heavily redacted, if ICE agents detained the man at his probation appointment.

Naranjo’s messages are among over 140 emails between Canyon County probation officers and ICE agents, obtained by InvestigateWest, from May to July 2026. They show how the probation department has recently coordinated with ICE’s Boise office, including by combing through its case files to compile a list for ICE of foreign-born people on probation, apparently without validating that those people are in the country illegally. People born outside the U.S. include individuals with green cards or pending asylum applications and naturalized U.S. citizens.

While Idaho law enforcement agencies have long worked with federal immigration agents to detain undocumented immigrants who are in jail or serving their sentence on probation, immigration attorneys and advocates are concerned that Canyon County’s “foreign born list” could lead to probationers with legal status getting detained, at a time when ICE agents have arrested U.S. citizens, people with pending green card applications and people with pending asylum claims.

Jeff Breach, the director of the county’s Misdemeanor Probation Department, declined to be interviewed for this story. In an email response to a list of questions, he said the list includes “individuals whose place of birth is a foreign country — and can also include individuals that have been previously flagged with an immigration hold.”

“Verifying and determining legal presence/status, along with any related enforcement, is within the purview of federal authorities,” Breach added.

ICE has requested a list of people that could be in the country without authorization “typically on an annual basis and across administrations,” Breach said. Steve Cushman, director of constituent services for Canyon County, said he didn’t know exactly when “those lists were first requested and provided, but it is my understanding that it goes back as far as the Obama administration.”

Breach said the probation department, which supervises misdemeanor offenders within the county, cooperates with ICE the same as it would any local or state law enforcement agency, by providing them “information to carry out their lawful duties.”

The county has faced criticism before for its efforts to help ICE detain people. In 2019, the Idaho Press, a local newspaper that covers the Boise area, reported the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office had a policy where staff were instructed to notify immigration officials of “all foreign born inmates” who were booked into the jail. Some of the people they flagged were U.S. citizens, according to the Idaho Press. The sheriff’s office is also facing a lawsuit from the ACLU of Idaho alleging the county and other agencies that participated in an October 2025 ICE raid racially profiled Latinos at a horse race track for immigration enforcement when they detained them, regardless of their immigration status.

Nikki Ramirez-Smith, an immigration attorney with Ramirez-Smith Law in Nampa, Idaho, said the county’s decision to compile and send ICE a list of foreign-born people on probation is “an invasion of privacy.”

“It’s one thing to know that someone is undocumented, it’s another thing to just start targeting every single person who was born in another country,” she said.

The “foreign born list”

On June 3, Naranjo emailed five ICE officers that she would speak to Breach about “the foreign born list.”

“We are working on a procedure to keep a list current for your agency,” Naranjo wrote. “I will get back to you on this as soon as we figure something out.”

Two days later, Breach sent an email to his staff:

“ICE has requested a list of offenders who are in the country illegally,” he wrote. “I need you to go through your caseload this month and send me a list of names of offenders who you believe are in the country illegally. I’ll review the names and put together a list that can be sent to ICE so that they can look into if the person is in the country illegally and if they want to take any action.”

Although most of the over 400 pages of emails obtained by InvestigateWest from May 1 to July 10 are heavily redacted — emails from immigration authorities appear to be redacted entirely — they show how probation officers used information in their case files to compile the list.

“That’s everyone in my cabinet that filled out (an) intake form and stated not born in US,” wrote Brandon Black, a Canyon County probation officer, in an email back to Breach on June 8.

Another officer, Justin Donovan, told Breach that he only identified one person under his supervision who “may be here illegally.” That man “only had an ID from Mexico during his last arrest,” Donovan said.

Naranjo, Black and Donovan did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Canyon County released to InvestigateWest a redacted version of the list, which contains information for 82 people on probation in Canyon County. It identifies the charges that people were placed on probation for, but blacks out names, addresses and dates of birth. Over half, or 54%, of the people on the list were on probation because of driving under the influence. Five people were on probation for drug-related crimes and nine people for disturbing the peace. Only seven people were identified as having an ICE hold, meaning ICE had already identified them for potential deportation.

Between May and July, the emails show probation officers were regularly notifying ICE agents about the dates and times that certain probationers would be at their office. In some instances, probation officers asked ICE if a person who had missed check-ins was in their custody. On two occasions, officers emailed agents right before and during the appointments to verify they were coming to apprehend a probationer. One probation officer also gave ICE agents the home address and make, model and license plate of a probationer’s car.

Breach estimated that in the last three months, ICE agents have “been present” at one or two probation appointments per month.

“All the law enforcement agencies we work with prefer to meet with offenders up in the office due to it being a controlled environment, which means it is safer for the offender, the officer, and the public,” he wrote. “There is an expectation from law enforcement agencies and the public that probation officers work cooperatively with law enforcement to ensure the safety of all parties involved.”

Asked whether the department is concerned that citizens or others with legal status might be included in the list, Breach referred to a previous statement that verifying a person’s status “is within the purview of federal authorities.”

Alycia Moss, an immigration attorney with Fennemore Law in Coeur d’Alene, said ICE agents should know if someone on the list is deportable or not, but she is still concerned they could mistarget someone on the probation department’s list.

“ICE may still target someone if they think the conviction is a deportable or removal offense even if they (have legal) status,” she said. “Sometimes, ICE doesn’t get that right.”

In Oregon, ICE agents arrested Juanita Avila, a 47-year-old legal permanent resident, last November. Last July, ICE agents also arrested and detained Mahdi Khanbabazadeh, a 38-year-old father who was married to a U.S. citizen and had a pending green card application, while he was dropping his child off at preschool in the Portland area.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security recently formed a new unit dedicated to reexamining immigrants who have green cards, according to the New York Times.

Ramirez-Smith, whose law firm is located in Nampa, Canyon County’s largest city, wasn’t surprised by how closely the Canyon County probation department was working with ICE. In previous years, Ramirez-Smith said she could often negotiate and get her client out of detention. But now ICE is quickly moving detainees out of state, leaving her little time to get clients out of detention.

“I’m getting a lot of people picked up from probation to the point now where if they have probation, I just prepare a habeas (petition) just to get ready,” Ramirez-Smith said, referring to the process to challenge the legality of someone’s detention.

Canyon County has been a recent target for immigration authorities

Canyon County is Idaho’s second-largest county by population, where Latinos make up about 27%. The county is an agricultural hub and one of the top five seed-producing regions in the world. Farms there rely heavily on an immigrant workforce.

The county was also the location of a high-profile immigration raid in Wilder last October, where over 100 people were detained at a horse racetrack, a popular gathering spot for Latino families in the area. According to witnesses of the raid, local police and Canyon County sheriff’s deputies assisted ICE agents by zip-tying children and detaining people without asking about their immigration status.

The raid shocked the community, leading to low attendance at the Wilder School District the day after the raid, according to reporting from the Idaho Statesman. The ACLU of Idaho also filed a lawsuit on behalf of three Latino families and their children, who are U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents, who were detained for four hours, alleging federal and local law enforcement racially profiled them during the operation.

Beyond the raid, Canyon County law enforcement has for years helped ICE by agreeing to hold people in jail for up to 48 hours past their release date. In 2019, the Idaho Press reported that Canyon County jail staff emailed ICE agents when they had booked someone into jail who they suspected was undocumented — in several cases flagging people who were U.S. citizens and holding them after they had posted bond. If inmates served jail time and posted bond, staff were instructed to contact immigration officials, the newspaper reported.

That year, Canyon County faced three lawsuits from people who alleged they were illegally held in jail, despite posting bond, because the county refused to release them due to their undocumented immigration status. The county settled with at least one man for $13,000.

In an email, Breach said the probation department does not have a written policy addressing how to interact with ICE, but instead follows a “long-standing practice” of cooperating with federal law enforcement agencies. He said the department has worked with immigration authorities since at least 2008.

ICE has relied on county and state probation departments across the country to coordinate arrests of undocumented people, according to the Immigrant Legal Resource Center. Many states have passed laws barring this type of cooperation between probation departments and ICE, including Colorado and New Mexico, after probation departments were found to be flagging ICE agents about the appointment times for undocumented people.

Idaho Gov. Brad Little encouraged state and local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration agents in an executive order last year. Eleven Idaho law enforcement agencies have signed up to participate in a program to help with immigration enforcement, known as the 287(g) program, with some agencies receiving tens of thousands of dollars in incentive payments for their cooperation.

In neighboring Washington and Oregon, immigration lawyers say the level of coordination happening in Canyon County would never fly, because of the states’ sanctuary laws barring local and state law enforcement from working with federal immigration agents to detain and deport people.

“In Washington, this would never be allowed because the state has protections in place to prevent this kind of information sharing,” Aaron Korthuis, an attorney with the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, said in an email. “In Idaho, it’s permitted (and likely even encouraged). I think it is simply another tactic ICE has developed to identify easy and low-risk environments for the agency to detain people.”

text:
If ICE were to sign "surge parking" leases in Boston, it would "constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation," Mayor Michelle Wu said.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu sent a letter to the city’s parking garage and lot owners Tuesday, asking them to reject efforts from the Trump administration to lease “surge parking” facilities for ICE. The move prompted a sharp reaction from the Department of Homeland Security, which called Wu’s actions “unhinged.”

Wu’s letter is a response to a “sources sought notice” posted by DHS to a government procurement website late last month. It seeks “sources capable of providing surface and/or structured vehicle parking spaces in the vicinity of existing or planned ICE facilities.”

Boston is one of 14 cities included in the notice. Federal officials are apparently interested in leasing 249 parking spaces in the city for ICE operations.

Wu, a frequent adversary of federal immigration authorities, said over the weekend that the city would be contacting private property owners directly to dissuade them from engaging with the DHS request. She also said that the city would submit a Freedom of Information Act request to ICE in order to identify those that submitted responses to the notice.

Wu followed through with both actions Tuesday.

“Were ICE to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region,” she wrote in her letter.

Wu accused the Trump administration of using ICE operations to “attack” otherwise peaceful American cities. She referenced operations in Maine and Texas, where ICE agents shot and killed men earlier this summer.

“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,” Wu wrote to the parking lot owners.

In a social media post Tuesday morning, DHS officials said Wu was targeting private property owners instead of working to remove criminals from Boston.

“She knows she has NO authority to block us from using private property,” DHS wrote. “So she’s hunting down private property owners and threatening them for working with ICE — because she’d rather intimidate law-abiding Bostonians than get criminal illegal aliens OFF the street.”

After the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota earlier this year, Wu prohibited ICE from using municipal property to stage operations and directed local police to investigate all allegations of criminal conduct, even by ICE agents.

The FOIA request submitted by the city asks ICE to provide all submissions the agency received in response to its “surge parking” notice.

As ICE ramped up operations in and around Boston last summer, the Wu administration began filing FOIA requests asking for information about people being detained in Boston. ICE has not been forthcoming in providing this information, Wu has said.

Gov. Maura Healey signed legislation earlier this month that restricts ICE operations in schools, hospitals, and courthouses. Healey has also limited civil immigration enforcement in nonpublic areas of state buildings and barred state agencies from entering into agreements with DHS that allow local authorities to conduct immigration enforcement.

Wu urged the parking lot owners to reject ICE’s proposition by advocating for a citywide response in her letter.

“In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity,” the mayor wrote. “When government, business, and community leaders stand together, we protect public safety and advance the economic vitality that makes Boston thrive.”

text:
FAIR shows they remain detained by their own choice

WASHINGTON—The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has filed a brief in the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, sitting en banc, in three cases about whether illegal aliens, subject by statute to mandatory detention pending their removal from the United States, nevertheless have a right, under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, to a bond hearing, and possible release into this country, pending that removal.

Under a statute, aliens who are in this country but have not been lawfully admitted are to be removed from the United States. Congress made their detention without bond while their removal is pending mandatory, to prevent them from disappearing into the country before their removal.

In its brief, FAIR shows that, to make out a due process claim, one must be deprived of what courts call a “fundamental liberty interest.” But aliens the law says have no right to be in the country at all have no fundamental liberty interest in moving about the country freely. Nor do they have a fundamental liberty interest in being released into the United States, as opposed to their home country.

Also, FAIR points out that detained aliens may leave detention at any time, merely by ceasing to contest their removal and going back to their home country. Since they are not detained against their will, they are not deprived of any due process right to release.

“Nothing forces illegal aliens to stay in this country pending their removal by the federal government,” said Dale L. Wilcox, executive director and general counsel of FAIR. “They can leave detention at any time simply by not contesting their removal and going home. We hope the court sees that it is not the United States that deprives these aliens of their liberty, and upholds the statute.”

The cases are Rodriguez v. Ortega, No. 26-50183, Angel v. Mullin, No. 26-50219, and Alvarado v. Vergara, No. 26-50221 (Fifth Circuit).

text:
The Treasury Department and the IRS on Wednesday proposed stronger restrictions on certain immigrants’ ability to claim refundable tax credits — the latest in the Trump administration’s efforts to curb access from non-U.S. citizens to federal benefits.

The department suggested the refunded portion of four tax credits be classified as “federal public benefits,” potentially disqualifying noncitizens with Social Security numbers who are eligible to work in the U.S. The department said the move would address “abuse” in the tax refund system.

If implemented, the joint proposal may prevent immigrants residing in the U.S. under temporary protected status (TPS) or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) from collecting certain tax breaks.

The proposed change would apply to the adoption tax credit, the child tax credit, the American opportunity tax credit and the earned income tax credit, according to the Treasury.

“Under President Trump, the days of illegal aliens collecting taxpayer-funded benefits are over. The federal law is clear, and Treasury is enforcing it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Wednesday press release.

“American taxpayers should not be forced to foot the bill for benefits going to those who are barred by law from receiving them,” he continued. “These proposed regulations end the abuse, protect the integrity of the tax system, and put Americans first.”

Wednesday’s proposal is not the Trump administration’s first attempt to leverage the tax system in efforts to curb unauthorized immigration. In February, a federal court ruled against attempts to block the IRS from using tax data to identify immigrants lacking permanent legal status and share results with the Department of Homeland Security.

This new Treasury proposal also aligns with guidance shared by the Justice Department last year for interpreting a 1996 budget law, which is currently under litigation.

The Justice Department’s opinion memo argued some non-U.S. citizens’ use of government benefits “contradicts the textually expressed congressional policy that aliens must not rely on taxpayer support or burden the public benefits system.”

The Treasury Department estimated in Wednesday’s release that this move could save between $700 million and $2.6 billion annually

According to Social Security Administration data, around 200,000 to 700,000 taxpayers — with less than 3 percent of those claiming this tax benefit — could be impacted by this change, the department wrote in its proposal.

title: Independent ICE flight tracker marks 5000th detainee flown out of MSP
authors: Madison McVan, Max Nesterak, Alyssa Chen, Nicole Neri
description:

text:
On the hot tarmac of Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport on Tuesday afternoon, a man in a gray sweatsuit slowly climbed the steps to board an Eastern Airlines flight bound first for Alexandria, Louisiana, then El Paso, Texas.

He was chained at the ankles, wrists and stomach — and he was the 5,000th immigrant detainee shipped out of Minnesota’s flagship airport since November, according to independent tracking.

Nick Benson watched from the top floor of an airport parking garage, two cameras with zoom lenses trained on the plane, recording video as 14 men and two women boarded the flight in chains.

One of the women struggled up the stairs, leaning on a worker in a bright yellow vest for support. This was the 147th “ICE Air” flight — planes shipping detainees on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement — Benson had observed since he began tracking deportations in November.

The database he built late last year has provided some of the most accurate, timely information to the concerned public during Operation Metro Surge, which the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has described as the largest immigration enforcement operation in U.S. history. (Benson later checked his data against data obtained from Homeland Security by the Deportation Data Project and estimated that his margin of error was fewer than one person per flight.)

In January and February, at the peak of the federal operation, Benson watched three flights per day take off, filled with detainees, typically bound for large detention centers in the South.

Since Operation Metro Surge wound down, ICE is back to a regular twice-a-week flight schedule, Benson said. His work remains the same: tracking flight schedules using open source information, lugging his camera equipment to the top of the parking garage, filming as the detainees are brought up the stairs onto the plane, then heading home to update his database.

Benson ran for a seat on the Burnsville City Council, but lost the election on Aug. 11. It’s a good thing he lost, he said — he was spread too thin.

“I ran as myself, and if the electorate didn’t like it… that was their decision,” Benson said.

Benson is a member of Minnesota 50501, the state chapter of the progressive organization behind the massive “Hands Off” and “No Kings” protests that emerged during President Donald Trump’s second term. The organization pays for his parking garage fees.

Minnesota 50501 is among the nearly 20 organizations investigated by the Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Department of Justice of being involved in a conspiracy to impede and assault federal agents during Operation Metro Surge.

An undercover agent attended a meeting of Minnesota 50501 at Augsburg Park Library in Richfield on Feb. 2. Around 60 people were in attendance, including Benson. The undercover agent’s report — included in a court filing in the case of 15 Minnesotans charged in the alleged conspiracy — mentions volunteers handing out whistles and literature about various roles available to people who wanted to protest ICE.

It also describes a “heavy-set male” — name redacted — who “introduced himself as monitoring deportation flights leaving the Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport.”

Benson, according to the agent, “bragged that there were only 19 people that got onto deportation flights yesterday, when in the past there were hundreds per day.”

Benson said it was strange to see himself described by an undercover agent, and that other than the use of the word “bragged,” the notes were accurate.

“There was nothing nefarious going on there,” Benson said. “It’s all just so profoundly ridiculous, that they’re going after us.”

Benson has no plans to stop monitoring the flights — unless the state Legislature passes a bill to mandate that the boarding process for immigration flights be livestreamed and publicly available. (This already occurs at Seattle’s Boeing Field.)

Benson’s state representative, Rep. Kaela Berg, DFL-Burnsville, introduced a bill in the 2026 legislative session that would do just that. The bill gained the maximum number of co-sponsors — 35 DFL lawmakers signed on — but it didn’t advance.

Benson has heard from the families of people who were detained, who were grateful that someone cared enough to watch over the immigrants as they were shuttled to camps before, in most cases, being deported.

“It’s the most important work I’m ever going to get a chance to do,” Benson said. “And I’m looking forward to not having to do it anymore.”

Outside on the tarmac, workers packed lengths of chains into the back of the convoy vans to be used on the next round of detainees.

text:
By Anastasia Mungaray

LOS ANGELES — A federal judge on Monday appointed two independent monitors with broad authority to investigate whether U.S. Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement are complying with the Flores Settlement Agreement and court orders governing the detention and treatment of children in federal immigration custody.

Chief U.S. District Judge Dolly M. Gee appointed Andrea Sheridan Ordin as special master and Dr. Paul Wise as independent monitor, giving them authority to examine government records, conduct visits to detention facilities and hotels, and interview federal employees, contractors, detained individuals and their families.

The Flores Settlement Agreement, reached in 1997, established requirements for the federal government regarding the detention, treatment and release of children in immigration custody.

Human Rights First explains, “The government is required to release children from immigration detention without unnecessary delay,” and “place children in the ‘least restrictive’ setting appropriate to their age and any special needs … and implement standards relating to the care and treatment of children in immigration detention.”

Ordin and Wise will remain in their positions for an initial term of 12 months.

This term may be extended if they or any parties involved seek an extension based on specific and ongoing concerns regarding the defendants’ compliance with the issues identified.

Barring the continuation of serious problems, an extended term is expected to last no longer than 36 months in total.

Ordin and Wise must submit a draft Monitoring Protocol within 15 days of their appointment, and the initial monitoring term begins following the finalization of the protocol.

The special master and independent monitor will not only monitor the length of time children are held in hotels but also the cumulative time a child may spend in an unlicensed facility before and after detention at Dilley detention centers in Texas.

Additionally, the monitors will verify data regarding time spent in custody and oversee the systems used by the Department of Homeland Security to track and calculate time in custody.

Ordin and Wise will also monitor conditions for compliance with the FSA and the court’s orders, including adequate temperature controls in the Rio Grande Valley, El Paso and San Diego, adequate sleeping conditions in San Diego and access to soap in the San Diego sector, including the Otay Mesa Port of Entry. Conditions at Dilley, including adequate access to medical care and provision of notice of Flores rights, will also be monitored.

Ordin and Wise will have access to ICE and CBP documents and records, along with the authority to make announced and unannounced visits to detention centers and hotels. They may also conduct interviews with CBP and ICE employees, contracted employees, detainees and detainees’ families.

Under the protective order, they are required to ensure that all information accessed and collected remains private and secure.

At a minimum, quarterly reports are to be prepared for and filed with the court and provided to the parties, evaluating the compliance of CBP and ICE. The reports will also recommend remedies for any violations observed.

Any observations are to be promptly reported to CBP, ICE and government attorneys. Issues that remain unresolved may be escalated to juvenile coordinators and counsel.

Provided the parties are given notice and an opportunity to respond, the monitors may recommend orders regarding the goals of monitoring, including contempt sanctions, but may not issue orders themselves, nor do they have the authority to intervene in or direct the defendants’ activities.

Ordin and Wise are directed by the court to proceed with all reasonable diligence to carry out the duties assigned to them. They are also to preserve and file materials reflecting essential activities in carrying out their monitoring duties.

text:
California U.S. Sens. Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff plan to investigate why U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents attempted to enter and inspect a Sacramento immigration law firm last week.

The incident, which was first reported by The Sacramento Bee, involved multiple armed ICE officers and the Morris Law Group office in North Natomas. On Friday morning around 9 a.m., at least four agents arrived and told employees of the law firm that they had received a list from Washington, D.C., which listed the building’s address as the primary mailing address for people they planned to arrest.

The ICE officers requested to tour the office for beds and stayed in the parking lot for roughly an hour, but were turned away multiple times after failing to provide a warrant. One ICE agent reportedly told an employee that they could return at 3 a.m. and break windows to enter if they received follow-up orders.

“I don’t put anything past the Trump administration to try to further terrorize immigrants,” Padilla told The Sacramento Bee on Tuesday.

In a written statement on Saturday afternoon, a U.S. Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that ICE officers approached “an unmarked door” and believed it was a “target address.” They departed after learning the address was a law firm, the DHS spokesperson said.

The law firm’s office has text in large bold letters that reads “Morris Law Group P.C.” above the front door. Clients of immigration lawyers also routinely use an office’s address as their mailing address.

The encounter was unusual even with a federal administration that has cracked down on both legal and undocumented immigrants in unprecedented ways. The visit also raised questions among legal experts and elected officials, given that law firm offices hold confidential information about clients and most lawyers are aware that a judicial warrant is needed to enter a house or non-public areas of a business.

“Law firms are sacred spaces where immigrants seek legal protection and exercise their constitutional rights,” said Sacramento Councilmember Lisa Kaplan, who represents the North Natomas area. “They are no backgrounds for political intimidation. Weaponizing federal agencies to bully advocates and scare vulnerable communities undermines justice for everyone.”

Schiff, in a written statement, called ICE’s actions “unconscionable” and said his office would investigate the incident.

“ICE should know they cannot enter private property without a judicial warrant,” Schiff said. “Instead of complying with the law, ICE agents chose to threaten violence against a law firm because of whom they represent.”

DHS has not responded to follow up questions on the incident, including about the alleged list from Washington, D.C., and if the visit was part of a broader operation against law firms.

Padilla said the agency should come forward with that information, if true. He also hoped they were responsive with responding to his request for more information.

“This administration clearly has a credibility problem,” he added.

text:
Liberia will accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the United States in a new agreement announced Tuesday by the African country.

The agreement is one of the largest under the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.

Liberia's Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said the deportees will be received within a year, with the first 20 expected to arrive on Thursday. The 1,200 deportees include Africans, as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of illegal migrants to nearly two dozen countries, with around 10 of them in Africa.

A point of contention in the agreements is that the deportations can include migrants with protection orders from a U.S. immigration judge not to be returned to their home countries over safety concerns. Piah did not say if the deportees had protection orders.

Liberian Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh said the country already screened the list of deportees and that most on the list had immigration violations and related offenses.

Piah said the migrants can seek asylum after their arrival or leave Liberia whenever they want.

Liberia will get support from the U.S. to manage the deportee program, as well as strengthen the migration system, Piah said.

"Liberia’s gesture is entirely humanitarian and in keeping with the country’s longstanding traditions," Piah said. "The government of Liberia intends to provide the transferred persons with the necessary support to seek protection in Liberia and to be safe during their stay here."

Immigration lawyers claim the Trump administration uses the third-country deportations as a loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries, with many migrants being deported to countries they've never been to.

Liberia's President Joseph Boakai was one of five leaders from West Africa who traveled to the White House to meet with President Donald Trump last year.

text:
A large federal contract that had funded the nonprofit legal organizations representing more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children expired on July 31. The end of the contract impacts a nationwide network of nearly 100 legal service providers that help migrant children navigate one of the most complicated legal systems in the country.

This is part of a series of actions the Trump administration has taken to end funding for these legal services. In March 2025, the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) moved to terminate the portion of its contract with the Acacia Center for Justice that funded direct legal representation for unaccompanied children. The government ordered Acacia to stop work, effectively cutting off the network of nonprofit organizations that had been representing children across the country. A federal district court subsequently ordered the government to continue to fund the program because the government had cancelled funding without providing a meaningful alternative for ensuring that children receive counsel.

The administration then sought additional information about the children represented by these organizations, including information that providers argued implicated attorney-client confidentiality, in exchange for payment. By June 2026, the federal government had withheld nearly $65 million for services performed since December 2025. The same federal district court ordered on August 6 that the government pay the nonprofits for their unpaid work.

When the administration allowed the Acacia contract to expire on July 31, it began to look for new providers through noncompetitive processes.

One agreement was awarded to Burke Law Group, a small Houston firm with limited experience in immigration law on August 6. Last week, however, the Burke Law Group withdrew from consideration. On August 7, the administration awarded a noncompetitive contract for up to $244 million to Our Rescue, for legal services for unaccompanied children. Our Rescue’s background raises its own questions about whether it has the immigration-law expertise necessary to represent thousands of children in complex immigration proceedings. ORR has stated that another group with experience providing immigration legal services, the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI), will be providing legal representation to unaccompanied children until Dec. 31.

For an administration pursuing a mass deportation agenda that seeks to maximize arrests and deportations, access to counsel is essential for those navigating the system. Legal representation is a significant indicator of success in immigration court despite noncitizens not having a right to government-funded representation. An American Immigration Council report showed that between FY 2019 and 2024, people without legal representation were overall more than 2.5 times more likely to receive an order of removal than their represented counterparts. For people in detention, that number grew to 10.5 times.

That is precisely why Congress has required the federal government to provide access to counsel to unaccompanied children “to the greatest extent practicable.” Without federally funded legal services, a child is expected to navigate immigration court against government attorneys while trying to understand statutes, regulations, court processes and complicated forms of immigration relief.

The expiration of ORR’s contract with Acacia is the latest chapter in a broader effort by the Trump administration to make it harder for immigrants to obtain legal assistance in immigration court proceedings.

Since the beginning of the Trump administration, it has repeatedly targeted federally funded immigration legal services. In January 2025, the Department of Justice (DOJ) issued stop work orders, which halted four programs that provide immigrants with information about immigration proceedings, referrals to pro bono attorneys, and other assistance. These include the Counsel for Children Initiative, the Legal Orientation Program (LOP), the Immigration Court Helpdesk, and the Family Group Legal Orientation Program. Congress has funded LOP since 2003, including allocating $27.5 million in FY 2026. Twelve nonprofit organizations sued arguing that the government’s actions violated federal administrative procedures and improperly disregarded Congress’s funding requirements.

While the administration rescinded the stop work orders in February 2025, two months later, it moved to terminate the underlying contracts with legal service providers receiving federal dollars to manage these programs. In court documents, declarations confirmed that the DOJ intended to end the Counsel for Children Initiative, the Immigration Court Helpdesk, and the Family Group Legal Orientation Program, while transferring the LOP program, and a similar program for custodians of unaccompanied children, LOP-C, away from civil society organizations with legal representation expertise and moving them “in-house” instead.

Two other legal access programs the administration tried to terminate are being operated under court orders. Those programs are the National Qualified Representative Program for people experiencing immigration court-recognized mental competency issues, and the Legal Access Services for Reunified Families program for family members under a settlement agreement who had been separated during the first Trump administration.

Instead of meeting its obligations by funding critical legal access programs, the Trump administration has repeatedly taken a different path: terminating existing providers, stopping and withholding payments, imposing new demands, and moving toward replacement arrangements with entities with no expertise in representing immigrants through complex legal processes, all with little public explanation. The result is a system in which Congress can appropriate money for legal services, but the administration can undermine the purpose of those appropriations through the contracting process itself.

text:
Where plaintiffs challenging the termination of the temporary protected status designation of South Sudan have moved to amend their complaint to add two new claims, their motion should be denied because the proposed new claims would be futile and unlikely to succeed.

“… On February 12, 2026, the Court postponed the termination determination under 5 U.S.C. §705 on the ground that the Secretary of Homeland Security violated the Administrative Procedure Act (‘APA’), 5 U.S.C. §551 et seq. … Following the Supreme Court’s June 25, 2026, decision in Mullin v. Doe, 146 S. Ct. 2121 (2026), which involved the termination of TPS for Syria and Haiti, the First Circuit summarily reversed the postponement order and remanded for further proceedings. …

“Now before the Court is Plaintiffs’ motion to amend their complaint to add two new claims (Dkt. 94), which were not raised to or addressed by the Supreme Court. Plaintiffs have also renewed their motion for postponement based on the proposed new claims (Dkt. 116). After a hearing on the motion to amend and full briefing, the Court concludes that Plaintiffs’ proposed new claims would be futile and unlikely to succeed. Plaintiffs’ motions therefore are denied. …

“Plaintiffs seek postponement of the termination of South Sudan’s TPS designation based on two new proposed claims: (1) a claim that former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem acted ultra vires in terminating the designation because that authority belongs exclusively to the Attorney General and (2) a procedural due process claim that former Secretary Noem’s alleged failure to consult with appropriate agencies and to publish the true basis for the termination determination deprived Plaintiffs of protected liberty and property interests without adequate process. …

“First, Plaintiffs request to amend their complaint to assert a claim that only the Attorney General, not the Secretary of Homeland Security, has statutory authority to terminate a TPS designation. Defendants argue that the Court is barred by 8 U.S.C. §1254a(b)(5)(A) from reviewing this claim. The Supreme Court has held that §1254a(b)(5)(A)’s ‘judicial-review bar applies to all non-constitutional claims.’ Mullin, 146 S. Ct. at 2137. Plaintiffs nevertheless contend that an ultra vires claim is not governed by this provision. The Court assumes, without deciding, that it has statutory authority to consider the merits of this proposed claim. … Even if such authority exists, the claim is futile and unlikely to succeed. …

“In the Court’s view, the ‘best reading’ of §1103 is the one initially espoused by Defendants. …

“The Court now turns to Plaintiffs’ proposed procedural due process claim. …

“Plaintiffs contend that former Secretary Noem violated their due process rights by failing to consult with appropriate agencies and to publish the true basis for her termination determination in the Federal Register, as required by the TPS statute. In other words, Plaintiffs repackage their previously asserted APA claims — which they concede are not reviewable by this Court in light of Mullin, see 146 S. Ct. at 2133-37 — as constitutional ones under the label of procedural due process. But the Supreme Court rejected materially identical challenges under the APA, and Plaintiffs have no liberty or property interests left other than those provided by statute or regulation based on their individual circumstances through other statutory provisions.”

text:
Silver Spring, MD — HIAS is a plaintiff in a new lawsuit challenging a Trump administration rule that allows asylum seekers to be sent to immigration court without first having an opportunity to participate in an asylum interview. For people fleeing persecution, violence, and other dangers, that interview can be their only opportunity to sit across from an asylum officer and explain, in their own words, why they cannot safely return home.

“U.S. law gives every asylum applicant who is seeking safety the right to tell their story and explain the dangers they faced in their home countries and why it would be unsafe for them to return. The asylum interview is at times the only way ordinary people fleeing persecution have to be heard – to feel that their stories matter. But this rule will deny many people their voice and their due process, and the result will be devastating. People fleeing violence and persecution must be able to find safety, and this country must be able to treat them with respect, compassion, and dignity,” said HIAS President & CEO Beth Oppenheim.

The asylum process can be difficult to navigate, particularly for people who have fled their homes under traumatic circumstances. Many asylum seekers have limited English proficiency, little understanding of the U.S. legal system, limited access to legal representation, or difficulty meeting the complex requirements of a written application. An interview gives people a chance to explain what happened to them, clarify their applications, and make sure their stories are heard by the person evaluating their request for protection.

The administration published the interim final rule on July 28, 2026. The rule eliminates the previous guarantee that certain affirmative asylum applicants will receive an asylum interview and allows U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to refer their cases directly to immigration court without one. Under the new process, hundreds of thousands of current and future asylum seekers could be referred straight into deportation proceedings without ever being able to state their case. It is a way to fast-track vulnerable people through a process increasingly designed to deport them.

HIAS is proud to be a plaintiff in the lawsuit, filed by the National Immigrant Justice Center, Human Rights First, the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, alongside Immigration Equality, Oasis Legal Services, and Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, challenging the rule and its impact on asylum seekers’ due process rights.

For more than 140 years, HIAS has witnessed both the devastating consequences of turning people away and the life-saving power of welcome. Today, HIAS provides services to refugees, asylum seekers, and other forcibly displaced and stateless people around the world and advocates for their fundamental rights. HIAS’ legal and pro-bono teams provide legal assistance to thousands of people annually, and we are suing now because our ability to do that could be gravely affected by this rule change.

This lawsuit is one of multiple legal challenges that HIAS has filed against the Trump administration’s attacks on refugees and asylum seekers. We will continue to fight for a system in which people fleeing persecution have a meaningful opportunity to seek safety, tell their stories, and be treated with dignity.

For press inquiries, contact media@hias.org

text:
A protest camp in the small border town of Lochiel, Arizona, is seeking to stop federal contractors from building another portion of President Trump’s border barrier with Mexico. At the center of the protest camp is a 200-year-old cottonwood known as a “grandmother” tree, with activists sitting in the tree to physically stop its destruction.

“People are successfully forcing the government to stop, to slow down, or at least change course on border wall construction,” says journalist John Washington, a staff writer for the queer news outlet Lookout and author of multiple books about immigration. “They’ve been very clear that this is both an environmental and a political fight.”

TRANSCRIPT

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We go now to southern Arizona, where protests against another section of border wall construction are ongoing. A protest camp, predominantly led by queer and fem activists in the small town of Lochiel, is seeking to protect ancient cottonwood trees from demolition by federal contractors. At the center of the protest camp is a 200-year-old cottonwood known as a “grandmother” tree. Democracy Now! spoke with one of the activists last evening. This is Refugio.

REFUGIO: We are here protecting a 200-year-old grandmother cottonwood tree. They are sacred to the Tohono O’odham and Yaqui people, who are some of the original stewards of this land. The San Rafael Valley, where these cottonwood trees sit, is one of the most beautiful, most important places for migration of animals, wildlife. It’s one of the freest places, I think, in my heart, that exists still along these borderlands. …

There is a binational tree-sit happening. We have folks on the other side of what has not been constructed yet. They’re on the — they’re on the México side, La Noria side. And right now we have this zone, this stretch where the wall has not appeared, has not been constructed, and it’s because we’ve been halting it by being here.

We are being surveilled by private security, which ironically is called VisionQuest. We are being surveilled by Border Patrol. We are being surveilled by the Army. They’re the 101st post. And we’re being surveilled by the sheriff’s office, the Santa Cruz Sheriff’s Office.

AMY GOODMAN: Shortly after Refugio spoke to Democracy Now!, another activist, as well as Refugio, were temporarily detained by Mexican state police. In a statement released afterwards, the protesters said they had seen the tree-sit on the Mexican side of the border, quote, “attacked by Mexican state police” and that they had mobilized to support their Mexican comrades. They were released without arrest.

For more, we go to Tucson, Arizona, where we’re joined by John Washington, journalist, staff writer for Lookout. Washington is the author of a number of books, his latest, How to Close a Camp: Dispatches from the Fight Against Immigrant Detention.

John, if you can talk about the significance of this tree-sit, as we move from Big Bend in Texas, like 600 miles away, to grandmother, to this tree, what people are so concerned about on the border?

JOHN WASHINGTON: Good morning.

Yeah, I think what we’re seeing is that the story right now is becoming increasingly not where the Trump administration is building a border wall, but where people are successfully forcing the government to stop, to slow down, or at least change course on border wall construction.

So, the activists on the ground in Lochiel that we just heard from a moment ago, they’ve been very clear that this is both an environmental and a political fight. They remind people that the border wall is a tool that deliberately inflicts suffering and death, and they cite the government’s own policies in that claim through the 1994 policy of Prevention Through Deterrence.

Right now the Trump administration, in attempts to make the border wall and the border line more rigid, what we’re seeing, it’s becoming, because of the resistance, more binational, multinational and transborder. So, for now more than three weeks, someone has been up tree-sitting in this ancient cottonwood, what they’re calling a grandmother. And just last night, for the first time, just across the border in northern Sonora, a Mexican activist joined that person in a tree on the Mexican side. And they strung a rope briefly between the two trees, hanging from it a banner that says — that read, “From Minnesota to Mexico, resistance is fertile.” And they have been pushing back. And we see that there are now these connections between the Big Bend, between Lochiel, between further west in Arizona the fight to stop border wall construction on the Tohono O’odham Nation.

You know, right where the people are right now in Lochiel is just about a dozen miles from another huge standoff in 2022, where some of the same activists pushed back against the former Arizona Governor Doug Ducey’s border wall, constructing — constructed out of these old shipping containers, and they successfully pushed back. The state of Arizona was forced to remove those shipping containers, costing taxpayers here about $200 million. And, you know, historians and activists I talked to at the time, when I was covering that, told me that it was the first time since the fall of the Berlin Wall that a border wall, an international barrier, has actually been removed.

And right now this is what the activists are again pushing for. Another sign in Lochiel reads, “All walls fall.” And while that may seem like a hard thing to achieve at the moment, they, in response to the arrests, brief arrests last night, are calling for more people to come down and support these and other movements.

AMY GOODMAN: Do the Mexican police and the U.S. police, the Border Patrol — are they working together?

JOHN WASHINGTON: That is unclear. I think that we have certainly seen — that is unclear in this exact moment, but we have seen certainly many instances in the past in different parts of the border wall where they absolutely collaborate.

AMY GOODMAN: The Tohono O’odham Nation recently issued a no-trespassing order to block wall construction in its tribal land. Can you talk about the significance of this?

JOHN WASHINGTON: That’s right. So, they filed a lawsuit. So, they have always been opposed, or long been opposed, to the border wall that is being constructed on their ancestral homeland. Right now the government is trying to build, as in Lochiel, a double barrier, so two giant border walls, threatening both, you know, pristine, beautiful deserts, fragile ecosystems, archaeological sites, graveyards, etc. They filed a lawsuit to try to stop this.

Just last week, a federal judge ordered the — ruled that the construction can continue, saying that the Tohono O’odham Nation should defer to the federal government, which is a little bit galling, given the long history of incursions into ancestral homelands here. They have also posted — the Tohono O’odham have also posted, as you mentioned, no-trespassing signs on their land, and this is pretty explicitly targeting people who are going to be engaged in any sort of construction.

Right now one of the most threatened sites is the Quitobaquito Spring, which is this stunning oasis in the desert where a number of species live only right there. And so, right now people trying to protect this land understand that there’s, you know, the Sonoran — the mudfish, the — sorry, the pupfish, the Quitobaquito spring snail, that these things, if the border wall construction continues, may be wiped off the face of this Earth. So, this is a —

AMY GOODMAN: I just —

JOHN WASHINGTON: — very high-stakes fight.

AMY GOODMAN: I just have one last question. We have 30 seconds. You’ve documented the Prevention Through Deterrence strategy implemented in the ’90s that funnel migrants deliberately into deadly corridors. How does the Lochiel border project fit into that historical pattern of lethal border enforcement?

JOHN WASHINGTON: Well, at this point, there’s very few areas in Arizona that are not walled off. But it is an ongoing attempt to further punish and inflict suffering and death on migrants, absolutely. However, like in Big Bend, very, very few people cross in this corridor. I mean, people, I think, are right to point out that this very much smells of a boondoggle, that no one is crossing here, and yet they are spending maybe a half a billion dollars on just this about 27-mile segment of wall to devastate the local ecosystem.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, John Washington, I want to thank you so much for being with us, staff writer for Lookout, Washington speaking to us from Arizona, author of the new book How to Close a Camp: Dispatches from the Fight Against Immigrant Detention.

That does it for our show. I’ll be in Middlebury, Vermont, on August 28th to speak at the Q&A after the screening of the film about Democracy Now!, Steal This Story, Please! I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks for joining us.

text:
Maine law enforcement leaders say their departments are following a new law that limits coordination with federal immigration agencies, but some are concerned the restrictions go too far.

The law, which took effect July 29, restricts Maine’s police and sheriff’s deputies from inquiring about a person’s immigration status, or sharing their personal information with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or U.S. Customs and Border Protection, unless it’s for an investigation into a state or federal criminal matter, like human trafficking or terrorism. At jails, staff are not allowed to honor hold requests from ICE if they’re only for civil detention purposes.

Multiple law enforcement officials raised concerns about the law, saying it cuts them off from members of the Department of Homeland Security who they’ve relied on for translation services and information that doesn’t show up in a criminal background check, such as details about when a person crossed the border or any known history abroad. Immigrants’ rights advocates have argued the new restrictions are a way to prevent local resources from being misused and say the law, which includes exceptions for when police can interact with the federal agencies, is reasonable.

“It’s always better to have open lines of communication with other agencies,” said Androscoggin County Sheriff Eric Samson. “Sometimes collaborative issues fall by the wayside because you can’t do that.”

The American Civil Liberties Union of Maine sent letters on July 30 to more than 100 Maine police departments, all 16 sheriff’s offices and various state agencies, explaining what the new laws require, prohibit and still allow.

“People are free to have their own opinions on the law — the important thing is that the law is followed,” said Anahita Sotoohi, an attorney for the ACLU of Maine, which was involved in introducing the legislation and its passage.

The restrictions come as federal immigration enforcement has ramped up across the country. On July 13, roughly two weeks before the law took effect, an ICE agent shot and killed a 25-year-old father in Biddeford. ICE has said it was “conducting targeted surveillance” on the address of a person with a final order of removal.

A lawyer for the family of the man who was killed, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, said there was never such an order against him. Sen. Angus King told reporters that DHS confirmed Durán Guerrero was never the agents’ intended target.

ICE also carried out a statewide, week-long enforcement operation in January that resulted in roughly 200 immigration arrests. A majority of those detained had no criminal history, according to a review of ICE data, and many were later ordered released by U.S. District Court judges who deemed the detentions unconstitutional. Maine is one of several states that have enacted laws limiting cooperation with ICE, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

Advertisement

“The reason why these states are coming up with these laws is because the administration is letting these ICE agents do whatever they want, however they want,” said Sharon Gandarilla-Javier, an assistant professor of police science at John Jay College of Criminal Justice.

Some in Maine law enforcement have taken issue with ICE’s recent practices. Cumberland County Sheriff Kevin Joyce said earlier this month that he’s noticed the agency is less transparent and it’s detaining immigrants who aren’t a public safety risk.

Joyce said he also has concerns with the new law, which he believes takes away discretion from local police.

“Law enforcement has a lot of discretion,” Joyce said. “When you get laws that take away discretion, there are going to be bad outcomes. And I think we’re going to, at some point, see a bad outcome that was not thought of.”

HOW AGENCIES PREPARED

Weeks into the new restrictions, Samson said he’s already seen consequences. He said this includes the case of a man from Auburn, who has been accused of sexually assaulting a woman and bailed out of the Androscoggin County Jail, despite a request from ICE to hold him there.

“It would be a good public safety practice to notify immigration if somebody they have interest in was due to be released and they were a danger to society, so they can act on that,” Samson said. “We can’t do that anymore.”

Some agencies began following the new restrictions months before they took effect and some consulted lawyers, including those with the Maine Sheriffs’ Association.

Advertisement

Several municipal governments have enacted broader ordinances that prohibit staff, including local police, from sharing residents’ data with ICE. That includes Portland, Lewiston and Waterville.

Maine State Police announced it would follow the law in December. A spokesperson said last month the agency has had no issues so far.

The Sanford Police Department said its staff attended three trainings about the new law, including one held by state police and the other by Dirigo Safety, an independent consultant for police work. Brunswick police Chief Scott Stewart, who is also president of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association, said his department enacted the rule in March to prepare staff.

Stewart said he sent a memo and a copy of the law to officers and told them to “familiarize yourself with the restrictions associated with it.”

He said the law has required his officers to take extra steps where they would have contacted immigration authorities — like using a translation service rather than calling a Border Patrol agent.

In Fort Fairfield, Police Chief Matthew Cummings said the law hasn’t changed much in his community, where Border Patrol agents have traditionally filled in when there’s only one local police officer on duty.

Advertisement

The Maine Criminal Justice Academy said it has certified 400 federal officers to enforce Maine laws. A list of those officers and their roles was not available Wednesday. The new law doesn’t impact those federal officers, who are allowed on a limited basis to enforce state law.

Cummings said Border Patrol agents have helped direct traffic at accidents and fires, respond to domestic disturbances and offering back-up at traffic stops.

“Many times, they are the first on scene,” he said.

He said his officers have already begun using a professional translation service over the phone, instead of relying on Border Patrol agents to help.

“We will obviously comply with every portion of state law,” Cummings said.

EXCEPTIONS IN THE LAW

The law includes exceptions for local police who work on task forces with federal agents, as long as the primary focus is not on immigration enforcement.

Advertisement

Emmylou Manwill, a professor for the Immigrants’ Rights and Human Trafficking Program at Boston University School of Law, said that the flowing of information between local police and federal investigators is essential when dealing with trafficking operations.

“Historically, it was best practice to have local law enforcement working alongside those federal agencies,” Manwill said. “But I think now we’re in a reality where the local immigrant community trust has really eroded, and now people are very suspect of anybody who’s working with federal officers.”

Under President Donald Trump, the division of DHS that typically investigates transnational crime, like terrorism and human trafficking — known as Homeland Security Investigation — has been diverted to conduct more civil immigration arrests. As a result, it’s been harder for immigrants who have been trafficked to report what happened to them.

Manwill said laws like Maine’s, and the similar “PROTECT Act” in Massachusetts, will help restore some trust in local law enforcement.

“The last thing we want to happen is, you know, us helping a client report to law enforcement and our client ending up in removal proceedings or ICE detention,” Manwill said.

Sotoohi, from the ACLU of Maine, said that she hopes agencies will view the organization as a resource if they need help understanding their new obligations under the law, which she described as complicated. So far, she said, the ACLU has mostly received brief responses, thanking them for the letters and how they explain the new laws.

The ACLU also sent letters to state-run healthcare sites, libraries and schools that are affected by other recently enacted laws, prohibiting the sharing of Mainers’ data with ICE.

Sotoohi said there “have been positive trends” even before the new restrictions took effect.

“Our motivation with these letters,” she said, “is our belief that these new laws have made strides in protecting people in Maine, and making sure our state and local resources stay in our communities.”

title: Ceuta: Madrid to transfer 500 vulnerable youths to mainland - DW.com
description:
Spanish immigration and youth services officials have come up with a plan to transfer roughly 500 particularly vulnerable unaccompanied youths from the North African Spanish exclave of Ceuta to mainland Spain.
Migration Minister Saiz emphasized the fact that the "overriding welfare of the children" must be protected at all cost.
UNICEF Spain's Lara Contreras said the approach would see Ceuta retain legal guardianship of the girls until they were transferred to child protection organizations "willing to take them in" on the Spanish mainland.
Contreras says it is "urgent" that authorities properly identify unaccompanied children and denounced the fact that "hundreds of them are wandering the streets alone, in unsanitary conditions."
Though most migrants have since returned to Morocco, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska recently said that around 5,000 remain in Ceuta.

Spanish immigration and youth services officials have come up with a plan to transfer roughly 500 particularly vulnerable unaccompanied youths from the North African Spanish exclave of Ceuta to mainland Spain.

Spain's Ministry of Youth and Children says the plan has a mechanism that will allow "child protection organizations to take in and care for the most vulnerable individuals — including girls — in adapted facilities on the mainland, without the need to transfer custody to [regional authorities]."

Spain's EFE news agency quoted government officials saying that a royal decree would establish "the binding and solidarity-based reception of minors by all regions."

Contreras said that 97 of the 500 girls selected — aged 9 to 17 — have already been moved to improved facilities and will be transferred as soon as possible.

Contreras says it is "urgent" that authorities properly identify unaccompanied children and denounced the fact that "hundreds of them are wandering the streets alone, in unsanitary conditions."

What is the situation in Ceuta?

The children are among the roughly 80,000 individuals who crossed into Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 in hopes of starting a better life in Europe.

Though most migrants have since returned to Morocco, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska recently said that around 5,000 remain in Ceuta.

Spain's national police have reportedly identified 2,168 unaccompanied minors living on the streets since the border crossing and handed them over to local authorities on July 30.

text:
Washington, D.C.— Today, immigration legal service providers and advocacy organizations filed a federal lawsuit challenging a new interim final rule that allows U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to send people seeking asylum directly to immigration court without first assessing their legal claims in an affirmative asylum interview.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC), the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS), and Human Rights First on behalf of Immigration Equality, Oasis Legal Services, HIAS, and the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project. The organizational plaintiffs represent thousands of people with affirmative asylum applications pending before USCIS.

The new rule allows asylum officers to refer cases to immigration court for deportation proceedings, based only on their written application, without ever speaking to the asylum seeker about the persecution they fled. The rule took effect July 28, 2026 and applies to new and pending applications.

For decades, the affirmative asylum process has given people an opportunity to explain their asylum claims and answer questions in a non-adversarial interview with a trained asylum officer. The asylum officer has then decided whether to grant the application or refer it to immigration court, where the applicant must defend themself against deportation. The new rule allows USCIS to eliminate the interview entirely.

This rule further restricts access to asylum in the United States and is a massive and unlawful departure from established procedures that many asylum seekers had relied on when they filed their applications. It was published without advance notice or a meaningful opportunity for public comment.

The government estimates that up to 31 percent of the more than 1.4 million cases in the affirmative asylum system may be impacted by this rule. The consequences will be severe for people who have survived violence and trauma, many of whom have been waiting years for an interview. Sending them directly to deportation proceedings will increase the case backlog in the already overburdened immigration court system, where the Trump administration has made it clear immigration judges should deny even the strongest asylum applications before the applicants can submit evidence. As a result of this rule, many more people will be detained and ordered deported to places they fear persecution and torture without the opportunity to have their evidence considered by a neutral decisionmaker.

The lawsuit asks the court to declare the interim final rule procedurally invalid and vacate the rule in its entirety.

Co-counsel and organizational plaintiffs in the case provided the following statements:

"With this rule, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) continues to erode asylum seekers' rights," said Mary Georgevich, senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “This rule eliminates the right to an interview, which is a critical part of the asylum application process for millions of people. Instead, based on incomplete information, DHS will refer cases to immigration court, increasing the likelihood that eligible refugees will be denied asylum and deported to persecution or torture.”

“This rule is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to accelerate deportations at the expense of due process,” said Melissa Crow, director of litigation at the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies (CGRS). “After adopting numerous measures to stack the deck against people in deportation proceedings, they now seek to funnel more asylum cases into our broken immigration court system. At every step, their goal is to deprive people seeking protection of the opportunity to tell their stories and have their claims adjudicated fairly. In cases with life-or-death stakes, the consequences will be devastating.”

“This Interim Final Rule is part of a multi-layered attack on the U.S. asylum system. The Asylum Office was established as an institution in the early 1990’s to provide asylum seekers coming forward of their own volition to request protection with the opportunity to have their cases adjudicated in a non-adversarial setting by officers with specialized training in the field,” said Anwen Hughes, senior director of legal strategy, refugee programs, at Human Rights First (HRF). “Many people, including children, survivors of torture and trauma and of various forms of gender-based harm, speakers of rare languages, and people with cognitive challenges, among many others, have applied with the expectation that they will be able to explain their experiences and fears of persecution in an interview to an officer whose only job is to elicit and understand the relevant facts. Now, this rule would allow asylum officers to forward broad categories of cases into removal proceedings without interview. Before the immigration courts, as those are currently operating, many of these people may never get a hearing at all. This rule must be invalidated and the right to seek asylum in a fair process must be protected.”

“An asylum application can tell the government what happened to a survivor, but an interview helps the government understand the context, meaning, and severity of what happened. It is a safeguard against cultural misunderstandings, assumptions, and bias that can distort the written record. We do not all read the same words and reach the same understanding; why would we expect a written application to capture an entire human story? Meaningful protection requires us to listen before we judge. We have the means to process asylum claims without sacrificing lives for expediency,” said Adam Ryan Chang, executive director of Oasis Legal Services.

“Every asylum seeker who chooses to come forward and ask for safety in the United States is entitled by law to a full and fair interview at the asylum office. This is an essential right for LGBTQ people fleeing persecution,” said Aaron C. Morris, executive director of Immigration Equality. “This rule attempts to take that critical opportunity away and undermines the due process that asylum seekers are entitled to. The rule is illegal and must be struck down.”

"U.S. law gives every individual who is seeking safety the right to tell their story and explain the dangers they faced in their home countries and why it would be unsafe for them to return,” said Beth Oppenheim, president & CEO of HIAS. “The asylum interview is at times the only way ordinary people fleeing persecution have to be heard - to feel that their stories matter. But this rule will deny many people their voice and their due process, and the result will be devastating. People fleeing violence and persecution must be able to find safety, and this country must be able to treat them with respect, compassion, and dignity."

"This rule is the latest in a series of attacks by this administration on the rights of people seeking protection in the United States, including children,” said Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project. “By eliminating the right to an asylum interview, this rule needlessly forces potentially hundreds of thousands of people into the overburdened, broken immigration court system, subjecting survivors of trauma, including children, to re-traumatizing proceedings, instead of allowing them to share their experience with a trained asylum officer in a less adversarial setting. This rule puts child survivors of trauma at increased risk of immigration detention and deportation back to the very conditions of danger that they fled. The stakes for immigrant children and all asylum seekers could literally be life or death."
